en: [First Chapter] Having approached Manu as he sat with a concentrated mind, the great seers honored him according to custom and spoke these words: 1.1.
O Blessed One, you ought to explain to us the dharmas of all castes, as they truly are and in their proper sequence, as well as those born of mixed origins.
For you alone, O Lord, are the knower of the true meaning and purpose of the effects of this entire self-existent ordinance, which is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Thus questioned by those great-souled ones, Amitaujas, having duly honored all those great seers, replied: "Listen. (1.4)
In the beginning, this was enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks, beyond the reach of logic, unknowable, as if entirely asleep. (1.5)
Then the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, the Unmanifest, who dispels darkness and whose power is manifested through the great elements and so forth, appeared, making this world manifest. 1.6.
He who is beyond the senses, ungraspable, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, composed of all beings, and inconceivable—he himself has appeared. 1.7.
Desiring to emit various kinds of creatures from his own body, he first created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed. (1.8)
That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun;
within it was born Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds.
The waters are called *nārāḥ*, for the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara;
since they were his primordial abode (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa. ||1.10||
That cause which is unmanifest, eternal, and composed of both the existent and the non-existent—the Puruṣa who was emitted from that is celebrated in the world as Brahman. ||1.11||
Having dwelt within that egg for a full year, the Blessed One,
by his own meditative power, split that egg into two.
From those two fragments, he fashioned heaven and earth;
in between, the sky, the eight directions, and the eternal abode of the waters.
And from himself he drew forth the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
and from the mind, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the self-conscious lord.
And [he perceives] the Great Self itself, all the three qualities (guṇas), and the five sense organs which gradually become the perceivers of objects. 1.15.
But having arranged the subtle constituent parts of those six beings of immeasurable power within the portions of his own self, he created all living beings.
The six subtle components of form resort to this [body];
therefore, the wise call his form "the body" (śarīra). 1.17.
Then the great elements, together with their functions, and the mind with its subtle constituents, enter that imperishable creator of all beings. 1.18.
But from these seven immensely powerful beings,
the perishable arises from the imperishable through subtle material particles.
Each subsequent one among these acquires the quality of each preceding one;
whichever of them occupies which position in the sequence, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities. (1.20)
But he, at the beginning, fashioned the names and the individual actions of all beings, as well as their distinct conditions, from the words of the Veda alone. (1.21)
The Lord created the gods whose nature is action, as well as living beings;
he also created the subtle host of the Sādhyas and the eternal sacrifice.
From Agni, Vāyu, and Ravi, he milked forth the threefold eternal Brahman,
characterized as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, for the sake of the perfection of sacrifice.
Time and the divisions of time, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets; the rivers, the oceans, and the mountains; and the level and uneven terrains. ||1.24||
Desiring to create these progeny, he emitted this creation: austerity, speech, pleasure, desire, and anger. (1.25)
For the sake of distinguishing between karmas, he separated dharma and adharma;
and he joined these creatures with pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain. (1.26)
The minute, perishable particles that are said to belong to the five elements—
along with these, all this universe comes into being in successive order.
Whatever task the Lord first assigned him to perform, that very same task he himself undertook again and again as he was being created. (1.28)
Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood—
whatever he ordained for each at the time of creation, that very thing entered into it of its own accord.
Just as the seasons themselves, at the change of seasons, naturally assume their own respective characteristics, so too do embodied beings undergo their respective actions. 1.30.
For the sake of the prosperity of the worlds, he brought forth from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Having divided his own body into two parts, he became male with one half and female with the other; with her, the Lord created Virāj.
O best of the twice-born, know me to be that Virāj Puruṣa who, having performed austerities, created himself; I am the creator of all this.
Desiring to create progeny, I performed most difficult austerities and first created ten great seers, the lords of creatures.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada. (1.35)
These [Manus], possessing great splendor, created seven other Manus,
as well as the gods, the hosts of gods, and the great seers of immeasurable power.
[He saw] the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas; the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Asuras; the Nāgas along with the Suparṇas; and the various hosts of the Pitṛs.
Lightnings, thunderbolts, and clouds; red portents and Indra’s bow; meteors, atmospheric crashes, and comets; and various celestial lights, both high and low. (1.38)
Kinnaras, monkeys, fish, and various birds;
domestic animals, wild beasts, humans, and fanged predators. || 1.39 ||
Worms, insects, and moths; lice, flies, and bugs; all gadflies and mosquitoes; and various kinds of stationary beings. || 1.40 ||
Thus, by my command, all this— the world of the moving and the non-moving— was created by those great-souled ones through the application of their ascetic power, according to each being's karma.
I shall describe to you exactly what kind of karma is proclaimed for these beings here, as well as the sequence of their births.
Domestic animals, wild beasts, and carnivorous predators with two rows of teeth;
Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and humans—all these are born from the womb. (1.43)
Birds born from eggs, snakes, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises—whatever other such beings there are, whether terrestrial or aquatic. (1.44)
The gadfly, the mosquito, the louse, the fly, and the bug are born from moisture;
and whatever else is of this kind arises from heat. 1.45.
All trees are born from sprouts, growing from seeds or cuttings;
herbs are those that perish after the ripening of their fruit and are endowed with many flowers and fruits. (1.46)
Those that bear fruit without flowers are known as vanaspatis;
those that bear both flowers and fruit are known as vṛkṣas. ||1.47||
Furthermore, there are various kinds of shrubs and clusters, as well as species of grasses, those that grow from seeds or from stems, as well as spreading creepers and climbing vines. (1.48)
Enveloped by manifold darkness caused by karma, these beings possess internal consciousness and are endowed with pleasure and pain. 1.49
These destinies, beginning with that of Brahmā, are declared to end here within this terrible cycle of existence for living beings, which is constantly and perpetually moving.
Having thus created all this and me as well, he of inconceivable prowess again withdrew himself into his own self, subduing time with time.
When that god awakens, this world stirs;
when he sleeps, his soul at peace, then everything closes its eyes.
But when that [Self] sleeps in its own state of composure, the embodied beings whose nature is action desist from their respective activities, and the mind falls into exhaustion. (1.53)
But when they all dissolve simultaneously into that Great Self, then this Soul of all beings sleeps happily and at peace. (1.54)
But having resorted to this darkness, he remains for a long time endowed with the sense-faculties;
yet he does not perform his own action, and then he departs from the body. (1.55)
When, having become as minute as an atom, it enters in conjunction with the seed— both the stationary and the moving— it then casts off its form.
Thus, through waking and dreaming, that imperishable one incessantly brings to life and causes the destruction of all this world of moving and non-moving beings.
Having composed this treatise himself, he first caused me alone to receive it according to the prescribed rule; I, in turn, [taught] the sages beginning with Marīci.
This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety;
for this sage has learned all of this from me without exception.
Then, having been addressed in that manner by Manu, the great seer Bhṛgu, with a joyful soul, spoke to all those sages: "Listen! (1.60)
Of this Svāyaṃbhuva Manu, there were six other high-souled and greatly powerful descendants who created their own respective progeny. (1.61)
Svārociṣa, Auttami, Tāmasa, Raivata,
the highly resplendent Cākṣuṣa, and the son of Vivasvat as well.
These seven Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, possessed immense splendor;
each, within his own interval, produced and protected all this world of moving and non-moving beings.
Eighteen nimeṣas make one kāṣṭhā, thirty of those make one kalā,
thirty karas make one muhūrta, and a day and night consists of as many [muhūrtas].
The sun divides day and night for both humans and gods:
night is for the sleep of beings, and day is for the performance of actions.
For the ancestors, a month constitutes a day and a night; its division is by the two fortnights.
The dark fortnight is their day for active duties, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep. 1.66.
For the gods, a year constitutes day and night; their further division is as follows:
the northern course (udagayana) is their day, and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night. 1.67.
Now learn in brief the measure of a day and night of Brahmā, and the duration of each of the Yugas in their proper order. 1.68.
They say that four thousand years constitute the Kṛta Yuga;
its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts as many hundreds of years, and its twilight (saṃdhyāṃśa) is of the same duration.
In the other three [ages], together with their twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
This set of four ages, which has been enumerated at the very beginning,
consisting of twelve thousand years, is called a yuga of the gods.
A thousand divine yugas, by calculation, should be known as one day of Brahmā; his night is of exactly the same duration.
Those people who know day and night understand that the holy day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas, and his night is of exactly the same duration.
At the end of that day and night, having fallen asleep, he awakens;
and once awakened, he creates the mind, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent.
Impelled by the desire to create, the mind undergoes transformation and brings forth the creation;
from that, space is born, and they know sound to be its quality. (1.75)
From ether, undergoing transformation, there arises the pure and powerful wind, which carries all fragrances; it is indeed considered to have the quality of touch. (1.76)
From wind, as it undergoes transformation, there arises luminous light that dispels darkness; it is said to have brilliance as its quality. (1.77)
And from light, undergoing transformation, water arises, whose essence is the quality of taste;
from water, earth arises, whose quality is smell—such is the creation from the beginning.
That divine age (*yuga*) which was previously stated to consist of twelve thousand [years], multiplied by seventy-one, is here called a *manvantara*. (1.79)
Innumerable Manvantaras, as well as creation and dissolution, the Supreme Lord performs again and again, as if in play. (1.80)
In the Kṛta age, the Dharma was complete in its four quarters and truth alone prevailed;
no acquisition whatsoever occurred through unrighteousness among human beings.
In other [ages], dharma exists by virtue of tradition (āgama), but it is diminished quarter by quarter; through theft, falsehood, and deceit, dharma likewise departs quarter by quarter. (1.82)
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, achieve all their goals, and have a lifespan of four hundred years;
however, in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one-quarter at each stage.
The lifespan ordained for mortals in the Vedas, as well as the blessings resulting from ritual actions, bear fruit in the world according to the age, as do the powers of embodied beings. (1.84)
The duties of men in the Kṛta age are of one kind, those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages another,
and those in the Kali age yet another, according to the decline of the respective ages.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, knowledge is said to be so;
in the Dvāpara age, they say sacrifice alone is supreme; and in the Kali age, charity alone is supreme.
But for the sake of protecting this entire creation, that one of great luster assigned distinct duties to those born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet. (2.87)
He ordained for the Brāhmaṇas teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving gifts and receiving them. (1.88)
He prescribed for the Kṣatriya the protection of subjects, the giving of gifts, the performance of sacrifices, the study of the Vedas, and non-attachment to sensual objects. (1.89)
The protection of cattle, giving gifts, performing sacrifices, studying, trade, moneylending, and agriculture are the duties of a Vaiśya. (1.90)
But the Lord assigned only one duty for the Śūdra: to serve these very same classes without malice. (1.91)
It is proclaimed that man is purer above the navel;
therefore, his mouth has been declared by the Self-existent One to be the purest of all. (1.92)
Because he was born from the highest limb, because of his seniority, and because he upholds the Veda, the Brāhmaṇa is by right the lord of this entire creation. (1.93)

For the Self-Existent One, having performed austerities, first created him from his own mouth for the purpose of conveying the oblations to the gods and the ancestors, and for the protection of this entire world.
What being is greater than he, whose mouth the dwellers of heaven always consume as sacrificial offerings (havya), and the ancestors likewise as offerings to the manes (kavya)? 1.95.
Among beings, those with breath are the best; among those with breath, those who live by intelligence;
among the intelligent, men are the best; and among men, Brāhmaṇas are traditionally held to be the best.
Among Brahmins, there are the learned; among the learned, those whose intellects are refined;
among those of refined intellect, the performers of action; and among the performers, the exponents of Brahman.
The very birth of a Brahmin is the eternal embodiment of Dharma;
for he is born for the sake of Dharma and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
For when a Brāhmaṇa is born, he is indeed born preeminent upon the earth;
he is the lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
"Everything that exists in this world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;
by virtue of his preeminence and noble birth, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this. (1.100)
A Brahmin eats only his own, wears his own, and gives away his own;
it is through the Brahmin’s compassion that other people eat at all. (1.101)
For the purpose of discerning that [dharma] and for the sake of the remaining [topics], the wise Svāyambhuva Manu composed this treatise in due order. (1.102)
This must be studied with great care by a learned Brahmin and correctly expounded to his disciples; it is not to be taught by anyone else. 1.103
A Brahmin who studies this treatise and whose vows are well-praised is never defiled by the defects of action born of mind, speech, or body. (1.104)
He purifies his lineage, seven ancestors and seven descendants;
indeed, even he alone is worthy of this entire earth. (1.105)
This is the most excellent means of securing well-being; this increases the intellect;
this constantly brings renown; this is the supreme state of ultimate bliss. (1.106)
In this [work], the Dharma has been taught in its entirety, as well as the virtues and faults of actions, and the eternal conduct of all four castes. 1.107.
Conduct is the supreme dharma, as declared in the Śruti and the Smṛti;
therefore, a self-possessed twice-born man should always be constantly devoted to it. 1.108.
A Brahmin who has fallen away from right conduct does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas;
however, one who is endowed with right conduct is declared to be a partaker of the full fruit. 1.109
Having thus observed the course of Dharma through right conduct, the sages took up conduct as the supreme root of all austerity. 1.110
And [he taught] the origin of the world, the very procedure for the formative rites (saṃskāra),
the practice and observance of vows, and the supreme rule for ritual bathing.
The acquisition of a wife, the characteristics of marriages, the rules for the great sacrifices, and the eternal ritual for ancestral offerings (śrāddha). 1.112.
The characteristics of the various modes of livelihood, as well as the vows of a Snātaka, what may and may not be eaten, purity, and the purification of ritual substances. 1.113.
The application of the duties of women, asceticism, liberation, and renunciation;
as well as the entire duty of kings and the determination of legal cases.
The rules for questioning witnesses, the law concerning husband and wife, the law of partition, gambling, and the removal of thorns [criminals]. ||1.115||
Furthermore, [he taught] the conduct of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the origin of the mixed castes,
the duties for times of distress, and likewise the rules for expiation for the merchants.
The journey through saṃsāra, which arises from the threefold karma, as well as the supreme good resulting from actions and the examination of their merits and defects. ||1.117||
In this treatise, Manu has declared the eternal laws of regions, the laws of castes, the laws of families, and the laws of heretical sects and groups. (1.118)
Just as Manu formerly spoke this scripture when questioned by me, so now do you also learn it from me. 1.119
Thus ends the first chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[The Second Chapter] Learn that Dharma which is practiced by the wise and the virtuous, who are always free from hatred and passion, and which is approved by the heart. 2.1.
To have desire as one's sole motive is not praised, yet in this world there is no such thing as being entirely free from desire;
for the study of the Vedas and the performance of Vedic ritual action are themselves objects of desire.
Desire indeed has its root in volition; sacrifices are born of volition;
vows, restraints, and duties—all are traditionally held to be born of volition.
No action whatsoever is ever seen here in this world that is performed by one who is free from desire;
for whatever one does, all that is the movement of desire. (2.4)
Behaving rightly toward these, one goes to the world of the immortals;
and here, one enjoys all desires exactly as they were intended.
The Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it, as well as the practice of the virtuous and self-satisfaction. (2.6)
Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone, all that is declared in the Veda, for it consists of all knowledge. (2.7)
But having examined all this in its entirety with the eye of knowledge, the wise man should indeed abide in his own duty according to the authority of the Vedas. 2.8.
For a person who practices the dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti attains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. 2.9.
The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Smṛti is indeed the Dharmaśāstra.
These two are not to be questioned in any matter, for from them the Dharma shone forth.

Any twice-born man who, relying on the treatises of logic, would despise both of these [the Veda and the Smṛti], he is an atheist and a reviler of the Veda; he is to be excluded by the virtuous. (2.11)
The Veda, the Smṛti, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—they say that this fourfold set is the direct definition of Dharma. (2.12)
For those who are unattached to wealth and sensual pleasures, the knowledge of Dharma is prescribed;
for those desiring to know Dharma, the supreme authority is the Śruti. 2.13
But where there may be a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are recorded as Dharma;
for both of those are rightly declared to be Dharma by the wise. (2.14)
Whether the sun has risen, has not yet risen, or is at the juncture of day and night, the sacrifice proceeds in every way; such is the Vedic revelation.
He for whom the ritual procedure—from conception to the cremation ground—is prescribed by means of mantras, should be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever. (2.16)
The region between the two divine rivers, the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, that land created by the gods is called Brahmāvarta. (2.17)
Whatever conduct has come down through a line of tradition in that region for the social classes (varṇas) and the intermediate castes (antarālas), that is called right conduct (sadācāra). ||2.18||
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and Śūrasena—this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣi), which follows immediately after Brahmāvarta. 2.19.
From a Brahmin born in this region, all men on earth should learn their respective duties. (2.20)
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, to the east of Vinaśana and to the west of Prayāga, is celebrated as Madhyadeśa. (2.21)
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean, between those very two mountains, the wise know the land to be Āryāvarta. (2.22)
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as the land fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas. 2.23.
The twice-born should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
but a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any place whatsoever.
This origin of Dharma has been proclaimed to you in brief, as well as the source of all this; now learn the duties of the social classes.

For the twice-born, the purifying refinement of the body, beginning with the rite of impregnation (*niṣeka*), must be performed through meritorious Vedic rituals; it is sanctifying both in this world and after death. (2.26)

By means of domestic fire-sacrifices, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle, the taint derived from seed and the taint derived from the womb are wiped away for the twice-born. (2.27)

By the study of the Vedas, by vows, by burnt offerings, by the knowledge of the three Vedas, by sacrifices, by sons, and by the great sacrifices and other rites, this body is made fit for Brahman. (2.28)
The birth-rite (jātakarma) is prescribed for a male before the cutting of the umbilical cord;
it includes the ritual feeding of him with gold, honey, and clarified butter accompanied by sacred mantras.
One should perform the naming ceremony for him on the tenth or the twelfth day,
or on an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable moment, or under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities.
The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya, endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya, connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra, contemptible. (2.31)

The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end in a word meaning "shelter" (śarman); that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with a word meaning "protection" (rakṣā); that of a Vaiśya should be connected with a word meaning "prosperity" (puṣṭi); and that of a Śūdra should be connected with a word meaning "servant" (preṣya). ||2.32||
For women, [the name] should be easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, captivating, auspicious, ending in a long vowel, and containing words of benediction. (2.33)
In the fourth month, the child’s first exit from the house should be performed;
in the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food, or whatever auspicious rite is desired in the family.
The tonsure ceremony for all twice-born classes must be performed according to the law in either the first or the third year, as enjoined by the Veda. (2.35)
One should perform the initiation ceremony for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
for a Kṣatriya, in the eleventh year from conception; and for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception. (2.36)
The initiation of a Brahmin who desires spiritual luster should be performed in the fifth year;
that of a Kṣatriya seeking power in the sixth; and that of a Vaiśya desiring worldly prosperity in the eighth.
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth. (2.38)
Beyond this time, all three of these, having failed to perform the consecration at the proper time, become Vrātyas fallen from the Sāvitrī, despised by the Āryas. ||2.39||
A Brāhmaṇa must never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the prescribed rules. (2.40)
Students of the Veda should wear, in their respective order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat; as well as garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of Mūrvā fiber; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads. (2.42)
In the absence of muñja grass, however, they should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja;
they should have three strands and be tied with one, three, or five knots. (2.43)
The sacred thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upwards and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads. (2.44)
According to the law, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pīlu or Udumbara. (2.45)
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose. (2.46)
All of them should be straight, without blemishes, and pleasant to behold;
they should not cause alarm to men, possessing their bark intact and unscorched by fire. (2.47)
Having accepted his desired staff and having worshipped the sun,
he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
An initiated man of the highest twice-born class should go for alms using "bhavat" at the beginning;
a Kṣatriya, however, should use it in the middle; and a Vaiśya, "bhavat" at the end. (2.49)
He should first beg for alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt—whichever of these would not treat him with contempt. (2.50)
Having collected that alms-food according to his needs without guile, and having offered it to his teacher, he should eat while facing the east, pure and having sipped water. 2.51.
One who eats facing east gains long life; facing south, one gains fame;
facing west, one enjoys prosperity; and facing north, one enjoys truth. (2.52)
Having sipped water, a twice-born man should always eat his food with a concentrated mind;
having eaten, he should sip water properly and touch the cavities of his head with water.
One should always honor food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way. (2.54)
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten unhonored, it destroys both of these. (2.55)
One should not give the remains of one's food to anyone, nor should one eat between [meals];
one should not overeat, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from food.
Excessive eating leads to ill health, lack of longevity, and loss of strength; it is unwholesome and despised by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. ||2.57||
A Brahmin should always perform his ritual sipping (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma tīrtha;
he may use either the Kāya or the Traidaśika tīrtha, but never the Pitrya.
They declare that the Brāhma tīrtha is at the base of the thumb;
the Kāya is at the roots of the fingers, the Daiva at their tips, and the Pitrya is below those two.
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should also touch the cavities with water, as well as the self and the head. (2.60)
Desiring purity, one who knows the Dharma should always sip water that is neither hot nor frothy, using the proper part of the hand, in a secluded place, facing either the east or the north. (2.61)
A Brahmin is purified by water reaching the heart; a Kṣatriya, by water reaching the throat; a Vaiśya, by water that has been sipped; and a Śūdra, by water merely touched at the extremity. 2.62.
When the right hand is raised, the twice-born is called *upavītī*;
when the left is raised, he is *prācīnāvītī*; and when it hangs from the neck, he is *nivītī*. (2.63)
Having cast his girdle, deer-skin, staff, sacred thread, and water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others with the appropriate mantras. (2.64)
The tonsure ceremony (keśānta) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year;
for a member of the royal caste (rājanya), in the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya, two years after that. (2.65)
This entire cycle of rites for women must be performed without omission, for the sake of purifying the body at the proper time and in the proper order. (2.66)
The marriage rite is declared to be the Vedic sacrament for women;
their service to the husband is their residence with the teacher, and the tending of the sacred fires is their domestic duty. (2.67)
This has been declared as the sacred rite of initiation for the twice-born, which manifests their true birth; now learn the application of their duties. 2.68.
Having initiated his pupil, the teacher should first instruct him in purity, as well as in proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and the twilight devotions. (2.69)

But when about to be taught, having sipped water according to the scriptures and facing north, he should be instructed with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali*, wearing light garments, and with his senses subdued. (2.70)
At the beginning and at the end of the recitation of the Veda, one should always clasp the feet of the teacher;
having joined the palms together, one should study, for that is known as the *brahmāñjali*. (2.71)
The salutation of the teacher must be performed with crossed hands:
the left [foot] is to be touched with the left [hand], and the right [foot] with the right [hand]. (2.72)
But when about to study, always alert, he should say to his teacher, "Sir, please teach! and he should conclude the lesson by saying, "May there be a pause. (2.73)
One should always place the Praṇava at the beginning and at the end of the Veda;
that which is not preceded by Oṃ slips away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart. (2.74)
Sitting upon grass-blades pointing eastward, purified by means of purifiers,
and cleansed by three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he is then worthy of the syllable Om.
Prajāpati extracted from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. (2.76)
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out one quarter from each; that is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse. (2.77)
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, by muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda. (2.78)
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
One born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes who is deprived of this Ṛc and of his own timely ritual action incurs censure among the virtuous. (2.80)
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable Oṃ, together with the three-footed Sāvitrī, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. (2.81)
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness attains the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity; there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī verse; and truth excels silence. 2.83.
All Vedic acts of oblation and sacrifice flow away; but the Imperishable (akṣara) is to be known as the Imperishable, as Brahman, and as Prajāpati. 2.84.

The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (vidhiyajña); the whispered (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold. 2.85.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña). ||2.86||
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a true Brahmin. (2.87)
A wise man should exert effort in restraining the senses as they roam among alluring objects, just as a charioteer restrains his horses. 2.88
I shall correctly explain, in due order and as they truly are, those eleven faculties which the wise of old have taught. (2.89)
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth; the anus, the generative organ, the hands and feet, and speech is recorded as the tenth. (2.90)
Of these, the five sense organs are the ear and so forth in their respective order;
the five organs of action are said to be the anus and so forth. (2.91)
The eleventh, the mind (manas), should be known as being of a dual nature by virtue of its own quality;
when it is conquered, these two groups of five [the senses] become conquered. (2.92)
Through attachment to the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault; but by fully restraining them, one attains perfection. (2.93)
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. (2.94)
Between one who might attain all these [desires] and one who might renounce them entirely, the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment. (2.95)
These senses, corrupted by sense-objects, cannot be restrained so effectively by abstinence as they can by constant application of knowledge. (2.96)
The Vedas, renunciation, sacrifices, observances, and austerities never lead to success for one whose disposition is corrupted. 2.97
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
But if among all the senses even a single sense leaks away, through that his wisdom flows out, like water from the foot of a leather water-skin. (2.99)
Having brought the collection of senses under control and likewise restrained the mind, one should accomplish all goals through yoga, as if [protecting] the body with one's own eyes. (2.100)
One should stand reciting the Sāvitrī during the morning twilight until the sun appears; but one should sit properly during the evening twilight until the stars become visible. (2.101)
Chanting during the morning twilight while standing removes the sin committed at night;
sitting during the evening twilight, however, destroys the impurity created during the day. (2.102)
But he who does not stand at the former [time] and does not worship at the latter [time] should be excluded from all the duties of the twice-born, like a Śūdra. (2.103)
Restrained and established in the daily rite near water, he should go to the forest with a concentrated mind and recite even the Sāvitrī. (2.104)

Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding the study of the Vedas as an auxiliary science, nor in the daily private recitation, nor indeed in the mantras for the burnt-oblation (homa), even on days when study is otherwise forbidden. ||2.105||
In the daily obligatory recitation there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as a "Brahma-sacrifice";
it is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, even when marred by the occurrence of a day unfit for study. (2.106)
For him who, being self-restrained and pure, studies his sacred lesson for a year according to the prescribed rule, this [Veda] constantly yields milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey. (2.107)

A twice-born man who has undergone the initiation ceremony shall, until his formal return home, maintain the sacred fire, subsist on alms, sleep on the ground, and perform what is beneficial for his teacher. (2.108)

The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, trustworthy, capable, a provider of wealth, virtuous, and one's own kinsman—these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma. (2.109)
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;
for even though he knows, a wise man should behave among people like one who is dull-witted. (2.110)
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two dies, or incurs enmity. (2.111)
Where neither virtue nor wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve, there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil. (2.112)
A knower of Brahman should, if necessary, die together with his knowledge;
for even in the midst of terrible calamity, he must never sow it in barren soil.
Knowledge approached a Brahmin and said: "I am your treasure; guard me.
Do not give me to a scorner, so that I may remain most powerful. (2.114)
But speak to that Brahmin alone whom you know to be pure, self-restrained, and a celibate student—a guardian of the treasure who is free from negligence. (2.115)
He who acquires the Veda from one who is reciting it without permission becomes guilty of the theft of the Veda and falls into hell. (2.116)
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received. 2.117.

A Brahmin who is well-restrained, even if his essence consists only of the Sāvitrī, is better than one who is unrestrained, even if he knows the three Vedas, eats all things, and sells all things. (2.118)
One should not occupy a bed or seat already used by a superior;
rather, while remaining on one's own bed or seat, one should rise to meet him and salute him. (2.119)
For the vital breaths of a young man indeed depart when an elder approaches; he recovers them again by rising to meet him and by saluting him. 2.120.
For one who is habitually respectful and constantly serves the elders, four things increase correctly: lifespan, wisdom, fame, and strength. (2.121)
After the salutation, a Brahmin greeting an elder should announce his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name. (2.122)
To those who do not understand the meaning of his name, a wise man should say, "I am he," and he should do the same for all women. (2.123)
In a formal salutation, one should utter the word "bhoḥ" at the end of one's own name;
for the sages have declared that the nature of the word "bhoḥ" is the very essence of names. (2.124)
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one.
At the end of his name, the vowel 'a' should be pronounced with the preceding syllable protracted. (2.125)
That Brahmin who does not know how to return a greeting is not to be saluted by a learned man; he is exactly like a Śūdra. (2.126)
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, regarding his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, regarding his prosperity; and a Śūdra, regarding his health alone. (2.127)
One who knows the Dharma should address an initiated person by name only if he is younger; otherwise, he should address him using the honorifics "bhoḥ" or "bhavat" placed before his name. (2.128)
But toward a woman who is another's wife and not related by birth, he should address her as "Madam," or as "Fortunate Lady," or as "Sister. (2.129)
Upon rising, one should address maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers who are younger than oneself, saying, "It is I, [Name]. (2.130)
A maternal aunt, the wife of a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law, and a paternal aunt are to be honored like the wife of one's guru; they are equal to the wife of a guru. (2.131)
The wife of one’s brother, if she is of the same caste, may be saluted day after day;
however, the wives of paternal kinsmen and maternal relatives must be saluted only after one has returned from a journey abroad. (2.132)
Toward his father’s sister and his mother’s elder sister, he should maintain the same conduct as toward his mother; yet the mother is more venerable than they. (2.133)
Friendship with fellow citizens is established by ten years; that of those skilled in the arts, by five years;
and that of Vedic scholars, by three years—even by a shorter period in the case of those born of the same lineage. (2.134)
One should recognize a ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king as father and son; yet of these two, the Brahmin is the father. (2.135)
Wealth, kinship, age, action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding. (2.136)
Among the three castes, he who possesses the greatest number of excellent qualities is worthy of honor here, even if he be a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade. (2.137)
The way must be yielded to one who holds a wheel, to one who has reached his tenth decade, to the sick, to one carrying a burden, to a woman, to a *snātaka*, to a king, and to a bridegroom. (2.138)
But among those assembled together, the Snātaka and the king are to be honored.
Only the royal graduate and the [ordinary] graduate are entitled to receive honor from the king. (2.139)
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda together with the Kalpas and the Rahasyas, him they call an Ācārya. (2.140)
But he who teaches a portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas, for the sake of his livelihood, is called an Upādhyāya. (2.141)
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the student] with food, is called a guru. (2.142)

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, is called his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world. (2.143)
He who truly fills both ears with the Veda is to be known as mother and father; one should never bear him malice. (2.144)
Ten preceptors are equal to one teacher; a father is equal to a hundred teachers; but a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in terms of venerability. (2.145)
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for the Brahmin, both after death and in this world. (2.146)
One should understand that the birth of this person—which occurs when his mother and father produce him through their union—is merely his physical manifestation within the womb. (2.147)
But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule with the Sāvitrī—that is real, and it is free from old age and death. (2.148)
One should know that person as a teacher in this world by virtue of that service of learning, who benefits one with what has been heard, whether it be little or much. (2.149)
One who effects a Vedic birth and is an instructor of his own duty becomes, according to dharma, the father of an elder even if he is a mere child. (2.150)
The child Kavi, the descendant of Aṅgiras, taught his fathers;
having encompassed them with his knowledge, he said to them, "O little sons! (2.151)
Filled with indignation, they questioned the gods regarding that matter;
and the gods, having assembled, said to them, "The child has spoken what is right for you. (2.152)
The ignorant one is indeed a child, while the giver of sacred knowledge is the father;
for they call the ignorant one a "child" and the giver of sacred knowledge a "father. (2.153)
The seers did not establish dharma on the basis of years, nor grey hair, nor wealth, nor kinsmen; he who is learned in the Vedas—he is great to us. (2.154)
The seniority of Brahmins is by knowledge, that of Kṣatriyas by valor, that of Vaiśyas by grain and wealth, and that of Śūdras alone by birth. ||2.155||
One does not become an elder merely because his head is gray;
even if he is young, the gods recognize him as an elder who has studied the Vedas. 2.156
As is an elephant made of wood, as is a deer made of leather, so is a Brahmin who has not studied; these three merely bear the name. (2.157)

Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a cow is fruitless with another cow, and just as a gift given to an ignorant man is fruitless, so too is a Brahmin who knows not the Rigveda fruitless. ||2.158||
The instruction of living beings toward their highest good must be carried out through non-violence alone;
and one who desires dharma should employ speech that is sweet and gentle. (2.159)
He whose speech and mind are pure and always perfectly guarded indeed attains the entire fruit taught in the Vedānta.
One should not be a wounder of others even when afflicted; one should not have a mind intent on actions that harm others.
One should not utter that speech by which another is agitated, for such speech does not lead to the higher worlds.
A Brahmin should always tremble at honor as if at poison;
he should always long for dishonor as if for nectar. (2.162)
For he who is held in low esteem sleeps in comfort and wakes in comfort;
he moves about this world in comfort, while the scorner perishes. 2.163
By this sequential method, the twice-born man, having refined his self, should gradually accumulate the austerity conducive to the attainment of Brahman while dwelling with his guru.
The entire Veda, together with its secret portions (the Upanishads), must be acquired by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule. (2.165)
A twice-born man of the highest order, desiring to perform austerity, should always practice the Veda;
for the study of the Veda is said to be the supreme austerity for a Brahmin in this world. (2.166)
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even to his very fingertips who, though wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability. (2.167)
That twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits, quickly becomes a Śūdra even while still alive, along with his descendants. (2.168)

The first birth of a twice-born man is from his mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of muñja grass; the third is at the initiation for sacrifice, according to the injunction of the Śruti. (2.169)
In that regard, his birth as a Brahmin is marked by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
at that time, Sāvitrī is said to be his mother and the teacher his father. (2.170)
They call the teacher "father" because of his imparting of the Veda;
for no ritual duty whatsoever is enjoined upon him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass. (2.171)
One should not utter the Veda except when offering the svadhā libations;
for he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born to the Veda. (2.172)

For one who has undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the instruction in the observances (vratādeśana) is prescribed, as well as the formal acquisition of the Veda (brahmagrahaṇa), in due order according to the rules. (2.173)
Whatever skin, whatever sacred thread, and whatever girdle is prescribed for each, and whatever staff and whatever garment—each of these remains his even during his religious observances. (2.174)
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules, fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own austerity. (2.175)
Having bathed daily and become pure, he should perform the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the sacred fire. (2.176)
He should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, women, all fermented acids, and indeed the harming of living beings. (2.177)

Anointing the body, applying collyrium to the eyes, wearing shoes and carrying an umbrella, as well as desire, anger, greed, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments—(these he should avoid). 2.178.
Gambling, gossip about people, slander, as well as falsehood; gazing at and touching women, and the harming of others. (2.179)
One should always sleep alone and never spill one's semen;
for by spilling semen out of desire, one destroys one's own vow. ||2.180||
If a twice-born student practicing celibacy should involuntarily emit semen during sleep, he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with "punar mām. (2.181)
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass—as much as required—and he should go out for alms every day. (2.182)
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, who are praiseworthy in their own duties. 2.183.
One should not beg for alms in the family of one's guru, nor among the families of one's paternal or maternal kinsmen.
If houses from others are unavailable, however, one should avoid each preceding house in preference for the next. (2.184)

Or, if those previously mentioned are unavailable, he may wander through the entire village, restraining his speech and remaining self-controlled, while avoiding those who have been accused of crimes. 2.185.
Having fetched fuel-sticks from afar, he should place them in the open air;
and evening and morning, he should unwearyingly offer oblations into the fire with them. (2.186)
If one has not gone out for alms and has not kindled the sacred fire, being free from illness, one shall observe the Avakīrṇi-vow for seven nights. (2.187)
One who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and should not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the livelihood of a vow-holder sustained by alms is equal to fasting. (2.188)
At a rite for the gods, he may eat like one observing a vow; at a rite for the ancestors, he may eat like a seer (ṛṣi).
If requested, he may eat at his pleasure; his vow is not thereby violated. (2.189)
This duty has been taught by the wise as belonging solely to the Brāhmaṇa;
they do not declare this duty to belong to the Rājanya or the Vaiśya. (2.190)
Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged, he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher. (2.191)
Restraining his body, speech, organs of perception, and mind, he should stand with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of his teacher. (2.192)
He should always have his right hand raised, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the teacher.
In the presence of his teacher, he should always have inferior food, clothing, and attire;
he should rise before him and go to bed after him. (2.194)
One should not engage in conversation or respond to a greeting while lying down, nor while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor with one's face turned away. (2.195)

Standing, one should attend to one who is seated; approaching, one should attend to one who is standing; going forward to meet, one should attend to one who is coming toward oneself; and running after, one should attend to one who is running. (2.196)
Facing one who has turned his back, approaching the presence of one who is far away, bowing down before one who is lying down, and standing at the command of one who is seated. (2.197)
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat must always be low;
and within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases. (2.198)
One should not utter his name alone, even in his absence;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures. (2.199)
Wherever censure or even slander of the guru arises, one should cover one's ears or depart from that place to another. (2.200)
Through reviling one becomes a donkey; indeed, through censuring one becomes a dog; an enjoyer of others' goods becomes a worm, and an envious person becomes an insect. (2.201)

One should not salute him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of a woman; likewise, if one is seated in a vehicle or on a seat, one should descend before saluting him. 2.202.
One should not sit with one's teacher either to the windward or to the leeward;
nor should one say anything at all that cannot be heard by the teacher. (2.203)
He may sit together with his teacher on vehicles drawn by oxen, horses, or camels, on a palanquin, on a stone slab, on mats, or on a wooden plank or a boat. (2.204)
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
nor, unless permitted by his teacher, should one salute one's own teachers. (2.205)
This same constant conduct is due toward teachers of knowledge, toward one's own kinsmen, and toward those who forbid unrighteousness as well as those who impart what is beneficial. (2.206)
One should always behave toward those who are superior as one does toward the guru—toward the guru’s sons, toward venerable persons, and toward the guru’s own kinsmen. (2.207)
Whether he be of equal age, a child, or a pupil, the son of a teacher who teaches during a sacrificial rite deserves honor as the teacher himself. (2.208)
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing, the eating of leftovers, or the washing of the feet for the teacher’s son. (2.209)
The wives of the teacher who belong to the same caste (varṇa) should be honored like the teacher himself;
those of a different caste, however, should be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation. (2.210)
Anointing, bathing, massaging the limbs, and the dressing of the hair—these should not be performed for the wife of one's guru. (2.211)
But a young wife of the guru should not be saluted by touching her feet here by one who is twenty years of age and capable of discerning virtues and faults. (2.212)
This is the very nature of women: to corrupt men in this world.
Therefore, the wise do not become heedless on account of women. (2.213)
For in this world, women are capable of leading astray both the ignorant man and even the wise man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger. (2.214)
One should not sit in seclusion with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man. (2.215)
However, on this earth, a young man may at his pleasure perform the formal salutation to the wives of his gurus who are themselves young, saying, "I am so-and-so. (2.216)
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wife every day and offer salutations, remembering the dharma of the virtuous. (2.217)
Just as a man obtains water by digging with a spade, so does one who desires to listen obtain knowledge residing in the teacher. 2.218
Whether he be shaven-headed or wear matted locks, or have his hair tied in a topknot, the sun should never set or rise while he remains within a village. 2.219.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own will,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting prayers.
For he who goes to sleep after the sun has set, or wakes up when the sun has risen, and fails to perform the penance, becomes joined with great sin. (2.221)
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always, with a concentrated mind, attend to both twilights in a clean place, reciting the prayers to be recited according to the rule. (2.222)

If a woman, or even a person of lower birth, should perform any act that leads to spiritual welfare, one should practice all of that with diligence, provided that one's mind finds delight therein. (2.223)

Some say that the good consists of dharma and artha; others, of kāma and artha; or even that dharma alone is the good; or that artha alone is the good in this world—such is the established position regarding the three aims of life (trivarga). ||2.224||
The teacher, the father, the mother, and the elder brother must not be treated with disrespect, especially by a Brahmin, even if he is himself in distress. (2.225)
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati;
the mother is indeed the embodiment of the Earth; and one's own brother is the embodiment of oneself. 2.226
The suffering that parents endure for the birth of human beings cannot be repaid even in a hundred years. (2.227)
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times; for when these three are satisfied, all ascetic toil is fully accomplished. (2.228)
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity;
one should not practice any other duty without being authorized by them. (2.229)
For these indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three stages of life (āśramas);
these indeed are the three Vedas; and these are said to be the three sacred fires. ||2.230||
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher, however, is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable. (2.231)
By being heedful in these three, a householder shall conquer the three worlds;
shining with his own body, he rejoices in heaven like a god. (2.232)
Through devotion to one's mother one attains this world; through devotion to one's father, the middle world; but through service to the teacher alone, one reaches the world of Brahmā.
All duties are honored by him who honors these three;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless. (2.234)
As long as those three live, she shall not practice with another;
devoted to their pleasure and welfare, she should constantly perform service for them alone. (2.235)
Whatever one may do for the sake of the next world, provided it does not conflict with their interests, that very thing one should announce to them through thought, word, and deed. (2.236)
For a man's duty is completed within these three;
this is the supreme dharma directly perceived, while any other is called a secondary dharma. 2.237

One who possesses faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a person of low status; one should learn the highest dharma even from the lowest, and take a jewel of a woman even from a base family. (2.238)
Even from poison, one should take the nectar; even from a child, a well-spoken word;
even from an enemy, virtuous conduct; and even from filth, gold. (2.239)
Women, jewels, as well as knowledge, righteousness, purity, eloquent speech, and various arts—these are to be acquired from everywhere. (2.240)
In times of distress, study from one who is not a Brahmin is permitted;
however, he must follow after and serve that teacher for as long as the study lasts. (2.241)
A student desiring the unsurpassed goal should not dwell for life with a teacher who is not a Brahmin, nor with a Brahmin who has not mastered the Vedas. (2.242)
But if he should choose to dwell permanently in the family of his teacher,
he should attend upon him with diligence until the liberation of the body.
But that Brahmin who serves his teacher until the completion of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahmā. (2.244)
One who knows the Dharma should not provide any service to the teacher beforehand;
however, when about to perform the final bath, being commanded by the teacher, he should procure wealth for the teacher's sake according to his ability. 2.245.
He should bring pleasure to his teacher by offering a field, gold, a cow, a horse, or at least an umbrella and sandals; or grain, garments, or even vegetables. (2.246)

But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who is endowed with good qualities, or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, exactly as toward the teacher. (2.247)
When these are not available, one who is capable of standing, sitting, and moving about should perfect his own body by performing service to the sacred fire. 2.248
The Brahmin who conducts himself in this way, with his vow of celibacy unbroken, goes to the highest station and is not born here again. ||2.249||
Thus ends the second chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

[The Third Chapter] One should practice the vow pertaining to the three Vedas under a teacher for thirty-six years, or for half that time, or for a quarter, or even until they have been mastered. (3.1)
Having studied the Vedas— either all of them, two of them, or even one— in due order,
and having remained firm in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of the householder.
One should first honor with a cow that son who is renowned for his own duty, who inherits the father’s Brahmanic estate, and who is seated upon the couch wearing a garland.
Having been permitted by his teacher and having performed the ceremonial bath according to the rules upon returning home,
the twice-born man should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.

A woman who is not a sapinda of one's mother and not of the same gotra as one's father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage, provided she is not of a sexual nature [with the groom]. (3.5)
Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, wealth, and grain—one should avoid these ten families in forming a marriage alliance. (3.6)

Families that neglect their religious duties, those lacking male progeny, those devoid of Vedic study, those with hairy armpits or hemorrhoids, and families afflicted by consumption, chronic disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, or leprosy; 3.7.
One should not marry a girl who is tawny, nor one with an extra limb, nor one who is diseased;
nor one who is hairless, nor one with excessive body hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown.

One should not marry a girl whose name is that of a lunar mansion, a tree, or a river; nor one whose name is that of a low-caste person or a mountain; nor one whose name is that of a bird, a snake, or a servant; nor one whose name is terrifying.

One should marry a woman whose limbs are unimpaired, who has an auspicious name, who walks with the gait of a swan or an elephant, and whose body hair, hair, and teeth are fine, and whose limbs are soft. (3.10)
But a wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother, or whose father is unknown, for fear of the practice of *putrikā* (the sonless father making his daughter his heir). (3.11)
For the twice-born, a wife of the same caste is recommended for the rite of marriage;
however, for those who proceed out of desire, these following women shall be the preferred wives in their respective order. (3.12)

A Śūdra woman alone is prescribed as a wife for a Śūdra; she and one of his own caste (svā) are prescribed for a Vaiśya; those two and one of his own caste are for a Kṣatriya; and those three and one of his own caste are for a Brāhmaṇa. ||3.13||
For even in times of distress, while remaining steadfast, no instance whatsoever is recorded in which a Śūdra woman is prescribed as a wife for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya. (3.14)
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth, quickly reduce their own families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras. (3.15)
According to Atri and the son of Utathya, one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste];
according to Śaunaka, by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, by having offspring from her. (3.16)
By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he falls from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa. (3.17)
But for him whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are dominated by that [wealth], neither the ancestors nor the gods eat; he does not go to heaven. (3.18)
For one who has drunk the saliva of a *vṛṣalī*, for one who has been defiled by her breath, and for one who has procreated with her, no atonement is prescribed. (3.19)
Learn now, in brief, these eight forms of marriage for women, which are beneficial or harmful both in this world and after death for all four castes. (3.20)
The Brāhma, the Daiva, as well as the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, and the Āsura; the Gāndharva, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca, which is the eighth and lowest. ||3.21||
I shall declare to you all that which is the duty for each caste, as well as the virtues and faults pertaining to each, and the merits and demerits associated with procreation. (3.22)

One should know that for a Brahmin there are six [marriages] in order; for a Kṣatriya, four, excluding the last two; and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, those same [four], which are righteous and not demonic. (3.23)
The wise know that the first four [forms of marriage] are recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone for a Kṣatriya; and the Āsura for both Vaiśyas and Śūdras. (3.24)
Of these five, however, three are considered lawful and two unlawful here;
the Paiśāca and the Āsura forms should never be performed under any circumstances. (3.25)
Whether performed separately or mixed together, the two forms of marriage previously mentioned—the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa—are recorded as lawful for the Kṣatriya. (3.26)
Having clothed and honored her himself, and having invited a man endowed with learning and virtue, the giving away of a daughter is declared to be the Brāhma rite. (3.27)

When a sacrifice has been properly extended and the officiating priest performs his duty, the giving away of a daughter after she has been adorned is declared to be the divine (daiva) form of marriage. (3.28)
Having taken one or two pairs of cattle from the bridegroom according to the law, the giving away of the maiden in accordance with the rule is called the Ārṣa rite. (3.29)
Having addressed the words, "May you both perform dharma together," and having honored the gift of the maiden, this is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite. (3.30)
Having given wealth to the kinsmen and to the bride herself according to one's ability, the giving away of the daughter at one's own will is called the Āsura dharma. (3.31)
The mutual union of the maiden and the groom through desire is to be known as the Gāndharva rite; it arises from passion and has sexual intercourse as its purpose. (3.32)
The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home, while she cries out and weeps, after having slain, wounded, or broken down [her guardians], is called the Rākṣasa rite. (3.33)
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that is the most sinful of marriages, known as the eighth, the Paiśāca.
For the foremost of the twice-born, the gift of a daughter is praised as being performed with water alone; for the other castes, however, it is by mutual desire. (3.35)
O Brahmins, listen as I duly proclaim all those virtues which Manu has declared for each of these forms of marriage. (3.36)
The son of a Brāhmaṇa who has performed meritorious deeds delivers ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first from sin. (3.37)

A son born of a woman married according to the Daiva rite causes seven generations of ancestors and seven of descendants to be purified; a son born of a woman married according to the Ārṣa rite purifies three ancestors and three descendants; and a son born of a woman married according to the Kāya (Gāndharva) rite purifies six ancestors and six descendants.
In the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma, sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born in due order. (3.39)
Endowed with beauty, strength, and virtue, wealthy and renowned, possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years. (3.40)
But from the remaining improper marriages, sons who are cruel, speakers of falsehood, and haters of the Veda and dharma are born. (3.41)

Through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they become objects of reproach for men. Therefore, one should avoid those that are blameworthy. (3.42)
The sacramental rite of taking the hand is prescribed for women of the same caste; this following rule is to be known regarding the marriage ceremony for women of different castes. (3.43)
An arrow should be grasped by a Kṣatriya woman, a goad by a Vaiśya maiden, and the hem of a garment by a Śūdra woman when marrying a man of higher caste. (3.44)

He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may approach her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days. 3.45.
The natural menstrual period of women is said to consist of sixteen nights, together with four other days that are forbidden. (3.46)
Of these, the first four, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth nights, are censured; the remaining ten nights are recommended. (3.47)
Sons are born from women on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one desiring a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night. (3.48)

A male is born when the semen is in excess; a female when the female element is in excess. When they are equal, a neuter is born, or sometimes both a male and a female. When they are diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs.
A man should avoid women on the eight censured nights and the other [inauspicious] nights;
he remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) regardless of which stage of life (āśrama) he dwells in. (3.50)
A wise father shall not accept even the slightest bride-price for his daughter;
for by accepting a price out of greed, a man becomes a seller of his offspring. (3.51)
But those kinsmen who, out of delusion, live off the property of women—whether it be their vehicles or their clothing—are sinners who go to a downward state. (3.52)
Regarding the rite of the Ṛṣis, some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price; but that is surely false.
Whether it be small or even great, it remains nothing other than a sale. (3.53)
When the kinsmen do not take a bride-price for them, that is not a sale;
it is merely a token of honor for the maidens and an act of pure compassion. (3.54)
These women must be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire abundant welfare for them. (3.55)
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, there all ritual acts are fruitless. (3.56)
Where the female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes; but where they do not grieve, that family indeed prospers forever. (3.57)
Those houses which female relatives, when not honored, curse, perish on all sides as if struck by a magical spell (kṛtyā). ||3.58||
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should always worship these [goddesses] with ornaments, clothing, and food, both at regular ceremonies and during festivals. (3.59)
In that family where the husband is content with his wife and the wife likewise with her husband, prosperity is indeed certain and constant.
For if a woman does not find pleasure, she will not delight the man; and from a lack of mutual delight, procreation does not proceed. (3.61)
When a woman is pleasing, the entire family is pleased;
but when she is displeasing, nothing at all is pleasing. (3.62)
Families quickly perish through ill-arranged marriages, the omission of sacred rites, the failure to study the Vedas, and by showing disrespect toward Brahmins. (3.63)
By means of crafts, commerce, and solely through the offspring of Śūdra women;
by means of cattle, horses, vehicles, agriculture, and service to the king. (3.64)

By officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, by atheism regarding ritual acts, and by being deficient in sacred mantras, families fall from their noble status to that of commoners. (3.65)
But those families that are enriched by the power of mantras, even if they possess little wealth, are reckoned among the noble lineages and draw great renown to themselves. (3.66)
In the marriage fire, the householder should perform the domestic rites according to the rules,
as well as the performance of the five great sacrifices and the daily cooking of food.
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; by using these, he is bound [by sin]. (3.68)
For the sake of expiating all of these in their proper order, the great seers ordained five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day. (3.69)

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation of water is the sacrifice to the ancestors; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali offering is the sacrifice to the spirits; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men. (3.70)
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability, even while constantly living at home, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse. (3.71)
He who does not offer sustenance to these five—the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself—does not truly live, even though he breathes. (3.72)
The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the likewise well-offered sacrifice (prahuta),
the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmya-huta), and the consumed sacrifice (prāśita)— these are declared to be the five sacrifices.

Recitation is the *huta* offering; the fire sacrifice is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits is the *prahuta*; the oblation to the elemental beings is the *bhautika-bali*; worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmya-huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*. (3.74)

One should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Vedas and in rites directed toward the gods; for it is by being engaged in rites directed toward the gods that one sustains this world of moving and unmoving beings. (3.75)
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. (3.76)
Just as all living beings depend upon the wind to live, so do the other stages of life depend upon the householder. 3.77
Since members of all three other stages of life are daily supported by householders alone with both knowledge and food, therefore the householder’s stage is the most excellent. (3.78)
It must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven, and by one who desires ultimate happiness here, for it is difficult to maintain when the senses are weak. (3.79)
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests—these expect [support] from householders; therefore, one who understands his duty should act toward them. (3.80)

One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas, the gods with burnt offerings according to the rule, the ancestors with śrāddha rites, men with food, and the elemental spirits with the bali offering. (3.81)
Day after day, he should offer the śrāddha with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors. (3.82)
One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of the ancestors during the fivefold sacrifice;
however, one should not feed any twice-born man specifically for the Vaiśvadeva rite.
A Brahmin should daily perform the oblation (homa) into the domestic fire for these deities from the prepared Vaiśvadeva food, according to the prescribed rule. (3.84)
First for Agni and for Soma, then for those two together, for the Viśvedevas, and for Dhanvantari; || 3.85 ||
And to Kuhū, to Anumati, and to Prajāpati;
together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and likewise finally to Sviṣṭakṛt. ||3.86||
Having thus properly offered the oblation, he should present the bali-offering in a clockwise direction toward all quarters to Indra, Antaka, Appati, and Indu, along with their followers.
One should offer at the door with the words "To the Maruts," and likewise in the water with "To the Waters";
one should offer upon the pestle and mortar with "To the Vanaspatis."
One should offer an oblation to Śrī at the head of the bed, to Bhadrakālī at the foot;
and one should present an offering to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the middle of the dwelling.
And one should cast an offering into the air for all the gods,
as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night.
One should offer the bali on the back part of the house for the prosperity of all food;
however, one should carry all the remainder of the bali to the south for the ancestors.
One should slowly place [the food] on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers (Cāṇḍālas), those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and worms. (3.92)
Thus, the Brahmin who constantly honors all beings goes by a straight path to the supreme abode, his very form consisting of light.
Having thus performed this rite of offerings, he should first feed his guest;
and he should give alms according to the rule to a mendicant and to a student of sacred knowledge.
Whatever merit one obtains by giving a cow according to the prescribed rule, that same merit a twice-born householder obtains by giving alms. 3.95
One should offer even alms or a vessel of water with respect and according to the prescribed rule to a Brahmin who knows the true meaning of the Vedas. (3.96)
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish when given out of delusion by donors to Brahmins who have become like ashes. (3.97)
An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, who are enriched by knowledge and austerity, delivers one from distress and even from great sin. (3.98)
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water, as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him with due ceremony and in accordance with the prescribed rule. (3.99)
Even for one who constantly gathers grains by gleaning or offers oblations into the five fires, a Brāhmaṇa who dwells unhonored takes away all his merit. (3.100)
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—these things are never lacking in the homes of the virtuous. (3.101)
A Brahmin staying for even a single night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest. (3.102)

One should recognize as a guest who has arrived at the house a Brahmin from another village, as well as a traveling companion, or even one where the sacred fires are maintained, including the wife. (3.103)
Those foolish householders who subsist on the food of others go, after death, to the state of cattle for those who provide them with that food. (3.104)
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by a householder;
