whether he arrives at the proper time or an improper time, he must not remain in the house without eating. (3.105)
One should certainly not eat oneself that food for which one causes a guest to eat;
honoring a guest brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven. (3.106)

One should provide a seat, lodging, a bed, attendance while walking behind, and respectful service; for those who are superior, one should perform these in a superior manner, for those who are inferior, in an inferior manner, and for those who are equal, in an equal manner. (3.107)

But when the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed, if another guest should arrive, one should give him food according to one's ability; one should not, however, perform the Bali offering [for that guest]. (3.108)
A Brahmin should not announce his own family and lineage for the sake of food;
for by proclaiming them for the sake of a meal, he is called by the wise a "vomit-eater. (3.109)
But for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya is said not to be a guest in his house;
nor are a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, kinsmen, or even a teacher [guests]. (3.110)
But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest, he may, if he so desires, feed him once the Brahmins have finished eating. (3.111)
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra also arrives at his household as a guest, he should feed them along with his servants, practicing compassion toward them. (3.112)
He should also, together with his wife, feed with affection his friends and others who have come to his house, providing them with food according to his means and their rank. (3.113)
One should feed these—married women, young maidens, the sick, and likewise pregnant women—immediately after the guests, without hesitation. (3.114)
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these, while eating, does not realize that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures. (3.115)
But when the Brahmins and his own servants have finished eating, the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains. (3.116)
Having honored the gods, the seers, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains. (3.117)
He who cooks for his own sake alone eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice. (3.118)
One should honor with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) a king, a sacrificial priest, a snātaka, a guru, a dear father-in-law, and a maternal uncle, again after a full year has passed.

When a sacrificial rite is about to take place, both a king and a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is the established rule that this does not apply when no sacrifice is being performed. (3.120)
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer a Bali oblation without mantras;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.
But having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should, at the waning of the moon, perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha monthly. (3.122)
The wise know the monthly Śrāddha for the ancestors as the Anvāhārya;
that should be performed with effort using commendable meat. (3.123)

In this regard, I shall describe in their entirety those who are to be fed and those who are to be avoided among the best of the twice-born, as well as how many there are and with what kinds of food. 3.124.
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large gathering.
Hospitality, the proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.
This rite for the deceased, known as the ancestral offering (pitrya), is celebrated at the waning of the moon;
for one engaged in that [meditation], the worldly rite for the deceased becomes constant. (3.127)
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy brahmin yields great fruit. (3.128)
One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors; one obtains abundant fruit thereby, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras. (3.129)
One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; he is a sacred ford for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*, and he is remembered as a guest. (3.130)
For where a thousand times a thousand who are ignorant of the Ṛgveda may eat, a single man who knows the mantras, being pleased, is worth all of them according to dharma. (3.131)
The offerings for the ancestors (kavya) and the sacrificial oblations (havis) should be given to one preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not cleansed by blood alone. (3.132)
As many morsels as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows at offerings to the gods and ancestors, so many glowing spikes, spears, and iron balls shall he swallow after death. (3.133)
Some twice-born ones are established in knowledge, others likewise in austerity; some are established in austerity and Vedic study, and others similarly in ritual action. (3.134)
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established among those devoted to knowledge;
however, offerings to the gods (havya) should be given according to the rule to all four [orders] alike. (3.135)
If one's father is not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya) but the son has mastered the Vedas (vedapāraga), or if the son is not learned in the Vedas but the father has mastered the Vedas; || 3.136 ||
One should know that he whose father is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) is superior, even if he lacks noble character;
however, the other deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras. (3.137)
One should not feed a friend at a śrāddha; rather, one should win him over with wealth.
One should feed at a śrāddha that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend. (3.138)
For him whose śrāddha rites and sacrificial oblations are dominated by friends, there is no fruit after death for those śrāddhas nor for those oblations. (3.139)
That lowest of the twice-born who, out of delusion, forms friendships through a funeral feast (śrāddha) falls from the heavenly worlds; he is a friend to the śrāddha, not to the gods. (3.140)
That sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which is given for a communal feast is declared by the twice-born to be of the Piśācas;
it remains right here in this world like a blind cow in a single house.
Just as a sower who has sown seed in barren soil does not obtain fruit, so too a donor who offers an oblation to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda does not obtain the fruit. 3.142.
It makes both the givers and the recipients partakers of the fruit;
a sacrificial fee given according to rule to a learned man [yields reward] both in this world and after death. (3.143)
At a śrāddha ceremony, one may certainly honor a friend even if he is not highly distinguished, but never an enemy;
for an oblation consumed by an enemy becomes fruitless after death. (3.144)
One should diligently feed at the śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda, or an Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his branch, or a Chandoga who has completed his study. (3.145)
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at his *śrāddha*, the satisfaction of his ancestors shall be eternal, extending through seven generations. (3.146)
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of oblations to the gods and the ancestors;
however, this secondary rule should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a kinsman, as well as the officiating priest and the person for whom one performs a sacrifice.
One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods;
however, when a rite dedicated to the ancestors is at hand, he should examine him with great care. (3.149)
Those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and those who follow the lifestyle of atheists—Manu has declared these Brahmins to be unworthy of offerings to the gods and the ancestors. (3.150)
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who have matted hair but do not study, nor those with shaggy hair, nor gamblers, nor those who officiate as priests for large groups. (3.151)
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers, and those who live by trade—these should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors. (3.152)
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer; 3.153.

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who has been cast out, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, and one who belongs to a religious guild (gaṇa)—these are indeed [unfit]. (3.154)
One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vows, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour; 3.155.
One who teaches for a fee, one likewise taught by a fee-payer, one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one who is a teacher of a Śūdra, one of foul speech, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka; 3.156.
Having abandoned, without cause, one's mother, father, or teacher; and having entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial alliances. (3.157)
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats the food of a harlot, a seller of Soma, one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger; 3.158.
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard, one afflicted with a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (such as poison). (3.159)

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is still unmarried, a betrayer of friends, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher of his own son; 3.160.

One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one afflicted with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise a reviler of the Vedas—these are to be avoided. (3.161)
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by the stars;
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare. (3.162)
One who diverts watercourses, one who delights in obstructing them, a builder of houses, a messenger, and likewise a planter of trees; 3.163.
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, one who is cruel, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for guilds (gaṇas). ||3.164||
One devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, a constant beggar, one who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous—these are likewise excluded. (3.165)
A sheep-butchers, a buffalo-herder, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and one who carries out the dead for a fee—these must be avoided with great effort. (3.166)
A learned man, the best among the twice-born, should avoid both of these lowest of the twice-born, who are of censurable conduct and unworthy of the company at a meal. (3.167)
For a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes. (3.168)
I shall describe in its entirety that result which arises for the giver after death from giving to one unworthy of the company at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors. (3.169)
Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, as well as by those such as the *parivetṛ* and others who are unworthy of the row, that indeed the *rakṣasas* consume. (3.170)

He who enters into the union of marriage and the sacred fire while his elder brother remains [unmarried] should be known as a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder), and the elder brother as a *parivitti* (the one superseded). (3.171)
The elder brother who remains unmarried, the younger brother who marries before him, she with whom he marries, as well as the giver and the officiating priest—the fifth—these all go to hell. (3.172)
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of his deceased brother—even though she has been authorized by dharma—is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. (3.173)
Two types of sons, the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, are born from another's wife:
the Kuṇḍa when the husband is alive, and the Golaka when the husband is dead. (3.174)
Those two beings, born in the field of another, destroy both in this world and after death the offerings of sacrificial oblations (havya) and ancestral rites (kavya) given by their donors. (3.175)
As many members of a company as an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating, for that many the foolish donor receives no fruit from that act. (3.176)

A blind man, upon seeing [the gift], destroys the fruit of ninety [gifts]; a one-eyed man, of sixty; a leper, of a hundred; but one afflicted with a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousand for the donor. (3.177)
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift.
Even a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, by accepting a gift from him out of greed, quickly goes to destruction like an unbaked clay vessel in water. (3.179)
What is given to a seller of Soma becomes excrement; to a physician, pus and blood; what is given to a temple-attendant is lost; and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation. (3.180)
That which is given to a merchant, however, yields no fruit either in this world or the next;
it is like an oblation poured into ashes, and likewise so for one who is a twice-born man born of a remarried woman.
But regarding other unworthy persons, those unfit for the company at a meal as previously specified, the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone. (3.182)
Learn now in full about those foremost of the twice-born, the purifiers of the assembly, by whom a row defiled by those unworthy of the company is purified. (3.183)
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the sacred texts], and who are born of a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly. (3.184)

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymns, one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas, one born of a lineage where the gift of a daughter in marriage was made according to the Brahma rite, and one who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman; || 3.185 ||

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a reciter, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand [cows], and one who lives for a hundred years—these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly. 3.186.
On the day before or on the very day when the Śrāddha rite is to take place, he should properly invite at least three Brahmins who possess the qualities previously described. (3.187)
A twice-born man invited to a rite for the ancestors should always remain self-restrained;
he should not recite the Vedic hymns, and that [rite] shall be his Śrāddha. (3.188)
For the ancestors attend upon those twice-born who have been invited;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit. (3.189)

But the best of the twice-born, having invoked [the ancestors] according to the rule for offerings to gods and ancestors, if he should somehow transgress, that sinner shall go to the state of a pig. (3.190)
But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha feast, rejoices with a Śūdra woman, incurs all whatever evil deed the giver has committed. (3.191)
Free from anger, devoted to purity, always practicing celibacy, having laid down their weapons—these highly fortunate Pitṛs are the deities of the past. (3.192)
Since the origin of all these [impurities] is entirely without exception, learn now those rules by which they are to be treated. 3.193.
The sons of all those sages— Manu Hiraṇyagarbha’s progeny, such as Marīci and the others— are recorded as the groups of Pitṛs.
The sons of Virāṭ, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are those of the gods, the offspring of Marīci.
The Barhiṣads, born of Atri, are recorded as the progenitors of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kiṃnaras.
Among the Brahmins they are called Somapas; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaiśyas, Ājyapas; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins. (3.197)
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha. (3.198)
One should designate the *anagnidagdha*, the *agnidagdha*, the *kāvyas*, the *barhiṣads*, as well as the *agniṣvāttas* and the *saumyas*, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins. (3.199)
Furthermore, regarding these principal groups of ancestors that have been proclaimed, it should be understood that their sons and grandsons here are infinite. (3.200)
From the sages the ancestors were born; from the ancestors, the gods and demons;
and from the gods, the entire world—both moving and stationary—in due order. (3.201)
Even water, when given with faith using silver vessels or those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible results for them. (3.202)
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors is more important than the rite for the gods;
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors. (3.203)
One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the Rākṣasas plunder a Śrāddha that is devoid of protection. (3.204)
One should seek that which has the gods at its beginning and end; it should not have the ancestors at its beginning and end.
For one who seeks that which has the ancestors at its beginning and end perishes quickly, along with his lineage. (3.205)
One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung, and one should diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south. ||3.206||
In open spaces, on clean riverbanks, and indeed in secluded places, the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered. (3.207)
When separate seats provided with sacrificial grass have been prepared, he should cause those Brahmins, who have duly sipped water, to sit down upon them. (3.208)
Having seated those blameless Brahmins upon their seats,
he should honor them with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with the gods.
Having brought water for them, along with sesame seeds and purifiers, the Brāhmaṇa, being authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, should perform the rite in the fire. (3.210)
Having first performed the satiation of Agni, Soma, and Yama, he should afterwards satisfy the ancestors with the sacrificial food (havirdāna) according to the rule. (3.211)
But in the absence of fire, one should place the offering in the hand of a Brahmin;
for that twice-born man is called "fire" by the Brahmins who perceive the sacred mantras. (3.212)
The ancients speak of these best of the twice-born as being free from anger, easily propitiated, intent on nourishing the world, and the gods of the śrāddha. (3.213)

Having performed the entire circumambulation with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya) around the fire, he should pour water upon the ground with his hand in the aprasavya manner. 3.214.
Then, having formed three pindas from that remainder of the oblation, being composed in mind, he should offer them according to the rite for water-libations while facing the south. (3.215)

Having offered those rice-balls (piṇḍas) then, being self-restrained and according to the prescribed rule, he should wipe that hand upon those Darbha grasses for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāginaḥ).
Having sipped water and turned toward the north, having slowly restrained his breath three times, he should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors with the appropriate mantras. (3.217)
He should slowly pour the remaining water near the funeral cakes;
then, being composed, he should smell those cakes in the order they were placed. (3.218)
Having taken small portions from each of the lumps of food in due order, he should first cause those very Brahmins who are seated to eat according to the rule. (3.219)
While his father is still living, however, he should perform the offering for his ancestors alone;
or else, like a Brahmin, he may cause his own father to partake in that Śrāddha.
But if one's father has passed away while the grandfather is still living, he should pronounce his father’s name and then proclaim the name of the great-grandfather. (3.221)
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared;
or, with permission, he may perform it himself at his pleasure. (3.222)
Having placed the water with sesame seeds and the *pavitra* grass in their hands, he should offer the first portion of that *piṇḍa*, saying, "May there be *svadhā* for them. (3.223)
Having himself taken the increased portion of food with both hands, he should place it slowly near the Brahmins while meditating upon the ancestors. (3.224)
The food that is brought forth and released from both hands, the evil-minded Asuras suddenly snatch away. (3.225)
And with self-restraint and concentration, he should properly place on the ground itself the various condiments such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey. (3.226)
Various kinds of food and drink, roots and fruits, as well as savory meats and fragrant beverages. (3.227)
Having brought all that, he should serve it slowly and with great composure, being pure and extolling all its qualities. (3.228)
One should never shed tears, nor become angry, nor speak untruth;
one should not touch food with the foot, nor should one shake it. (3.229)
Tears cause the departed spirits to depart; anger, the enemies; falsehood, the dogs;
the touch of one's foot, the rākṣasas; and shaking [the head], the evildoers. (3.230)
Whatever may please the learned Brahmins, that he should give without envy; and he should engage in discourses on the Veda, for this is what is desired by the ancestors. (3.231)
At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause the recitation of the Veda, the treatises on Dharma, as well as narratives, histories, Purāṇas, and supplementary texts. (3.232)
Being satisfied himself, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them food gradually;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and praise for their qualities. (3.233)
One should diligently feed even a daughter’s son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.
Three things are purifying at a Śrāddha: a daughter’s son, a blanket made of goat’s hair, and sesame seeds;
and three things they praise therein: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste. (3.235)
All the food should be very hot, and they should eat while remaining silent;
nor should the twice-born, when asked by the giver, speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
As long as there is heat in the food, as long as they eat while restrained in speech, so long do the ancestors eat, until the qualities of the sacrificial offering have been described. (3.237)
Whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south, and whatever one eats while wearing shoes—that indeed the Rākṣasas consume. (3.238)
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog, a woman in her menses, and a eunuch—these should not look at twice-born men while they are eating. (3.239)
Whatever is looked upon by these at the giving of a house, at a meal, or at an offering to the gods or the ancestors, that becomes ineffective. (3.240)
The pig destroys [the merit] by its smell, the cock by the wind of its wings, the dog by the casting of its glance, and one born of the lowest caste by touch. (3.241)
Whether he be lame or one-eyed, or even a servant of the donor, or one with deficient or redundant limbs—one should remove him from that place as well. (3.242)
When a Brahmin or even a mendicant has approached for the sake of food, he should, with the permission of the Brahmins, honor him according to his ability. (3.243)
Having gathered food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should cast it upon the ground in front of those who have eaten, scattering it about.
The leavings on the *darbha* grass and whatever food has been scattered should be the portion for those who have died an unnatural death, for renunciants, and for women of noble family. (3.245)
That which remains on the ground as leavings from one who is neither crooked nor deceitful is declared to be the share of the group of servants at a rite for the ancestors. (3.246)

When a twice-born man has died, however, one should perform the Śrāddha rite without the Sapiṇḍana ceremony; one should feed the Brahmins without an offering to the gods and offer a single funeral cake (piṇḍa). (3.247)
But once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the Dharma, the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by this very same procedure. (3.248)
That fool who, having eaten at a *śrāddha*, gives the leftovers to a *vṛṣala* goes headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell. (3.249)
If one who has partaken of a śrāddha feast approaches the bed of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) on that same day, his ancestors lie for that month in her excrement. (3.250)

Having asked, "Was it well-tasted?", he should then cause those who are satiated to rinse their mouths; once they have rinsed, he should dismiss them with the words, "May you be happy on all sides. (3.251)
Immediately after that, the Brahmins should say to him, "Svadhā astu.
For the utterance of "svadhā" is the supreme benediction in all rites for the ancestors. (3.252)
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food;
having been authorized by those twice-born ones, he should do exactly as they may direct. (3.253)
At a rite for the ancestors, one should say "svaditam"; at a rite in a cow-pen, "suśṛtam"; at a rite for prosperity, "saṃpannam"; and at a rite for the gods, "rocitam. (3.254)
The afternoon, as well as darbha grass, the preparation of the site, sesame seeds, abundance, refinement, and eminent twice-born men—these are the perfections in rites for the ancestors. (3.255)

Darbha grass, the purifier, the forenoon, and all kinds of sacrificial food (haviṣya), as well as whatever purifier was mentioned previously—these should be known as the requisites for the oblation. 3.256
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is not seasoned, and salt-free food—these are called by their very nature sacrificial oblations (havis). (3.257)

Having dismissed those brahmins, being self-controlled, restrained in speech, and pure, he should look toward the southern direction and request these boons from the ancestors: "O ancestors, may my lineage never fail; may wealth always be present; may the Vedas and progeny increase; and may faith never depart from us. (3.259) And having thus requested these boons, he should circumambulate them three times from left to right and then dismiss them with the words, "May you go as you please. (3.260) |||The provided text consists entirely of ellipses and does not contain any Japanese or Sanskrit content to translate. Therefore, there is no output to provide.
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (3.259)

Having thus performed the offering of water, he should immediately thereafter cause those rice-balls to be eaten by a cow, a Brahmin, a goat, or the fire, or else he should cast them into the water. (3.260)
Some perform the offering of the funeral cakes even beforehand;
others cause them to be eaten by birds, or cast them into fire or water. (3.261)
Then, the devoted and lawful wife, intent on the worship of the ancestors and desiring a son, should properly eat the middle *piṇḍa*. (3.262)
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence, wealthy, possessed of progeny, righteous, and likewise of a sattvic nature. (3.263)
Having washed his hands and sipped water, he should provide food primarily for his kinsmen;
having given hospitality to his kinsmen, he should also honor his relatives. (3.264)
That remnant of food should remain until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus is the law established. (3.265)
I shall now describe in its entirety that sacrificial offering which, when given to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves both for a long duration and for infinity. (3.266)
By the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits, according to the prescribed rule, the ancestors of men are gratified for one month. (3.267)
For two months with fish-meat, for three months with the meat of the deer, for four months with the meat of sheep, and for five months indeed with the meat of birds. (3.268)
For six months with the meat of a goat, for seven here with that of the spotted deer (pārṣata),
for eight with the meat of the black antelope (aiṇeya), and indeed for nine with that of the Ruru deer.
They remain satisfied for ten months with the flesh of boars and buffaloes, but for exactly eleven months with the meat of hares and tortoises. (3.270)
But by means of cow's milk, or milk-rice, or the meat of a vārdhrīṇasa, one’s satisfaction lasts for twelve years. (3.271)
Black potherb, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the rhinoceros and red deer, honey, and all kinds of food fit for sages lead to infinity. (3.272)
Whatever one may give mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too shall indeed be inexhaustible during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism.
"May there be born in our lineage one who would give us milk-rice with honey and ghee on the thirteenth lunar day, during the time when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east. (3.274)
Whatever one gives according to the rule, correctly and endowed with faith, that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the next world. (3.275)
In the dark fortnight, from the tenth day onwards—excluding the fourteenth—the lunar days are recommended for the śrāddha rite; other days are not so auspicious. (3.276)
Just as the latter fortnight is superior to the former fortnight, so too the afternoon is superior to the forenoon for a śrāddha ceremony. ||3.277||
Performing [the rites] on odd lunar days and under odd asterisms, one attains all desires;
but by worshipping the ancestors on even days, one obtains abundant progeny.

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder, with the offering turned properly to the left, and remaining alert, one should perform the ancestral rite according to the rules until its conclusion, holding *darbha* grass in the hand. (3.279)
One should not perform a śrāddha at night, for that time is declared to belong to the Rākṣasas; nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has just risen.
By this rule, one should perform the Śrāddha here three times a year—
during the winter, summer, and rainy seasons— and the five great sacrifices daily.
The oblation pertaining to the sacrifice for the ancestors is not prescribed for a common fire;
nor is there a Śrāddha without the Darśa sacrifice for a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires. (3.282)

Whatever merit the best of the twice-born obtains by satiating the ancestors with water after bathing, by that alone he attains the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña). //3.283//
They call the Vasus the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; such is the ancient Vedic revelation. (3.284)
One should always be an eater of *vighasa* and always an eater of *amṛta*;
for *vighasa* is that which remains after eating, and likewise *amṛta* is that which remains from a sacrifice. (3.285)
All this rule regarding the five sacrifices has been declared to you;
now hear the rule concerning the livelihoods of the foremost among the twice-born. (3.286)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[Chapter Four] Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher, the twice-born man should dwell in his house, having taken a wife, during the second quarter of his life. 4.1.
A Brahmin should live in times of non-distress by adopting a livelihood that involves no harm to living beings, or at least very little harm. (4.2)
For the sake of accomplishing the mere necessities of life, one should accumulate wealth through one's own irreproachable occupations, without causing distress to the body. (4.3)

One may live by means of the *ṛta* and the *amṛta*, or by the *mṛta* and the *pramṛta*, or even by the *satya* and the *anṛta*; but one should never, under any circumstances, live by the "dog's livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*).
Gleaning ears of grain is to be known as *ṛta*; what is obtained unasked is *amṛta*;
alms obtained by begging are *mṛta*; and agriculture is traditionally called *pramṛta*. (4.5)
Trade, however, consists of both truth and falsehood, and one may live by that as well;
service is declared to be the "dog's livelihood," therefore one should avoid it. (4.6)
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or even enough for a single jar;
or he may have enough for three days, or he may not even provide for tomorrow. ||4.7||
And among these four twice-born householders, each subsequent one should be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of the worlds. (4.8)
Among these, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmasattra).
Subsisting by means of gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, and being devoted to the Agnihotra,
he should always perform only the Iṣṭis prescribed for the new moon, the full moon, and the solstices.
One should never follow the ways of the world for the sake of one's livelihood; rather, one should live the pure life of a Brahmin, which is straightforward and free from deceit. 4.11
One who seeks happiness should remain self-restrained by relying upon supreme contentment;
for happiness has its root in contentment, while the opposite is the root of suffering. (4.12)
But a twice-born Snātaka living by any one of these modes of livelihood should observe these following vows, which lead to heaven, long life, and fame: 4.13.
One should constantly perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. (4.14)
One should not seek wealth through excessive attachment nor by contrary actions;
one should not seek it even when wealth is available, nor from hither and thither even in times of distress. (4.15)
One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire;
one should also turn the mind away from excessive attachment to them. 4.16
One should abandon wealth and even one's own kindred if they obstruct one's sacred study;
passing one's time in whatever manner is necessary, for that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of one's purpose. 4.17
One should conduct oneself here in accordance with the conformity of one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage, by adopting a corresponding appearance, speech, and disposition. (4.18)
For the sake of increasing his intelligence, he should constantly study the treatises that quickly bring wealth, prosperity, and benefit, as well as the Vedic scriptures. (4.19)
For in whatever measure a person masters the scripture, in that same measure he understands it, and his discernment finds delight in it. 4.20

One should never neglect the sacrifice to the sages, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to the ancestors, according to one's ability. (4.21)
Some people who know the scriptures on sacrifice constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from worldly desire. 4.22
Some offer the breath into speech and speech into breath at all times, perceiving within speech and breath the imperishable completion of the sacrifice. (4.23)
Other brahmins always perform these sacrifices with knowledge alone, perceiving with the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge. 4.24

One should always perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice at the beginning and end of day and night; likewise, one should perform it with the *darśa* at the end of the half-month and with the *paurṇamāsa*. (4.25)
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice of new grain; likewise, at the end of the seasons, he should perform the seasonal sacrifices;
at the end of the solstices, the animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, the Soma sacrifices.

A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and desires to live a long life must not eat new grain or meat without having first performed the sacrifice of the new harvest (navasasyeṣṭi) and the animal sacrifice (paśubandha). 4.27.
For his fires, greedy for new grain and meat, if not honored with the offering of fresh grain and animal sacrifice, truly desire to consume his very life-breaths. (4.28)
No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of one's ability with a seat, food, a bed, water, or roots and fruits. (4.29)

One should not honor, even with a mere word, those who belong to heretical sects, those who persist in improper occupations, those who act like cats, the deceitful, the sophists, and those who behave like herons. (4.30)

One should honor with offerings to the gods and ancestors those householders who are learned in the Vedas and have completed their studies and vows, but one should avoid those who are the opposite. 4.31.
To those who do not cook for themselves, the householder should give according to his ability;
and he should make a distribution among all beings without causing hardship to his own household. (4.32)
A Snātaka who is suffering from hunger may seek wealth from a king, or from his patron (yājya), or from a pupil; it is the settled rule that he must not seek it from anyone else. 4.33.
A learned Snātaka shall never suffer from hunger if he has the means;
nor, while possessing wealth, shall he wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (4.34)

Having trimmed his hair, nails, and beard, self-controlled, wearing white garments, and pure, he should be constantly engaged in the private recitation of the Veda and in what is beneficial for the self. 4.35.
He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot with water,
the sacred thread, the Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings.
One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky. (4.37)
One should not jump over a calf-roping cord, nor run while it is raining;
nor should one look at one's own reflection in water—this is the rule. (4.38)
One should circumambulate clockwise clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees. (4.39)
Even if he is intoxicated, he should not approach a woman during her menstrual period;
nor should he lie down with her on the same bed. (4.40)
For when a man approaches a woman overwhelmed by her menses, his wisdom, vigor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish. (4.41)
For him who avoids her when she is overwhelmed by the menses, wisdom, splendor, strength, vision, and even life itself increase. (4.42)
He should not eat together with his wife, nor should he look at her while she is eating,
sneezing, or yawning, nor when she is seated at her ease.
A twice-born man desiring luster should not look at a woman who is applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed with oil, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth. (4.44)
One should not eat food while wearing only a single garment, nor should one perform a bath naked.
One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen. (4.45)
Neither on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain; neither in a ruined temple nor ever upon an anthill. (4.46)
Neither in pits inhabited by living creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing;
neither having reached the bank of a river, nor on the summit of a mountain. (4.47)
While looking at the wind, fire, a Brahmin, the sun, water, or likewise cows, one should never discharge feces or urine. (4.48)
Having passed by [the village], he should void his excrement using wood, a clod of earth, a leaf, or grass;
restraining his speech, being pure, with his body covered and his head veiled. (4.49)
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night one should face south; and during the two twilights, one should face as during the day. (4.50)
In the shade or in the dark, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the ritual] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as well as when there is fear of danger to life. 4.51.
The wisdom of one who urinates facing a fire, facing the sun, facing the moon, water, or a twice-born man, or facing a cow or the wind, perishes. (4.52)
One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it. 4.53
One should not place it underneath, nor should one step over it;
one should not treat it with the feet, nor should one cause injury to living beings. (4.54)
One should not eat at the time of twilight, nor should one travel, nor should one lie down;
nor indeed should one scratch the ground, nor should one remove one's own garland.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or phlegm into water, nor anything else defiled by impurities, nor blood, nor poisons. (4.56)
One should not sleep alone in an empty house, nor should one wake a superior person from sleep; one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor go to a sacrifice unless invited. 4.57
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should keep the right hand raised.
One should not prevent a cow from suckling her calf, nor should one tell anyone [of it];
likewise, upon seeing a rainbow in the sky, a wise man should not point it out to anyone. 4.59
One should not dwell in an unrighteous village, nor in one where diseases are exceedingly prevalent;
one should not set out on a journey alone, nor should one reside for long on a mountain. (4.60)
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra, nor in one filled with people who neglect the sacred fires; nor in one overrun by heretics, nor in one infested by men of the lowest castes. (4.61)
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice excessive gluttony;
one should not eat too early, nor too late in the evening, nor having already eaten in the morning, should one eat again in the evening. (4.62)
One should not engage in futile exertion, nor drink water from one's cupped hands; one should not eat foods while holding them in one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity. 4.63
One should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments;
one should not clap hands, nor shout, nor utter cries when impassioned.
One should never wash one's feet in a vessel made of bell-metal;
nor should one eat from a broken dish, nor from one that is defiled by its nature.
One should not wear sandals, clothing, a sacred thread, ornaments, a garland, or even a water-pot that have been worn by others. (4.66)
One should not travel with draft animals that are untrained, nor with those afflicted by hunger or disease;
nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are mutilated. (4.67)
He should always travel with horses that are well-trained, swift, endowed with auspicious marks,
and perfect in color and form, without lashing them excessively with a goad.
The morning sun, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and a broken seat should be avoided;
one should not clip one's nails or hair, nor should one tear at the nails with the teeth. (4.69)
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with one's fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless action, nor any that results in future suffering. (4.70)
The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, or bites his nails, as well as the slanderer and the impure person, quickly goes to destruction. (4.71)
One should not engage in contentious debate, nor should one wear garlands outdoors;
riding on the backs of oxen is in every way censured. (4.72)
One should not enter an enclosed village or house by a way other than the gate; and at night, one should avoid the roots of trees from afar. (4.73)
One should never play with dice, nor should one carry one's sandals oneself;
one should not eat while reclining on a bed, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
One should not eat anything mixed with sesame until sunset;
nor should one sleep here naked, nor go anywhere while still impure from food.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet;
eating with wet feet, one shall attain a long life. 4.76.
One should never enter a difficult place that is beyond the range of sight;
one should not look at feces or urine, nor should one cross a river by means of one's arms.
One who desires to live a long life should not step upon hair, nor ashes, bones, or potsherds; nor should one step upon cotton seeds or husks. (4.78)
One should not dwell with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with outcasts, nor with those who live on the outskirts of society. (4.79)
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared for sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him. (4.80)
For he who teaches him the Dharma and he who likewise instructs him in the vow sinks into the darkness called "the unrestrained" along with that very person. (4.81)
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food, nor bathe without it [the head]. (4.82)
One should avoid seizing the hair or striking the head with these blows;
moreover, having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil. (4.83)
One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste, nor from those who possess slaughterhouses, oil-presses, or taverns, nor from those who live by prostitution. (4.84)
A cart is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a banner is equal to ten carts;
a courtesan is equal to ten banners; and a king is equal to ten courtesans. (4.85)
A king is considered equal to a butcher who operates ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, accepting gifts from him is terrible. (4.86)
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures will, in due course, go to these twenty-one hells. (4.87)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the hell of Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka. ||4.88||
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, Saṃpratāpana, Saṃghāta along with Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pūtimūrtika. ||4.89||
The Iron Stake, the Residue of Grain, the Path, the Śālmalī River,
the Forest of Sword-leaves, and the Iron Cage.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and who desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king. (4.91)
One should wake up during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as the bodily afflictions rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas. (4.92)

Having risen and performed the necessary duties, purified and composed, he should stand for a long time reciting the morning twilight prayer at its proper time, and likewise the evening prayer at its own time. 4.93.
By virtue of their long twilight devotions, the seers attained long life,
as well as wisdom, fame, renown, and spiritual luster.

Having performed the ritual commencement according to the rule on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedic hymns for four and a half months. 4.95.
Under the Puṣya asterism, the twice-born should perform the external dismissal of the Vedas (chandasām utsarjana),
or when the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha has arrived, during the forenoon.

Having thus performed the ritual dismissal of the Vedic meters outside according to the scriptures, one should cease [the study] for a night with its two flanking days (pakṣiṇī), or for that single day and night. 4.97.
From this point forward, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic meters during the bright fortnights,
and one should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights.
One should not study indistinctly, nor in the presence of Śūdras; having studied the Veda at the end of the night while exhausted, one should not go back to sleep. 4.99.
A twice-born man who is disciplined should always recite the Veda composed in meters according to the prescribed rule, provided there is no time of distress. (4.100)
One who is studying should always avoid these days of suspension from study, as should one who is teaching students according to the prescribed rule. (4.101)
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, and when there is a cloud of dust by day—
those who know the rules of study declare these two occasions during the rainy season to be times unfit for study.
Manu has declared that when there is lightning, thunder, and rain, or when there is a falling of great meteors, there shall be no study for the remainder of the day. 4.103.
But when these [phenomena] appear while the sacred fires have been kindled, then one should know that there is no study; likewise, when clouds appear out of season. (4.104)

In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly bodies, one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) lasting until the same time the following day, even during the proper season. 4.105.

But when the fires have been kindled, if there is the sound of lightning and thunder, there shall be a suspension of study for as long as the light lasts; for the remainder of the night, it is as if it were day.
For those who desire proficiency in dharma, there shall be a perpetual suspension of study in villages and cities, and in the presence of any foul odor whatsoever. (4.107)
There is no study when a corpse is inside a village, nor in the presence of a low-caste person (vṛṣala), nor while there is weeping, nor in a crowd of people. 4.108.
While in water, at midnight, when voiding excrement or urine, while impure from food, or after eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha), one should not entertain [impure thoughts] even in the mind. 4.109.

Having accepted an invitation to an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, a learned twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days, nor during the period of ritual impurity following the death of a king or an eclipse of Rāhu.
As long as the scent and the smear of a funeral meal (ekānudiṣṭa) remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long should one not recite the Veda. 4.111
One should not study while lying down, nor with one's feet raised, nor having crossed one's legs; nor after eating meat, nor food from a house where a birth-impurity (sūtaka) has occurred. 4.112.
In mist, or when the sound of an arrow is heard, during both twilights, on the new moon day and the fourteenth day, and on the full moon days and the Aṣṭakā festivals. ||4.113||
The new moon day destroys the teacher, and the fourteenth day destroys the disciple; the Brahma-aṣṭakā and the full moon day likewise destroy them; therefore, one should avoid those days. 4.114.

A twice-born man should not recite while there is a shower of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, when jackals howl, or when dogs, donkeys, or camels are barking, nor while standing in a row.

One should not study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen; nor after wearing a garment used for sexual intercourse, nor after accepting food offered at a funeral rite (śrāddha). 4.116.

Whether it be animate or inanimate, whatever may be offered at a *śrāddha* ceremony, upon touching that, there is a suspension of study; for the twice-born is traditionally said to have his hand as his mouth. (4.117)
One should know that there is no study for the remainder of the day when a village is plundered by thieves, when there is a panic caused by fire, or during all extraordinary portents. (4.118)
At the Upakarman and the Utsarga ceremonies, a fast of three nights is prescribed;
at the Aṣṭakās and on the nights marking the end of the seasons, a fast of one day and night is prescribed.

One should not study while mounted on a horse, nor on a tree, nor on an elephant; nor on a boat, nor on a donkey, nor on a camel; nor while standing on barren ground, nor while traveling in a vehicle. 4.120.
Not during a dispute, nor in a quarrel, nor in an army, nor in battle;
not immediately after eating, nor while indigestion persists, nor after vomiting, nor when there is sour eructation. (4.121)
Nor should one study without having first taken leave of a guest, while a strong wind is blowing, when blood is flowing from the body, or when one has been wounded by a weapon. (4.122)
One should never recite the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda while the sound of Sāman chanting is heard;
likewise, after having completed the study of a Veda, or after having studied the Āraṇyaka.
The Ṛgveda has the gods as its deities; the Yajurveda, however, belongs to humans;
the Sāmaveda is remembered as belonging to the ancestors; therefore, its sound is impure. (4.124)
Knowing this, the learned, extracting the essence of the three Vedas, first practice it daily in due order and afterwards study the Veda itself. (4.125)
If cattle, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, a mongoose, or a rat pass between [the teacher and the student], one should know that there is no study for a day and a night. (4.126)
A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions for the suspension of study:
an impure place of study and an impure self. (4.127)
On the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth, a twice-born Snātaka must always remain celibate, even during the period favorable for conception. (4.128)
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight; nor should one bathe constantly with one's clothes on, nor in an unknown body of water. (4.129)
One should not intentionally step on the shadow of deities, a teacher, a king, a *snātaka*, an *ācārya*, a tawny man (*babhru*), or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice. (4.130)
At midday, at midnight, after eating a śrāddha meal containing meat,
and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads.
One should not intentionally step upon fragrant unguents, bath-water, feces, urine, blood, phlegm, spittle, or vomit. (4.132)
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companion of an enemy, nor an unrighteous person, nor a thief, nor the wife of another. (4.133)
Indeed, nothing in this world is so detrimental to longevity as a man's pursuit of another's wife in this world. (4.134)
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they are weak. (4.135)
For these three, when treated with contempt, utterly consume a man;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt. (4.136)
One should not despise oneself because of former failures; until death one should seek prosperity, nor should one consider it unattainable. (4.137)
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpleasant;
nor should one speak an untruth that is pleasant—this is the eternal dharma.
One should say "bhadraṃ bhadram" (well-being, well-being), or simply say "bhadram" (well-being);
one should not engage in dry enmity or dispute with anyone. (4.139)
One should not travel too early, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is high noon;
one should not go with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with outcasts.
One should not despise those who have missing limbs or extra limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those deficient in beauty or wealth, or those of low birth. (4.141)
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire;
nor, while remaining in his natural state, should he, being impure, look at the host of luminaries in the sky. (4.142)
Having touched these while impure, one should always touch the vital breaths with water, as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand. (4.143)
Unless he is ill, he should not touch his own bodily apertures without a specific reason; he should avoid all the hair on his private parts as well. (4.144)
He should be devoted to auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have his senses conquered;
he should constantly mutter prayers and offer oblations into the fire without weariness. (4.145)
For those who are devoted to auspicious conduct, who are ever self-restrained, and who engage in recitation and burnt offerings, no misfortune exists. (4.146)
One should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without weariness; for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary one. 4.147
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity, and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth. (4.148)
Remembering his former birth, the twice-born practices the Brahman;
and by the constant practice of the Brahman, he enjoys infinite bliss. (4.149)
He should constantly perform the Sāvitra oblations and the propitiatory fire-sacrifices on the Parvan days;
and he should always worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakā days and the Anvaṣṭakā days.
One should discharge urine at a distance from one's dwelling, as well as the water used for washing the feet and the remnants of food; indeed, one should perform these acts far away. (4.151)
One should perform acts of friendliness, grooming, bathing, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, and the worship of the deities during the forenoon alone. (4.152)
On the sacred festival days (parvan), a twice-born man should visit the deities, righteous brahmins, the sovereign for the sake of protection, and his teachers. (4.153)
He should salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart. 4.154.
One should, unwearied, always practice the conduct of the virtuous, which is the root of dharma and is properly established in its own duties as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti. (4.155)
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. (4.156)
For a man of evil conduct is indeed censured in the world;
he constantly partakes of suffering, being diseased and short-lived. (4.157)
Even if he lacks all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct, is full of faith, and free from malice, lives for a hundred years. (4.158)
Whatever action depends on another, that one should avoid with effort;
whatever depends on oneself, that one should practice with diligence. (4.159)
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering. (4.160)
Whatever action one performs that brings satisfaction to one's inner self, that one should perform with diligence; but one should avoid the opposite. (4.161)
One must not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a guru, Brāhmaṇas, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever. (4.162)
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, disparaging the deities, as well as hatred, arrogance, pride, anger, and harshness. (4.163)
One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down; except for a son or a pupil, whom one may strike for the sake of discipline. (4.164)
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him shall wander for a hundred years in the Tāmisra hell. (4.165)
Having intentionally struck [another] even with a blade of grass out of agitation, one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in wombs of evil beings. (4.166)
By causing blood to flow from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting, a man, through his lack of wisdom, incurs very great suffering after death. (4.167)
For as many particles of dust as the blood takes up from the surface of the earth, for that many years shall the shedder of that blood be devoured by others in the hereafter. (4.168)
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body. (4.169)
For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is based on falsehood, and who is constantly devoted to violence—such a person does not prosper in happiness here in this world. (4.170)
Even if he should falter, he must not, on account of dharma, allow his mind to settle upon what is contrary to dharma;
for he sees that the unrighteous and the wicked swiftly meet with their downfall.
Unrighteousness practiced in this world does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow;
but returning slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer. (4.172)
If it does not ripen upon oneself, then upon one's sons; if not upon the sons, then upon one's grandsons; yet an unrighteous act never fails to bear fruit for the doer. (4.173)
By means of unrighteousness one prospers for a time; then one beholds auspicious things;
then one conquers one's rivals, but finally perishes along with one's very roots. (4.174)
One should always take delight in truth, righteousness, noble conduct, and purity;
and one should instruct disciples according to the Dharma, with speech, arms, and belly restrained. (4.175)
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of righteousness, and one should also abandon righteousness if it results in future suffering and is censured by the world. (4.176)
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor dishonest; one should likewise not be fickle with speech, nor have a mind intent on deeds that harm others. (4.177)
By that path by which his fathers have gone, by which his grandfathers have gone—by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by that way, he does not come to harm. (4.178)
By officiating priests, family chaplains, and teachers; by maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; by children, the elderly, and the sick; and by physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends. (4.179)
One should not engage in a dispute with one's mother or father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or the group of servants. (4.180)
By renouncing disputes through these [means], one is liberated from all evils;
and by conquering these, the householder conquers all these worlds. (4.181)

The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati; the guest is the lord of Indra’s world; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods. (4.182)
Female relatives belong to the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen belong to the world of the Viśvedevas; maternal uncles and mothers belong to the world of the waters and the earth. (4.183)
The young, the old, the emaciated, and the afflicted should be known as lords of space (ākāśa).
An elder brother is equal to a father; a wife and son are one's own body. (4.184)
One's shadow is one's own, as is the circle of servants; but a daughter is the ultimate object of pity.
Therefore, when insulted by these, one should always endure it without feverish resentment. (4.185)
Even if one is capable of accepting gifts, one should avoid attachment to them;
for by accepting gifts, one's Brahmanic luster is quickly extinguished. (4.186)
Without knowing the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of material gifts, a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger. (4.187)
One who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, food, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter without knowing the proper rules, is reduced to ashes like wood. (4.188)
Gold [purifies] life and food; land and a cow purify the body; a horse [purifies] the eyes; clothing [purifies] the skin; ghee [purifies] luster; and sesame seeds [purify] offspring. (4.189)

But that twice-born man who is without self-restraint, who does not study the Vedas, and who delights in accepting gifts, sinks along with that very recipient, like one in water using a boat made of stone. (4.190)
Therefore, an ignorant person should fear whatever gift he might receive;
for even by means of a very small thing, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud. (4.191)
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat, nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas. (4.192)
For wealth, even if acquired according to the law, when given to these three types of people, results in misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world. (4.193)
Just as one who attempts to cross water with a boat made of stone sinks beneath, so do both the giver and the recipient sink to the bottom when they are ignorant. 4.194

One who always carries the banner of Dharma while being greedy, hypocritical, and a deceiver of the world; one who is violent and a cheat toward all—such a person should be known as a "cat-vowed" practitioner (baiḍālavratika). ||4.195||
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own self-interest, dishonest, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow" (bakavrata). 4.196.
Those Brahmins who observe the vow of the heron and those who bear the marks of a cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful deed.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing the sin with a vow, one merely practices deception upon women and Śūdras. (4.198)
Such Brahmins, both in this world and after death, are censured by those who discourse on the Veda; for that vow practiced through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas. (4.199)
He who, being without the marks, subsists by wearing the dress of one who bears the marks, takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born in the womb of an animal. (4.200)
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others; for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the reservoir's builder. (4.201)
One who makes use of another's vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, or houses without them being given incurs a fourth part of the sin. (4.202)
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs. (4.203)

A wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not the observances (niyamas) exclusively; for one who fails to practice the restraints falls, while one who devotes himself solely to the observances likewise falls. (4.204)
A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice offered by one who is not learned in the Vedas, nor at one offered by a village priest, nor at one offered by a woman or a eunuch. (4.205)
This is offensive to the virtuous wherein these people offer oblations;
it is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it. (4.206)
One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted; nor that which is infested with hair or insects, nor that which has been intentionally touched by the foot. (4.207)
That which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a menstruating woman, pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog; 4.208.
Food smelled by a cow, and especially food proclaimed for sale, the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned—[these should be avoided]. (4.209)
The food of a thief and a singer, of a carpenter and a usurer, of one who has been initiated for a sacrifice, of a miser, and of one who is bound or fettered; 4.210.
The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite;
as well as sour gruel, stale food, and the leavings of a Śūdra—[these must not be eaten]. (4.211)
The food of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, or of one who eats leavings;

the food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, that which has been tasted by another, and that from a household within ten days of a death—[these should not be eaten]. (4.212)

Food that has not been honored, meat from an animal killed for no sacred purpose, the food of a woman who has no hero (husband), the food of an enemy, the food of a city-dweller, the food of an outcast, and food upon which someone has sneezed. (4.213)
The food of a slanderer and a liar, of one who sells the results of sacrifices, of an actor, of a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person—[these should be avoided]. (4.214)
[The food] of a blacksmith, of a Niṣāda, of a stage-player, of a goldsmith, of a basket-maker, and likewise of a seller of weapons; 4.215.
[One should not eat the food] of dog-keepers, of butchers, of a washerman of clothes, of a dyer, of a cruel man, or of one in whose house a paramour resides. (4.216)

Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely dominated by women, food from a deceased person before ten days have passed, and that which is simply unsatisfying—[these one should avoid]. (4.217)
The food of a king takes away one's vital energy; the food of a Śūdra, one's spiritual luster;
the food of a goldsmith, one's lifespan; and the food of a leather-cutter, one's fame. (4.218)
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds. (4.219)
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; the food of a seller of weapons is filth. (4.220)
Regarding those others who have been proclaimed in sequence as persons whose food should not be eaten, the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair. (4.221)
Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance. (4.222)
A learned twice-born man shall not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra who does not perform the ancestral rites (śrāddha);
however, in the absence of other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for one night.
Having deliberated upon both—the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer—the gods ordained that their food be equal. (4.224)
Prajāpati, having approached them, said: "Do not make the unequal equal!
That which is purified by faith belongs to the liberal giver; the other is struck down by lack of faith. (4.225)

One should constantly perform sacrifices and works of public utility with diligence and faith; for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired through righteous means, those two become inexhaustible. 4.226

One should constantly practice the duty of giving—both that pertaining to sacrifices and that pertaining to works—with a state of complete contentment, whenever a worthy recipient is encountered, according to one's ability. (4.227)
Whatever may be asked for should be given without malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who can deliver one from all [suffering]. (4.228)
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision. (4.229)
The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold obtains long life; the giver of a house obtains the finest dwellings; the giver of silver obtains supreme beauty. (4.230)
The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of an ox attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun.

The giver of a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty; the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman. (4.232)
Of all gifts whatsoever—water, food, cattle, land, clothing, sesame seeds, gold, and clarified butter—the gift of the Veda is preeminent. (4.233)
With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift, with that very same disposition one receives it back, duly honored. (4.234)
He who accepts what has been honored and he who gives what has been honored—both of them go to heaven; but in the opposite case, they go to hell. (4.235)

One should not be proud of one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth after performing a sacrifice; even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast after giving a gift. (4.236)
Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; life-span perishes through reviling Brahmins; and a gift perishes through boasting of it. (4.237)
One should gradually accumulate merit, like termites building an anthill, for the sake of a companion in the next world, without causing pain to any living beings. (4.238)
For in the next world, neither father nor mother remain for the sake of companionship;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsmen remain—dharma alone remains. (4.239)
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone it experiences the fruit of its good deeds, and alone likewise that of its evil deeds. (4.240)
Having cast the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; Dharma alone follows him. (4.241)
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate Dharma for the sake of a companion;
for with Dharma as a companion, one crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse. (4.242)
The radiant one, whose body is ethereal, swiftly leads that person who is devoted to dharma and whose sins have been destroyed by austerity to the next world.
One who desires to lead his family to excellence should always form alliances with the most eminent; he should avoid those who are base. (4.244)
By associating only with the most excellent and avoiding those who are inferior, a Brāhmaṇa attains preeminence; by the opposite conduct, he falls to the state of a Śūdra. (4.245)
Firm in action, gentle, and self-controlled, not associating with those of cruel conduct,
and non-violent through self-restraint and charity— one who maintains such vows shall likewise conquer heaven.
One may accept from anyone fuel, water, roots, fruits, food that is offered, honey, and the gift of safety. (4.247)
Prajāpati considered alms-food brought forward and offered spontaneously, without being previously requested, as acceptable even from one who has performed evil deeds. (4.248)
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years, nor does the fire carry his oblations, for him who treats such a woman with contempt. (4.249)
One should not refuse a bed, a house, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, parched grain, fish, milk, meat, or even vegetables. (4.250)
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources, but he himself must not be satisfied by them alone. (4.251)
But when the teachers have passed away, or if he lives at home without them, seeking his own livelihood, he should always receive it from virtuous persons. (4.252)
A partner in trade, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (4.253)
Whatever his nature may be, whatever he intends to do, and how he would treat him, in that manner should one offer oneself. (4.254)
He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is when among others is the greatest evildoer in the world; he is a thief who robs his own self. (4.255)
All objects of speech are fixed; they are rooted in speech and have issued forth from speech.
That man who steals this speech is a thief of everything. (4.256)

Having discharged his debts to the great seers, the ancestors, and the gods according to the prescribed rule, and having entrusted everything to his son, he should live established in equanimity. (4.257)
One should always reflect alone in solitude upon what is beneficial for oneself; for by reflecting alone, one attains the supreme good. 4.258
Thus has been declared the eternal mode of life for the Brahmin householder,
as well as the auspicious ritual of the Snātaka vows, which increases one's inner strength.
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras, is eternally freed from sin and is glorified in the world of Brahma. 4.260
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[The Fifth Chapter] Having heard these duties of the *snātaka* as they have been declared, the sages spoke thus to the high-souled Bhṛgu, who was born from fire: 5.1.
O Lord, how does death prevail over those brahmins who, as previously described, perform their own duty and are learned in the Vedas and the scriptures? (5.2)
That righteous-souled Bhṛgu, the son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Listen, by what fault Death seeks to slay the Brahmins. (5.3)
Through the lack of study of the Vedas, the abandonment of right conduct, laziness, and the defects of food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins. (5.4)
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms, as well as those things produced from impure substances, are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born. (5.5)
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions, and the *śelu* fruit, cow’s milk, and colostrum. 5.6.
One should not eat kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, or cakes in vain, nor meat that has not been consecrated, nor food intended for the gods, nor sacrificial oblations. (5.7)

The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals, that of a sheep, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has been taken away—[these are forbidden]. (5.8)
And among all wild animals, except for the buffalo, as well as the milk of females and all sour substances, these indeed are to be avoided. (5.9)
Curd is fit for consumption among sour substances, as is everything produced from curd;
and likewise those [liquors] which are distilled from auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits.
One should avoid all carnivorous birds, as well as those that dwell in villages; likewise, one should avoid those with uncloven hooves and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird. (5.11)
