The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the village cock, the sārasa, the rajjudāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina. (5.12)
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, birds that scratch with their claws, fish-eating aquatic birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat; 5.13.
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail, those that feed on fish, village pigs, and all kinds of fish. (5.14)
Whoever eats the flesh of any creature is said to be an eater of that creature's flesh; one who eats fish is an eater of all flesh; therefore, one should avoid fish. (5.15)
The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are the first two prescribed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*);
likewise, all *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *saśalka* fish are permitted. (5.16)
One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown, nor all five-toed creatures, even if they are among those designated as edible. (5.17)

The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare—these they declare to be edible among five-toed animals, as well as those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel. (5.18)
Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, village pigs, garlic, village cocks, onions, or leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]. (5.19)
Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa;
for the remaining cases, one should fast for a day.

The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, it must be performed with greater particularity for that which was known [to be forbidden]. (5.21)
"Commendable beasts and birds may be slain by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice, and also for the sake of maintaining their dependents; for so Agastya practiced in ancient times. (5.22)
For in ancient times, during the sacrifices of the seers and the rites of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the sacrificial cakes were made from the flesh of wild animals and birds. (5.23)
Whatever food, whether hard or soft, is mixed with oil or fat and is not otherwise censured, may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, as may whatever remains from an oblation. (5.24)

Even if it has been stored for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be consumed by the twice-born even if they have not been sprinkled with clarified butter. (5.25)
Thus has been declared in its entirety what is edible and what is inedible for the twice-born;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.

One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas, or when one is engaged according to the rule [in a sacrifice], or indeed when there is a danger to life. (5.27)
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa); both the stationary and the moving—all is the sustenance of the vital breath. 5.28
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs; the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave. (5.29)
The eater is not defiled by eating the creatures that are his food, even day after day; for both the eaters and the creatures to be eaten were created by the Creator himself. (5.30)
"The eating of meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine rule; any practice other than this is called the demonic rule. (5.31)
Having purchased it oneself, or having produced it, or even having received it from another, one does not incur fault by eating meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors. (5.32)
A twice-born man who knows the law should not eat meat contrary to the rule when he is not in distress;
for by eating meat contrary to the rule, he becomes a ghost and is helplessly devoured by those very creatures. (5.33)
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as grave as that of one who eats meat in vain after death. (5.34)
But that man who, though duly appointed according to the rule, does not eat meat, goes after death to the state of a beast for twenty-one births. (5.35)
A Brahmin should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, abiding by the eternal rule, he may eat those consecrated with mantras. (5.36)
In times of distress, one may perform a sacrifice with clarified butter as the victim, or likewise with a victim made of flour;
but one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body, so many times does the one who slaughters animals in vain undergo death after death in successive births. (5.38)
Animals were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world. Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing. (5.39)
Herbs, animals, trees, crawling creatures, and likewise birds, having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher rebirths once again. (5.40)
"Manu has declared that animals may be slain only in the offering of honey-mixture (madhuparka), in sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods; not elsewhere. (5.41)
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, when killing animals for these purposes, leads both himself and the animals to the highest state. (5.42)
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress. (5.43)
One should know that the violence ordained by the Vedas, which is restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings, is indeed non-violence; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, whether he is alive or even dead. (5.45)
He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage and death, seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness. (5.46)
Whatever he meditates upon, whatever he does, and wherever he fixes his delight—that he attains without effort, provided that he harms nothing at all. (5.47)
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat. (5.48)
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should abstain from the eating of all meat. (5.49)
He who does not eat meat, even while disregarding the [prescribed] rule like a Piśāca, becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases. (5.50)
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it—all these are slayers. (5.51)
There is no doer of unmeritorious deeds greater than he who, without having honored the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another. (5.52)
He who should perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years, and he who does not eat meat—the merit and fruit of these two are equal. (5.53)
One does not obtain that fruit by eating pure fruits and roots, nor by consuming the foods of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat. (5.54)
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world;
the wise declare this to be the 'meat-ness' of meat. (5.55)
There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; for these are the natural inclinations of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit. (5.56)
I shall now declare the purification for the deceased as well as the purification of objects, for all four castes, duly and in their proper order. (5.57)

When a child has teethed, when it has been named, or when its tonsure ceremony has been performed, all the relatives remain impure upon its death; the same is declared regarding birth-impurity (sūtaka). (5.58)
Impurity on account of a death is prescribed for ten days among the sapindas;
it may last for three days or even one day until the collection of the bones has taken place. (5.59)
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person; however, the status of being a samānodaka (a kinsman by water) persists as long as there is knowledge of the birth and the name. 5.60.
In the case of birth as well, it should be exactly the same; however, the *sūtaka* (impurity) belongs to both the mother and the father.
The *sūtaka* belongs to the mother alone, while the father becomes pure by performing ritual ablution (*upaspṛśya*).
But a man who has emitted semen becomes pure simply by performing ritual ablution after casting it out.
Due to the connection through the seed, one should observe the impurity for three days. 5.63.
Those who touch a corpse are purified in one day and night, or even in three periods of three nights; however, those who offer water for the deceased are purified after three days.
But when his guru has died, the disciple should perform the funeral rites for the ancestors;
he becomes pure there after ten nights together with those who consume the food offered to the deceased. ||5.65||
In the case of a miscarriage, a woman is purified in as many nights as there were months of pregnancy;
when her menstrual flow has ceased, a virtuous woman who is menstruating becomes pure by means of a bath. (5.66)
For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, impurity is declared to last for one night;
but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights. (5.67)
Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside, having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones. (5.68)
For him, no funeral rites with fire should be performed, nor should the water-libation be offered;
having abandoned him like a log in the forest, one should simply pass three days [in mourning]. (5.69)
The water-rite for one who has not reached three years of age should not be performed by his relatives;
however, they may perform it once a tooth has appeared or when the naming ceremony has been completed. (5.70)
For a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin), purification is prescribed after one day has passed;
however, for those who share the same funeral water (ekodaka) upon birth, purity is held to occur after three nights. ||5.71||
But for female relatives who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, those of the same lineage (sanābhayaḥ) become pure according to the very rule already stated.
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days;
they should not eat meat, and they should sleep separately on the ground. (5.73)
This rule for impurity due to death has been proclaimed for when one is present;
this procedure for relatives and kinsmen is to be understood as applying when one is absent. (5.74)
But he who hears that one residing in a foreign land has died within ten days shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights. (5.75)
If ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed, a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes. ||5.77||
If a child, one residing in another country, or a person belonging to a different family (pṛthakpiṇḍa) has died, one becomes pure immediately by plunging into water along with one's clothes. //5.78//
If death and birth should occur again within ten days, a Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that ten-day period has not yet elapsed. (5.79)
When a teacher has passed away, they say that impurity lasts for three nights;
for his son and for his wife, the rule is that it lasts for one day and night. (5.80)

Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has come to stay with him, he shall remain impure for three nights; likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, he remains impure for a night with its two wings (a pakṣiṇī rātri).
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm must remain impure for as long as the light lasts;
however, if the king is not learned in the Vedas, the impurity lasts for a full day, as does that for a teacher who is well-versed in the scriptures.
A Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kṣatriya in twelve days, a Vaiśya in fifteen days, and a Śūdra is purified in a month. (5.83)
One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one obstruct the rites performed in the sacred fires; and while performing that rite, even a kinsman does not become impure. (5.84)
Having touched a Divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a corpse, or one who has touched a corpse, one becomes pure by bathing. (5.85)
Having sipped water and being purified, he should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to his enthusiasm and *pāvamānī* verses according to his ability. (5.86)
Having touched a human bone that still has fat adhering to it, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of fat, he is purified simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.
One who has been initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
but once it is completed, having offered the water libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone. (5.88)
The water-libation ceremony shall be withheld for those born of improper unions, for those who persist in false ascetic orders, and for those who commit suicide. (5.89)
And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor; ||5.90||
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, the one observing a vow is not deprived of his vow. (5.91)
One should carry out a dead Śūdra by the southern city gate; those of the twice-born castes, however, by the western, northern, or eastern gates, as appropriate. 5.92.
There is no fault of sin for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those engaged in sacrificial sessions; for they always abide in the station of Indra, having become one with Brahman. 5.93
Immediate purification is ordained for a king in his high station;
the reason for this is his seat [of authority], for the sake of protecting his subjects. (5.94)
And for those killed in riots or battles, by lightning or by a sovereign, or for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for whomever the king so desires. ||5.95||
The king bears the body of the eight guardians of the world: Soma, Agni, Arka, Anila, Indra, Vittapati, Appati, and Yama. (5.96)
A king who is empowered by Lokeśa is not subject to ritual impurity;
for the purity and impurity of mortals arise from and dissolve into Lokeśa.
For one slain in accordance with the duty of a Kshatriya by weapons raised in battle, the sacrifice is immediately completed and so too is purification; such is the established rule. (5.98)
A Brahmin becomes pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya by his mount or weapon; a Vaiśya by his goad or reins; and a Śūdra, having performed his duties, by touching a staff. (5.99)
This purification regarding sapinda relatives has been declared to you, O best of the twice-born;
now learn the purification for the dead concerning all non-sapinda relatives. (5.100)
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who was not a relative, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one for the maternal relatives and kinsmen of his mother. (5.101)
If he eats their food, however, he becomes pure in ten days;
if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house.
If one follows out of desire a deceased person, whether a kinsman or even a stranger, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter. 5.103.
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that oblation, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven. (5.104)
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with clay], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents of purification for embodied beings. (5.105)
Among all forms of purity, purity of purpose is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in purpose is truly pure, not he who is merely purified by earth and water. (5.106)
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts by giving;
those whose sins are concealed by silent recitation; and those most learned in the Vedas by austerity. (5.107)

That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current; a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation. 5.108.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. 5.109
This decision regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the determination concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.
For luminous gems, for all things made of stone, and for objects made of metal,
purification has been declared by the wise to consist of ashes, water, and earth.
An unanointed golden vessel is purified by water alone, as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver, provided they are not otherwise tarnished. (5.112)
Gold and silver emerged from the conjunction of fire and water;
therefore, their purification by means of their own source is more effective. 5.113.
The purification of copper, iron, bronze, brass, tin, and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
For all liquid substances, purification is traditionally held to be straining;
for solid objects, it is sprinkling with water; and for wooden items, it is planing.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the purification of the sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand,
while that of the *camasa* cups and the *graha* ladles is by washing.

The purification of the *caru* vessels, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar, is by means of hot water. (5.117)
The purification of large quantities of grain and clothing is performed by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification is prescribed by washing them with water. (5.118)
The purification of skins is like that of cloth, and the same applies to woven articles;
for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is prescribed to be like that of grain. (5.119)
Silk and woolen cloths [are purified] with alkaline salts; blankets of Kutapa wool with Aṛiṣṭaka fruits; fine linen cloth with Bilva fruits; and linen garments with white mustard seeds. (5.120)
For conch shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory, purification should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow's urine or water, just as for linen cloth. (5.121)
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again. (5.122)

The ground is purified by these five means: by sweeping, by smearing with cow-dung, by sprinkling, by scraping, and by the dwelling of cows. [5.124] That which has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or spat upon—
That which is defiled by hair or insects is purified by the scattering of earth. ||5.125||
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impure matter do not depart from an object, so long must earth and water be applied in all cases of purifying substances. (5.126)
The gods have ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word. (5.127)
Water that has reached the ground is pure if it quenches the thirst of a cow, provided it is not contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste. (5.128)
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
almsfood received by a student of sacred knowledge is always pure—this is the settled rule. (5.129)
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game. (5.130)
Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure, as is the flesh of one killed by other carnivorous animals, or by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and other such bandits. (5.131)
Those apertures which are above the navel are entirely pure;
those which are below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body. (5.132)
One should specify that flies, droplets of water, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun, dust, the earth, life-force, and fire are pure to the touch. (5.133)
For the purpose of purification after the voiding of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken in appropriate quantities; likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities. (5.134)
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, snot, nails, phlegm, tears, and rheum from the eyes—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. (5.135)
One application of earth on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand, and seven on both hands should be applied by one desiring purification. (5.136)
This is the rule of purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics. (5.137)
Having voided urine or feces, one who has sipped water for purification should touch the cavities of the head;
likewise always before studying the Veda and while eating food. (5.138)
One desiring bodily purity should first sip water three times and then wipe the mouth twice; however, for women and Śūdras, this should be done once each. (5.139)
For Śūdras who live according to the law, shaving should be performed every month;
their rules for purification are like those of Vaiśyas, and their food consists of the remnants of the twice-born.
The principal [limbs] do not become defiled by food remnants, nor do droplets that fall upon the body;
nor do the beard hairs that enter the mouth, nor what remains stuck between the teeth. (5.141)
Those drops which touch the feet of one who is giving water for sipping to others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. (5.142)
If one who holds an object in his hand is somehow touched by something impure, he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that object down. 5.143.
One who has vomited or been purged should bathe and then consume clarified butter;
one who has eaten food should simply rinse the mouth, while bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse. (5.144)
Having slept, having sneezed, having eaten, having spat, having spoken untruthful words, or having drunk water—one who is about to study should sip water (ācamana), even if he is already pure. 5.145.
This entire rule for purification, as well as the cleansing of objects, has been declared to you for all classes; now learn the duty of women. (5.146)
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an old woman, a woman should not perform any action independently, even within her own home. (5.147)
In childhood she should remain under the authority of her father, in youth under that of her husband;
when her husband has died, she should remain under the authority of her sons; she must never enjoy independence. (5.148)
A woman should not desire separation from her father, her husband, or even her sons;
for by being separated from them, she brings reproach upon both families. (5.149)
She should always be cheerful and skillful in her household duties; she should keep the utensils well-maintained and be not wasteful in her expenditures. (5.150)

To whomsoever her father or her brother—having obtained the father’s consent—may give her, she shall serve him while he lives, and once he has passed away, she must not transgress against him. (5.151)
For their welfare, auspicious rites, benedictions, and sacrifices to Prajāpati are performed at weddings; the giving away [of the bride] is what establishes ownership. (5.152)

A husband who has performed the sacramental rite with mantras, whether during the period of menstruation or at other times, is the constant bestower of happiness upon his wife both in this world and in the next. (5.153)
Whether he be devoid of virtue, addicted to sensual desires, or lacking in good qualities, a husband must always be served by a virtuous wife like a god. (5.154)
For women there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast;
by that service which she renders to her husband, she is glorified in heaven. (5.155)
A virtuous wife, desiring the world of her husband, should do nothing whatsoever unpleasant to her husband, whether he is living or dead. (5.156)
She may indeed emaciate her body with pure flowers, roots, and fruits, but she must not even utter the name of another man once her husband has died. (5.157)
Let her remain patient and self-restrained until death, fixed in the practice of celibacy, desiring that unsurpassed dharma which belongs to women who have but one husband. (5.158)
Many thousands of brahmins who had practiced celibacy from their youth went to heaven without having produced offspring for the continuation of their lineage. (5.159)
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who are lifelong celibates. (5.160)
But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, transgresses against her husband, incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the world of her husband. (5.161)
No offspring born here belongs to anyone other than the father, nor does it belong to another's possession; for virtuous women, a second husband is nowhere ordained. (5.162)
She who, abandoning her own inferior husband, serves a superior man, becomes contemptible in the world and is called one who has had a previous husband. (5.163)
But through infidelity with her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases. (5.164)
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous. (5.165)
By this conduct, a woman who is restrained in mind, speech, and body attains supreme fame in this world and the world of her husband in the next. (5.166)

A twice-born man who knows the law should cause his wife—who is of the same caste, of virtuous conduct, and who dies before him—to be cremated with the *agnihotra* fire and the sacrificial implements. (5.167)
Having given the sacred fires to a wife who has died before him during the funeral rites, he may again perform the marriage ceremony and likewise the re-establishment of the sacred fires. (5.168)
By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
having taken a wife, he should dwell in his house during the second stage of life. (5.169)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

[The Sixth Chapter] Having thus remained in the stage of the householder, a twice-born man who has performed the ceremonial bath according to the rules should dwell in the forest, self-controlled, as prescribed, with his senses subdued. 6.1.
But when a householder perceives his own wrinkles and gray hair, and indeed the offspring of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest. (6.2)
Having completely renounced village food and all personal belongings,
and having entrusted his wife to his sons, he should go to the forest, either alone or with her.
Taking with him the *agnihotra* fire and the implements for the domestic fire, he should depart from the village to the forest and dwell there with his senses restrained. (6.4)
With various kinds of pure food fit for sages, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
he should perform these very great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should wear either a skin or a garment of bark; he should bathe in the evening as well as in the morning;
and he should always maintain his matted locks, beard, body hair, and nails.
From whatever he may eat, he should offer a portion as a bali-oblation and give alms according to his ability;
he should honor those who have come to his hermitage with water, roots, fruits, and alms-food.
One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas, self-controlled, friendly, and composed;
always a giver and never a taker, compassionate toward all living beings. (6.8)
And he should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice pertaining to the three sacred fires according to the rule,
not omitting the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices through the practice of yoga.
He should perform the Ṛkṣeṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices,
as well as the Turāyaṇa and the Dakṣāyaṇa in their proper sequence.
With pure foods fit for sages, gathered by himself during the spring and autumn seasons,
he should separately offer sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and cooked oblations (caru) according to the prescribed rules.
Having offered that most pure forest produce as an oblation to the deities, he should consume the remainder himself, along with salt prepared by his own hand.
One should eat vegetables grown on land or in water, as well as flowers, roots, and fruits produced from pure trees, along with oils derived from fruits.
One should avoid honey, meat, mushrooms growing from the earth,
bhūstṛṇa grass, śigruka, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree.
In the month of Āśvayuja, he should discard the food of sages previously stored, as well as worn-out garments, vegetables, roots, and fruits. (6.15)
One should not eat what has been ploughed by a plowshare, even if it has been abandoned by someone; nor should one eat flowers or fruits grown in a village, even if one is afflicted by hunger. (6.16)
He may eat food cooked by fire, or he may eat only what is ripened by time;
he may be one who grinds with stones, or even one who uses his teeth as a mortar.
He may be one who washes [his bowl] immediately after eating, or one who stores for a month;
he may be one who stores for six months, or even one who stores for a year. (6.18)
One should eat food at night or by day, having obtained it according to one's ability; or one may observe the practice of eating only every fourth mealtime, or even every eighth mealtime.
Or he should conduct himself according to the rules of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance during both the bright and dark fortnights;
or else, at the end of each fortnight, he should eat a single meal of boiled barley-gruel.
Or he may always subsist solely on flowers, roots,
and fruits that have ripened in due time and fallen of their own accord, remaining steadfast in the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas.
He should roll about on the ground or stand on his tiptoes for a day; he should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, approaching water at the times of the three libations.
In summer he should practice the penance of the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in winter, he should wear wet clothes, thus gradually increasing his austerity. (6.23)
Performing ablutions at the three sessions of the day, he should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
practicing most rigorous austerity, he should wither his own body.
Having duly internalized the sacrificial fires within himself,
he should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, a sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Exerting no effort for the sake of pleasures, he was a celibate student who slept upon the ground;
having no sense of "mine" regarding shelters, his dwelling was at the foot of trees.
He should practice the collection of alms for his sustenance only among ascetic Brahmins, and among other twice-born householders who dwell in the forest. (6.27)
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from the village,
receiving them either in the hollow of his hands, in a leaf-cup, or in a potsherd.
Living in the forest, a Brahmin should practice these and other initiations, as well as various Upaniṣadic scriptures, for the sake of self-perfection. (6.29)
These have been practiced by sages and brahmins, as well as by householders, for the sake of increasing knowledge and austerity and for the purification of the body. (6.30)
Or, having taken his stand in the Aparājita posture, he may proceed straight toward the [northeastern] direction, disciplined and subsisting on water and air, until the fall of his body. (6.31)
Having cast off the body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers,
the Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having thus spent the third part of his life in the forests, he should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant during the fourth part of his life. (6.33)
Having gone from stage to stage of life, having offered oblations, having conquered his senses,
and being exhausted by alms and offerings, one who renounces increases after death.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward. (6.35)
Having studied the Vedas according to the prescribed rules, having begotten sons in accordance with dharma,
and having performed sacrifices to the best of one's ability, one should direct the mind toward liberation.
A twice-born man who has studied the Vedas, yet fails to procreate offspring and fails to perform sacrifices, falls downward if he desires liberation. (6.37)
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa should renounce his home and go forth.
For him who, having bestowed fearlessness upon all beings, goes forth from his home, there are worlds consisting of splendor, O teacher of Brahman. (6.39)
Since not even the slightest fear arises for the twice-born from living beings, there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever for him who is liberated from the body. (6.40)
Having gone forth from the home, the sage, purified by his observances, should wander as a mendicant, indifferent even when sensual pleasures are presented to him. 6.41
One should always wander alone for the sake of accomplishment, without a companion; seeing that success belongs to the solitary one, he neither abandons [the path] nor is he abandoned. (6.42)
He should be without fire and without a dwelling; he may resort to a village for the sake of food.
Indifferent, free from accumulation, a sage whose mind is concentrated on the ultimate reality. (6.43)
An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged garments, solitude,
and equanimity toward all things— these are the characteristics of one who is liberated.
One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life; one should simply await the time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages. 6.45
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is purified. (6.46)
One should endure harsh words; one should not despise anyone.
Nor, depending upon this body, should one harbor enmity toward anyone. (6.47)
One should not respond with anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates. (6.48)

Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent to external objects, and free from worldly desires, one who seeks happiness should wander about in this world with the self alone as his companion. (6.49)
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by giving instructions or counsel. (6.50)
One should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants. (6.51)
With his hair, nails, and beard trimmed, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, never causing pain to any living beings.
His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice. (6.53)
The gourd, a wooden bowl, one made of clay, and likewise one made of split bamboo—these, Svāyambhuva Manu declared, are the vessels for ascetics. (6.54)
One should go for alms only once a day and not become attached to abundance;
for a mendicant who is attached to alms becomes attached to sense-objects as well. (6.55)

When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle lies still, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished their meal, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed, the ascetic should always go for alms. (6.56)

He should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should gain delight him; he should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, having emerged from attachment to material requisites. (6.57)
One should utterly despise gains obtained through being honored;
for even a liberated ascetic is bound by gains obtained through being honored. (6.58)
By consuming little food and by staying and sitting in solitude,
one should withdraw the senses that are being carried away by the objects of the senses.
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred, and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality. 6.60
One should contemplate the destinies of men arising from the defects of their actions,
as well as their falling into hell and the torments in the abode of Yama.
Separation from those who are dear, as well as union with those who are unpleasant, being overcome by old age, and being tormented by diseases. (6.62)
The departure from this body, the rebirth in a womb again, and the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of wombs—[all these he beholds]. (6.63)
The conjunction with suffering for embodied beings arises from unrighteousness,
while the inexhaustible union with happiness arises from righteousness and purpose.
And by means of yoga, one should contemplate the subtlety of the Supreme Self, as well as its manifestation within bodies, both high and low. (6.65)
Even if adorned, one should practice the Dharma while dwelling in whatever stage of life;
being equal toward all beings, the external mark is not the cause of righteousness.
Although the fruit of the *kataka* tree clarifies water, the water does not become clear merely by uttering its name. (6.67)
For the sake of protecting living beings, whether by night or by day, he should always walk after scanning the ground, even when his body is exhausted. (6.68)
Whatever living beings a mendicant kills unintentionally by day or by night, for the sake of purifying himself from those [karmas], he should perform six breath-restraints after bathing. (6.69)
Even three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) performed according to rule by a Brahmin,
joined with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, should be known as the supreme austerity.
Just as the impurities of metallic ores are burnt away when they are being smelted, so too are the defects of the senses burnt away through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa). 6.71

One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sin by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā); one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). 6.72.
Through the yoga of meditation, one may perceive the course of this inner self among beings of high and low status— a course that is difficult for those of unrefined soul to understand.
One endowed with right vision is not bound by actions;
but one devoid of vision enters into the cycle of transmigration.
By means of non-violence, detachment from the senses, Vedic rituals,
and the practice of severe austerities, they attain that state in this world.
It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by tendons, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement. (6.76)
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is overwhelmed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent. (6.77)
Just as a tree leaves the riverbank, or as a bird leaves a tree,
so too, abandoning this body, one is released from the crocodile of suffering.
Having cast off both good deeds toward those dear to him and evil deeds toward those unpleasant,
through the yoga of meditation, he attains the eternal Brahman.
When one becomes free from longing for all things through one's inner disposition, then one attains eternal happiness both in this world and after death. (6.80)
By this method, having gradually abandoned all attachments,
one who is liberated from all pairs of opposites abides in Brahman alone.
All this that has been described here is indeed meditative;
for no one who is not a knower of the inner self ever enjoys the fruit of ritual action.
One should constantly recite the Brahman pertaining to sacrifice, as well as that pertaining to the deities, that pertaining to the self, and whatever is declared in the Vedāntas. (6.83)
This is the refuge for the ignorant; this very same is for those who possess knowledge.
This is for those seeking heaven; this is for those seeking the infinite.
The twice-born man who wanders forth as a mendicant according to this sequential method shakes off all evil in this world and attains the supreme Brahman.
This dharma has been taught to you for ascetics of restrained self who have renounced the Vedas; now learn the yoga of action.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder. (6.87)
All these, when practiced in due order according to the scriptures, lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal. (6.88)
Moreover, according to the injunctions of Vedic revelation,
the householder is declared to be the best among all these [stages of life], for he indeed sustains these three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean, even so do all those in the various stages of life find their support in the householder. 6.90
Moreover, by these four classes of twice-born men belonging to the various stages of life, the tenfold dharma must always be practiced with diligent effort. (6.91)
Fortitude, forbearance, self-control, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, wisdom, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma. 6.92
Those brahmins who thoroughly study the ten characteristics of dharma, and having studied them, live in accordance with them, go to the supreme goal. (6.93)
Having practiced the tenfold dharma with a concentrated mind and having heard the Vedāntas according to the injunctions, the twice-born man, free from debts, should renounce the world.
Having renounced all actions and cast off the defects of action, he should dwell happily under the sovereignty of his sons, self-restrained and practicing the study of the Veda. (6.95)
Having thus renounced actions, intent on his own duty and free from desire, he destroys sin through renunciation and attains the supreme goal. (6.96)
This fourfold duty of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you, which yields imperishable fruit after death; now learn the duty of kings.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[The Seventh Chapter] I shall proclaim the duties of kings, how a monarch should conduct himself, how his origin comes about, and how his supreme success is achieved. (7.1)
Having received the Vedic consecration according to the prescribed rule, the Kṣatriya must provide protection for all this [world] in accordance with justice. (7.2)
For when this world was without a king and everyone fled in every direction out of fear, the Lord created a king for the protection of all this. (7.3)
Having extracted eternal portions from Indra, Anila, Yama, and Arka; from Agni and Varuṇa; and indeed from Candra and Vitteśa— 7.4.
Since this king was fashioned from portions of these lords of the gods, he therefore surpasses all beings in splendor. (7.5)
Like the sun, he scorches both eyes and minds;
no one on earth is able even to look upon him. (7.6)
He becomes fire and he becomes wind; he is the sun, he is the moon, and he is the King of Dharma; by his power, he is Kubera, he is Varuṇa, and he is the great Indra.
A ruler of the earth must not be despised even if he is a child, for thinking "he is merely a human being";
for he is a great deity dwelling in human form. (7.8)
Ordinary fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly;
but the fire of a king’s wrath consumes the entire family, along with its livestock and accumulated wealth. (7.9)
Having truly considered the task, his own power, and the place and time,
he repeatedly assumes various forms for the sake of accomplishing dharma.
In whose favor dwells the lotus-goddess Śrī, in whose prowess lies victory,
and in whose anger resides death— for he is composed of all splendor.
But whoever hates him out of delusion will undoubtedly perish;
for the king sets his mind upon that person's swift destruction. (7.12)
Therefore, O lord of men, that dharma which a ruler should establish for those he favors, and that which he establishes for those he disfavors—he should not deviate from that dharma. (7.13)
For its sake, the Lord first created Dharma, his own son, the protector of all beings, the staff consisting of the splendor of Brahman.
Out of fear of him, all beings, both stationary and moving, provide sustenance for his enjoyment and do not deviate from their own duties. //7.15//
Having truly considered the place, the time, the power, and the learning [of those involved], he should appropriately apply [punishment] toward men who act unjustly. (7.16)
That king is the personification of punishment; he is the leader and the ruler, and he is recorded as the guarantor of the dharma of the four stages of life.
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them.
The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be the very law (dharma). 7.18.
When properly supported after careful consideration, he delights all his subjects;
but when applied without due deliberation, he causes destruction on every side. (7.19)
If the king were not to tirelessly administer punishment to those deserving of it, the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit. (7.20)
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake, and likewise a dog might lick the oblation; there would be no ownership in anything at all, and the lower would prevail over the higher. (7.21)
The whole world is kept in check by the rod of punishment, for a man who is pure is hard to find;
indeed, through fear of the rod, the entire world is fit for enjoyment. (7.22)
Even the gods, dānavas, and excellent gandharvas, as well as the rākṣasas, birds, and serpents, are made to serve for one's enjoyment only when oppressed by punishment. (7.23)
All social classes would become corrupt and all moral boundaries would be shattered;
moreover, universal upheaval would arise from the misapplication of punishment. (7.24)
Where the dark-hued, red-eyed Punishment stalks, destroying evil, there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly. (7.25)
They say that the king who is its administrator should be a speaker of truth,
one who acts with circumspection, wise, and skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
A king who administers that [punishment] properly prospers through the three aims of life;
but one who is self-indulgent, unjust, and base is destroyed by that very punishment.
For punishment is indeed a very great power, difficult for those of undisciplined soul to wield;
it destroys the king himself, along with his kinsmen, if he deviates from righteousness.
Then he would afflict the fortresses, the kingdom, and the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.
Thus, he cannot be led by the right path by one who is without a companion, who is deluded, greedy, of unrefined intellect, and attached to the objects of the senses. (7.30)
Punishment can be rightly administered by one who is pure, true to his word, acting in accordance with the scriptures, wise, and well-supported by assistants. (7.31)
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies, straightforward toward friends, and endowed with patience toward Brahmins. (7.32)
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain, his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water. (7.33)
But for a king who acts contrary to this and has not conquered his own self, his fame in the world diminishes like a drop of clarified butter upon water. (7.34)
The king was created as the protector of all the social classes and stages of life, who are established each in their respective duties, in due order. (7.35)
Therefore, whatever must be done by one who protects his subjects along with his retinue,
all that I shall declare to you exactly and in due order.
Having risen in the morning, the king should attend upon the Brahmins;
he should stand by those who are learned and aged in the knowledge of the three Vedas, and abide by their instruction. (7.37)
One should always serve elderly Brahmins who are pure and learned in the Vedas;
for one who constantly serves the elderly is honored even by the Rākṣasas. (7.38)
From them he should constantly learn discipline, even though his own self is already disciplined;
for a king whose self is disciplined never perishes. (7.39)
"Many kings, together with their retinues, have perished through lack of discipline;
yet even those dwelling in the forest have obtained kingdoms through discipline. (7.40)
Vena was ruined through lack of discipline, as were King Nahuṣa, Sudās Paijavana, Sumukha, and Nimi. (7.41)
Pṛthu indeed obtained his kingdom through discipline, as did Manu;
Kubera obtained mastery over wealth, and the son of Gādhi obtained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
From those learned in the three Vedas, he learned the triple knowledge, the eternal science of government,
the science of inquiry, the knowledge of the self, and the practical applications of the arts from the world.
One should apply oneself day and night to the conquest of the senses;
for one who has conquered the senses is able to keep the subjects under control. (7.44)
One should diligently avoid these ten calamities arising from desire, as well as the eight born of anger, for they have miserable ends. ||7.45||
For a lord of the earth who is addicted to vices born of desire is deprived of both wealth and dharma; but one addicted to those born of anger is deprived even of himself. (7.46)
Hunting, gambling, sleeping by day, slander, women, intoxication, the three types of performance (song, dance, and music), and idle wandering—this is the tenfold group born of desire. (7.47)
Slander, violence, malice, envy, detraction, and the spoiling of property, as well as harshness of speech and of punishment—this is the eightfold group born of anger. (7.48)
One should strive with effort to conquer that greed which all poets know to be the root of both these; for both these two groups arise from it.
Drinking, dice, women, and hunting—in this sequence, one should know that this tetrad is the most grievous among the group of vices born of desire. (7.50)
One should always know that this triad—the infliction of punishment, verbal cruelty, and the violation of property—is likewise painful within the group born of anger. (7.51)
A self-possessed person should know that among this group of seven vices, which are everywhere interconnected, each preceding one is more grievous than the one following it. (7.52)
Between calamity and death, calamity is said to be the more grievous;
the one beset by calamity sinks lower and lower, while the one free from calamity goes to heaven even when dead. (7.53)
He should appoint seven or eight ministers who are hereditary, learned in the treatises, brave, skilled in hitting the mark, of noble birth, and thoroughly tested. (7.54)
Even an action that is easy to perform is difficult for one person alone;
how much more so a kingdom of great consequence, especially when undertaken without assistance? (7.55)
Together with them, he should constantly deliberate upon common matters: peace and war, stability, revenue, protection, and the consolidation of what has been acquired. (7.56)
Having ascertained their respective individual intentions,
he should act for his own welfare by attending to the affairs of all of them together.
But with a distinguished, wise Brāhmaṇa,
the king should deliberate upon the supreme counsel concerning the six measures of statecraft.
Always placing his trust in him, he should entrust all affairs to him;
having reached a decision together with him, he should then begin the work. (7.59)
He should also appoint other ministers who are pure, wise, steadfast, thoroughly tested, and capable of properly collecting revenue. (7.60)
He should appoint as many men—vigilant, skillful, and discerning—as are required to carry out his duties. (7.61)
For their sake, he should appoint those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth to the management of the mines;
and those who are pure and timid to the duties within the inner apartments. (7.62)
And he should appoint as his messenger one who is learned in all the scriptures, who understands gestures, facial expressions, and movements, and who is pure, capable, and of noble birth. (7.63)
Devoted, pure, skillful, mindful, and knowing place and time;
handsome, fearless, and eloquent—a messenger such as this is praised by kings. (7.64)

The power of punishment rests with the minister; the administration of discipline depends on punishment; the treasury and the kingdom belong to the king; and peace and its opposite depend upon the envoy. (7.65)
For it is the messenger indeed who unites those who are divided and divides those who are united;
the messenger performs that action by which men are alienated. (7.66)

He should discern, through secret signs, gestures, and movements, the master's facial expression, his inner disposition, his conduct, and what he intends to do regarding his undertakings and toward his servants. (7.67)
Having understood in truth everything intended by the enemy king, he should apply such effort as will not cause harm to himself. (7.68)
One should dwell in a country that is arid yet rich in crops, inhabited mostly by noble people, free from turmoil, delightful, with submissive vassals, and providing a means of livelihood. (7.69)
One should dwell in a city by taking refuge in a desert fort, an earth fort, a water fort, a forest fort, a human fort, or a mountain fort. (7.70)
But with every effort, one should take refuge in a mountain fortress;
for by virtue of its many advantages, the mountain fortress is distinguished above all others.
Among these, the first three are inhabited by wild animals, creatures of holes, and those that move in water; the latter three are inhabited, respectively, by monkeys, humans, and gods. (7.72)
Just as enemies do not harm those who have taken refuge in a fortress, so too do foes not harm a king who has taken refuge in a fortress. (7.73)
A single archer standing upon a rampart can fight a hundred; a hundred can fight ten thousand. Therefore, a fortress is superior. (7.74)
That city shall be well-provided with weapons, wealth, grain, and vehicles; it shall be endowed with brahmins, artisans, machines, fodder, and water. (7.75)
In its center, he should have his own residence constructed—spacious, well-protected against all seasons, bright, and provided with water and trees. (7.76)
Having occupied that [seat], he should marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks, born of a noble family, pleasing, and endowed with beauty and virtue. (7.77)
He should appoint a domestic priest and choose officiating priests; they shall perform for him the domestic rites as well as those pertaining to the sacrificial fires. (7.78)
The king should sacrifice with various rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
and for the sake of dharma, he should bestow enjoyments and wealth upon the brahmins. (7.79)
He should cause the annual tribute to be collected from the kingdom by trusted officials;
he should be devoted to the sacred tradition in this world and behave toward his subjects like a father.
He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the men as they carry out their work for him. (7.81)
Having returned from the teacher’s house, he should be a worshiper of the Brahmins;
for this inexhaustible treasure of the Brahman is ordained for kings. (7.82)
Neither thieves nor enemies carry it off, nor does it perish;
therefore, the king should deposit this inexhaustible treasure with the Brahmins. (7.83)
It overflows not, it does not fail, and it never perishes;
that which is offered into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifices. (7.84)

A gift given to one who is not a Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin it yields a twofold reward; to one who has studied the Veda it yields a thousandfold reward; and to one who has mastered the Vedas it yields an infinite reward. (7.85)
Indeed, depending specifically on the recipient and through faith alone, one obtains the fruit of a gift after death, whether it be small or great. (7.86)
When challenged by those who are his equals, superiors, or inferiors while protecting his subjects, the king, mindful of the duty of a Kshatriya, must not retreat from battle. (7.87)
Not retreating in battles, the protection of subjects, and service to the Brahmins—this is the supreme means for the welfare of kings. (7.88)
In battles, kings who desire to slay one another, fighting with their utmost strength and never turning their backs, go to heaven. (7.89)
While fighting his enemies in battle, he should not strike them with deceptive weapons, nor with barbed missiles, nor with poisoned ones, nor with those whose tips are ablaze with fire. (7.90)
One should not strike one who has climbed onto dry land, nor a eunuch, nor one with palms joined in reverence;
nor one with disheveled hair, nor one who is seated, nor one who says, "I am yours. (7.91)

Not one who is asleep, nor one who has not donned armor, nor one who is naked, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is not fighting, nor one who is looking on, nor one who has encountered another [in combat]. (7.92)

Remembering the dharma of the virtuous, he did not strike one who was suffering from a weapon-wound, nor one who was distressed, nor one who was severely mangled, nor one who was terrified, nor one who had turned away. (7.93)
But he who, out of fear, turns his back in battle and is slain by enemies, takes upon himself whatever evil deed his master has committed. (7.94)
Furthermore, whatever merit he has acquired for the sake of the hereafter, his master takes all of that from him when he is killed while turning back. (7.95)
Chariots, horses, elephants, parasols, wealth, grain, livestock, women, all kinds of goods, and base metals—whatever one conquers belongs to him. (7.96)
And they shall give a share to the king; such is the Vedic revelation.
And the king must give what has been won by the troops as a whole to all the warriors, rather than distributing it individually.
This eternal dharma of the warrior, unadorned by hypocrisy, has been declared; a Kṣatriya, slaying his enemies in battle, should not deviate from this dharma. (7.98)
One should seek to acquire what has not been acquired, protect with effort what has been acquired, increase what has been protected, and bestow what has been increased upon worthy recipients. (7.99)
One should know that this fourfold [dharma] is the means for achieving the goals of human life;
one should perform its constant practice correctly and without sloth. (7.100)

One should seek what is not yet obtained by means of force; one should protect what has been obtained with vigilance; one should increase what has been protected through growth; and one should bestow what has been increased as a gift. (7.101)
He should always have his rod of punishment raised, always display his manly prowess, always keep his secrets concealed, and always seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemy. (7.102)
The entire world trembles before one who constantly holds the rod of punishment uplifted;
therefore, he should bring all beings into subjection by means of that very rod alone. (7.103)
He should conduct himself with complete sincerity and never with deceit; remaining ever well-guarded, he should also recognize the guile employed by his enemy. (7.104)
An enemy should not discover one's own vulnerability, but one should discover the vulnerability of the enemy;
one should hide one's limbs like a tortoise and guard one's own weak points. (7.105)
One should deliberate on matters like a crane, spring forth like a hare, snatch away like a wolf, and exert prowess like a lion. (7.106)
While he is thus victorious, whatever adversaries he may have,
he should bring them all under his control by means of the expedients beginning with conciliation.
If, however, they do not abide by these [admonitions] through the first three expedients, one should bring them under control gradually by force, using punishment alone. (7.108)
Among the four expedients beginning with conciliation, the wise always praise conciliation and force for the constant prosperity of the kingdom. (7.109)
Just as a reaper pulls out the weeds while protecting the grain, so should a king protect his realm and slay those who stand in opposition. 7.110
That king who, out of delusion, exhausts his own kingdom through lack of oversight, shall before long fall from his kingdom and from life itself, along with his kinsmen. (7.111)
Just as the vital breaths of living beings diminish through the emaciation of the body, so too do the vital breaths of kings diminish through the emaciation of the kingdom. 7.112
One should always observe this rule for the consolidation of the kingdom;
for a king whose kingdom is well-consolidated prospers in happiness. (7.113)
He should establish a *gulma* (military outpost) among two, three, or five [villages], as well as among hundreds of villages, for the protection of the kingdom. (7.114)
One should appoint a lord of a village, as well as a lord of ten villages,
a ruler of twenty, a ruler of a hundred, and likewise a lord of a thousand.
The village headman himself should gradually report any faults arising in the village to the lord of ten villages;
the lord of ten should report them to the lord of twenty.
The lord of twenty should report all of that to the lord of a hundred;
the lord of a hundred villages, however, should himself announce it to the lord of a thousand.
Whatever is to be paid daily by the village dwellers to the king—such as food, drink, fuel, and so forth—the village headman shall receive those. (7.118)

The collector of ten villages should enjoy the produce of one village, the collector of twenty villages that of five villages; the superintendent of a hundred villages [should enjoy] a village, and the lord of a thousand [villages], a city.
Indeed, another minister of the king, who is affectionate and vigilant, should oversee their village affairs as well as their private matters. (7.120)
And in every city, he should appoint a single overseer of all affairs, stationed in a high place, formidable in appearance, like a planet among the stars. (7.121)
He himself should always personally inspect them all;
he should thoroughly ascertain their conduct in the realms through spies. (7.122)
For the king's protectors are generally deceitful servants who seize the property of others; from them he must guard these subjects. (7.123)
Those of evil intent who would grasp only the literal meaning of the verses, the king, having confiscated all their property, should banish them. (7.124)
He should provide daily maintenance for women and servants engaged in royal service, according to their rank and the nature of their work. (7.125)
A paṇa should be given as wages for the lowest servant, and six for the highest;
likewise, food and clothing every six months, and one droṇa of grain every month. (7.126)

Having carefully considered the buying and selling, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of acquisition and preservation, the king should cause merchants to pay taxes. (7.127)
Just as the king and the doer of deeds are joined with their respective fruits,
so should the king, having duly considered this, always apportion taxes within his realm.
Just as water-creatures, young calves, and bees consume their food little by little, so should the king take from his kingdom an annual tax that is small and small. (7.129)
The king shall take one-fiftieth as tax on cattle and gold;
one-eighth, one-sixth, or even one-twelfth on grain. (7.130)
Furthermore, he may take a sixth part of trees, meat, honey, and clarified butter;
and of perfumes, medicinal herbs, juices, flowers, roots, and fruits.
And for leaf-vegetables, grasses, hides, and split-bamboo articles, as well as for earthenware vessels and everything made of stone. || 7.132 ||
Even when dying, a king must not take a tax from a learned Brahmin (śrotriya),
nor should a learned Brahmin living in his realm suffer from hunger.
In whose kingdom a learned man of sacred knowledge perishes from hunger, his entire realm likewise perishes from that hunger before long. (7.134)
Having ascertained his learning and conduct, the king should provide him with a righteous livelihood;
he should protect him in every way, just as a father protects his own biological son. (7.135)
Whatever dharma he performs day by day while being protected by the king, by that the king’s lifespan, wealth, and kingdom increase. (7.136)
Whatever little one might cause to be paid annually under the designation of "tax" to the common people living by trade within the kingdom, that the king [should take]. (7.137)
The lord of the earth should cause artisans, craftsmen, and Śūdras who subsist by their own labor to perform work for one day each month. (7.138)
One should not, out of excessive greed, cut off one's own root nor that of others;
for by cutting off one's own root, one would afflict both oneself and them. (7.139)
A lord of the earth should be both severe and mild, having regard for what must be done;
indeed, a king who is both severe and mild becomes esteemed.
When weary from overseeing the affairs of men, he should appoint to that seat a chief minister who knows the Dharma, is wise, self-controlled, and of noble birth. (7.141)
Having thus performed all these duties of his own, he should protect these subjects, remaining both disciplined and vigilant. (7.142)
He from whose kingdom the subjects are carried off by bandits while they cry out for help—even as he looks on, along with his servants—he is dead; he does not truly live. (7.143)
The supreme duty of a Kṣatriya is indeed the protection of his subjects;
for a king who enjoys the prescribed fruits of his office is joined with righteousness through that very act.
Having risen during the last watch of the night, having performed his purifications and composed himself,
and having offered oblations into the fire and honored the Brahmins, he should enter the auspicious assembly hall.
Remaining there, he should bid farewell to all his subjects after greeting them;
and having dismissed all his subjects, he should deliberate together with his ministers.
Having ascended to a mountain ridge or a palace, or having gone to a secluded place,
or in a forest free from undergrowth, one should deliberate in secret, unobserved.
That king who, though lacking a treasury, enjoys the entire earth, while ordinary people, having come together, do not know his secret counsel. (7.148)
At the time of reciting the mantra, one should remove those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, or deaf; animals; those advanced in age; women; barbarians; the diseased; and the deformed. (7.149)
Those who are despised, as well as animals, and especially women, betray a secret; therefore, one should be cautious in that regard. (7.150)
At midday or at midnight, being rested and free from fatigue, one should contemplate virtue, pleasure, and wealth, either alone or together with them. (7.151)
The acquisition of those things that are mutually contradictory, the giving away of daughters in marriage, and the protection of sons. || 7.152 ||
The dispatching of messengers, as well as the remaining tasks to be performed,
the movements within the inner apartments, and the activities of the secret agents.
He should understand in truth the entire eightfold business and the five classes [of officials], as well as loyalty and disloyalty and the conduct of the circle of states. (7.154)
He should diligently investigate the conduct of the middle king, the activities of the one seeking conquest, the movements of the neutral king, and those of the enemy. (7.155)
In brief, these constituent elements are the root of the circle;
eight others are also enumerated, and thus they are traditionally remembered as twelve.
The five others known as ministers, the realm, the treasury, the purpose, and punishment—each of these has been described; in brief, they number seventy-two. (7.157)
One should know the enemy and likewise one who serves the enemy; next to the enemy is the friend, and beyond those two is the neutral party. (7.158)
He should win them all over by means of conciliation and the other expedients,
whether employed individually or collectively, through personal prowess and through statesmanship.
One should always deliberate upon the six measures of policy: peace, war, marching, halting, dividing the army, and seeking refuge. (7.160)
Having considered the matter at hand, he should employ sitting idle, marching, making peace, waging war, dividing his forces, or seeking refuge. (7.161)
A king should know that alliance and war are each of two kinds, as well as marching and sitting encamped, as well as the double policy and seeking refuge. (7.162)

When the undertaking is common to both parties, and likewise when it is the opposite, then that peace treaty should be known as having two characteristics, being connected with future consequences. (7.163)

War is declared to be of two kinds: that undertaken by oneself for the sake of one's own purpose, either out of season or at the proper time, and that waged against a friend who has committed an offense. || 7.164 ||
When an urgent matter has arisen by chance, marching alone or in alliance with a friend is said to be the two kinds of expedition. (7.165)

When one's own power has gradually diminished, whether due to fate or by one's own past actions, or out of consideration for a friend—these are recorded as the two types of neutrality (āsana). (7.166)
The maintenance of both the army and the master for the sake of accomplishing the task is declared to be of two kinds as "duplicity" by those who know the qualities of the sixfold policy. (7.167)
Seeking refuge with the virtuous for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose when oppressed by enemies is considered to be of two kinds. (7.168)
When one perceives that one's own superiority in the future is certain, while the suffering in the present is slight, then one should resort to peace. (7.169)
When he considers all his subjects to be exceedingly joyful and himself likewise highly exalted, then he may consider war. (7.170)
When he perceives his own army to be joyful and well-nourished in spirit, while that of the enemy is the opposite, then he should march against the foe. (7.171)
But when he is depleted of both mounts and troops, then he should remain diligent, conciliating the enemy with gifts. (7.172)
When the king considers his enemy to be stronger in every respect, then, having divided his army into two parts, he should accomplish his own purpose. (7.173)
But when he becomes most vulnerable to the forces of the enemy, then he should quickly seek refuge with a righteous and powerful king. (7.174)
One should always serve with every effort that man who subdues both his own subjects and the enemy's forces, just as one would a teacher. (7.175)
If he should perceive even there a fault arising from seeking refuge, he should engage in fair combat itself without hesitation. (7.176)
A king who understands policy should employ every means such that his friends, neutrals, and enemies do not become superior to him. (7.177)
One should examine the present state of all future undertakings, as well as the merits and defects of all past ones, according to their true nature. (7.178)
One who knows the merits and defects regarding the future, who makes swift decisions in the present, and who understands the remaining tasks from the past, is not overcome by enemies. (7.179)
He should arrange everything in such a way that friends, neutrals, and enemies do not overcome him; this is the summary of political strategy. 7.180.
But when the lord intends to set out toward the enemy's kingdom, he should then proceed slowly toward the enemy's city according to this following rule: 7.181.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the lord of the earth should set out on his journey;
or else, according to his strength, during the months of Phālguna or Caitra. (7.182)
Moreover, at other times as well, when he perceives certain victory, he should march forth after declaring war, or when a calamity has arisen for the enemy. (7.183)
Having performed the ritual arrangements at the base according to the rules, as well as those for the journey, and having secured a dwelling place and properly stationed spies; (7.184)
Having cleared the three types of roads and his own sixfold forces, he should advance slowly toward the enemy's city according to the rules for a protracted campaign. (7.185)
One should be especially vigilant regarding a friend who serves the enemy and one who remains hidden;
likewise, one who has gone and returned is an even more grievous foe. (7.186)
He should march along that path in the staff-array, or the wagon-array, or the boar-array, the crocodile-array, the needle-array, or the garuḍa-array. (7.187)
From whichever direction he anticipates danger, there he should extend his forces;
and he himself should always take up his position in the lotus formation. 7.188.
The commander-in-chief and the chief of the army should station themselves in all directions;
and from whichever direction he suspects danger, he should designate that as the eastern quarter. (7.189)
And he should station trusted men as outposts on all sides—men skilled in both their positions and in combat, who are fearless and steadfast. (7.190)
One should cause a small number of troops to fight in a compact formation, while a large number may be deployed at will;
having arrayed them in the needle or thunderbolt formations, one should cause them to fight.
One should fight with chariots and horses on level ground; likewise, with boats and elephants in marshy terrain;
with bows in places covered by trees and shrubs; and with swords, shields, and other weapons on firm ground. (7.192)
He should cause the Kaurukṣetras, the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, and those born in Śūrasena—men who are both tall and short—to fight in the vanguard ranks. (7.193)
Having arrayed his army, he should gladden it and examine them thoroughly;
he should also discern the movements of his enemies as they fight. (7.194)
Having besieged the enemy, he should remain there and harass his kingdom;
he should constantly corrupt his supplies of fodder, food, water, and fuel. (7.195)
He should break down the tanks as well as the walls and moats; he should launch a surprise assault upon him at night and likewise terrify him. (7.196)
He should instigate those who can be sowed with discord, and he should remain aware of their actions;
when fate is favorable, he who desires victory should fight, free from fear. (7.197)
One should strive to conquer enemies through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension—either collectively or individually—but never by means of war. (7.198)
Since victory is seen to be uncertain for two combatants, and defeat likewise in battle, one should therefore avoid war. (7.199)
When even the three previously mentioned expedients have been exhausted, he should fight with such diligence that he may conquer his enemies. (7.200)
Having conquered, he should worship the gods and righteous Brahmins;
he should grant exemptions and proclaim amnesties of safety. (7.201)
But having understood the intended purpose of all these people in brief, he should install a member of their own lineage there and establish a formal covenant. (7.202)
And one should establish authoritative standards for their duties as they have been declared;
and one should honor him with jewels, together with the principal men. (7.203)
Taking what is not given causes displeasure, while giving causes pleasure;
therefore, the timely acquisition of desired objects is highly praised. (7.204)
All this action is dependent upon the two ordinances, the divine and the human;
of these two, the divine is indeed inconceivable, but in the human there exists effort. (7.205)
Or, being prepared, he may even march together with him after carefully concluding a treaty, perceiving the threefold fruit consisting of an ally, gold, or land. (7.206)
Having observed the seizing of the rear and likewise the cry within the circle, one shall obtain the fruit of the expedition from either a friend or even an enemy. (7.207)
A king does not prosper so much by the acquisition of a land of gold as he does by gaining a firm friend who, though currently weak, is capable of future success. (7.208)
A friend who knows the dharma, is grateful, and is naturally contented; one who is devoted, steadfast in his undertakings, and light-hearted—such a friend is highly praised. (7.209)
The wise say it is difficult to find an enemy who is wise, of noble birth, brave, skillful, generous, grateful, and steadfast. (7.210)
Nobility, knowledge of men, heroism, and a sense of compassion; constant magnanimity and the arising of the qualities of one who remains impartial—[these are his traits]. (7.211)
A king should, without hesitation, abandon even land that is secure, always productive of crops, and conducive to the increase of cattle, for his own sake. (7.212)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
but one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (7.213)
