Having closely observed all calamities that have arisen together, the wise man should employ every means, both those joined with [favorable conditions] and those separated from them. (7.214)
Relying upon these three—the practitioner, the practice to be undertaken, and all the means in their entirety—one should strive for the accomplishment of the self. (7.215)
Thus, having deliberated on all this with his ministers, the king, after exercising and bathing at midday, should proceed to the inner apartments to eat. (7.216)

There, having thoroughly examined the food and other edibles with attendants who are like his own self, who know the proper time, and who cannot be led astray, he should eat it while reciting mantras that neutralize poison. (7.217)
One should neutralize all his substances with anti-poisonous medicines;
and being self-controlled, he should always wear red, anti-poisonous amulets. (7.218)
And women who have been thoroughly examined, purified by their dress and ornaments, and composed in mind, should touch him with fans, water, and incense. (7.219)
One should exert effort in this way regarding vehicles, beds, seats, and food, as well as in bathing, grooming, and all forms of personal adornment. (7.220)
Having eaten, he should indeed divert himself with the women in the inner apartments;
and having diverted himself at the proper time, he should again attend to his duties. (7.221)
And having adorned himself, he should inspect the armed men once more, as well as all the mounts, weapons, and ornaments. (7.222)
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should remain armed within his inner apartments and listen to the reports of those who disclose secrets and the activities of his spies.
Having gone to another chamber and dismissed those people, he should enter the inner apartments again, surrounded by women, for the purpose of eating. (7.224)
Having eaten there again a little, gladdened by the sounds of musical instruments, he should go to rest at the proper time and rise with his fatigue dispelled. (7.225)
A healthy lord of the earth should carry out this conduct;
however, when unwell, he should entrust all of this to his servants.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[The Eighth Chapter] But the king, desiring to examine legal cases, shall enter the court modestly, accompanied by Brāhmaṇas as well as ministers who are experts in counsel. 8.1.
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and being modest in dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal affairs of the litigants. 8.2.
Day by day, [these stories] were composed separately according to eighteen different paths, based on reasons observed in the world and observed in the scriptures. (8.3)
Of these, the first is non-payment of debt; then deposit, sale without ownership, joint enterprise, and the non-delivery of what has been given. (8.4)
Non-payment of wages, breach of contract, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between owners and herdsmen; 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes, verbal and physical assault, theft, violence, and the abduction of women; 8.6.
The duties of women and men, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—these eighteen topics constitute the basis for legal procedure here. (8.7)
In these matters, for men who are mostly engaged in disputes, one should determine the outcome of the case by resorting to the eternal dharma. ||8.8||
But when the king himself does not personally attend to the administration of justice,
then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee the legal proceedings.
Surrounded by three members of the assembly, he should examine his legal cases, having entered the foremost court and being either seated or standing. (8.10)
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together with a learned minister of the king, they know that assembly to be a *brahma-sabhā*. 8.11.
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly, and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (8.12)
One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is righteous; by neither speaking nor speaking falsely, a man becomes a sinner. (8.13)
Where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while the members of the assembly look on, there they too are slain. (8.14)
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, one must not violate Dharma, lest Dharma, being violated, slay us. (8.15)
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed a bull; the gods know him who treats that Dharma with contempt as a *vṛṣala* (outcaste). Therefore, one should not violate the Dharma. 8.16.
Dharma alone is the true friend that follows one even unto death;
for everything else goes to destruction along with the body. (8.17)
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness, one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king. ||8.18||
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the court are released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (8.19)
One who lives merely by his birth may, if he so desires, be called a "Brahmin" [in name];
however, a Śūdra can never be the expounder of dharma to a king. (8.20)
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow sinking in the mud while onlookers look on. (8.21)
That kingdom which is mostly composed of Śūdras, overrun by nihilists, and devoid of the twice-born, quickly perishes entirely, afflicted by famine and disease. (8.22)
Having occupied the Dharma-seat, with his body properly covered and his mind composed, he should bow to the world-protectors and begin the judicial investigation of cases. (8.23)
Having understood both the beneficial and the harmful, as well as dharma and adharma alone, he should examine all the cases of litigants according to the order of their castes. (8.24)
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
by their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, eyes, and movements. (8.25)
By means of outward forms, gestures, gait, movements, and speech, as well as by changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived. (8.26)
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor until he has returned from his teacher’s house or until he has passed his childhood. (8.27)

The same protection should be afforded to those who have daughters who are widows, to those whose families have perished, to women devoted to their husbands, to widows, and to those who are afflicted by illness. (8.28)
But if their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still living, the righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment prescribed for thieves. 8.29.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that period, the king shall take it. 8.30.
He who says "this is mine," when questioned according to the rule, deserves that property as its owner, provided he correctly identifies its form, number, and other characteristics. (8.31)
He who falsely reports the place, time, caste, appearance, and size of a lost article in its true nature deserves a fine equal to the value of that article. (8.32)
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth part, or even a tenth or a twelfth, of goods lost and then recovered. (8.33)
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
any thieves the king may catch therein, he shall cause to be executed by an elephant.
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it. (8.35)
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth, or a smaller fraction calculated according to the value of that very deposit. (8.36)
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited, may take it entirely, for he is the master of all. (8.37)
But whatever ancient treasure a king may discover buried in the earth, he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury. (8.38)
For the king is indeed the lord of the earth; by guarding the ancient treasures and the mineral ores within the soil, he receives half the share. (8.39)
The king must restore to people of all castes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.40)
One who knows the law, having carefully considered the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should establish the specific duty (svadharma) [of each]. 8.41
Even when they are far away, those men who perform their own duties and remain steadfast in their respective tasks become dear to the world. (8.42)
The king himself shall not initiate a legal case, nor shall his official;
nor shall he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another. (8.43)
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king trace the path of dharma through inference. 8.44
Abiding by the rules of legal procedure, he should examine the truth, the matter at hand, himself, the witnesses, the place, the time, and the form of the case. (8.45)
Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, that one should establish as long as it is not in conflict with the customs of one's country, family, and caste. (8.46)
When urged by a creditor for the sake of recovering his debt from a debtor, the king shall cause the debtor to pay the amount established as due to the creditor. (8.47)
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth, by those very means he should, having won over the debtor, compel him to pay. 8.48.
One should recover a debt through legal process, through trickery, through customary conduct, and by force as the fifth means. (8.49)
If a creditor recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means, he must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own. (8.50)
But one who denies the debt when it has been proven by evidence shall be made to pay the creditor's claim and a small fine according to his ability. (8.51)
When the debtor denies the debt in the assembly after being told "Pay it," the complainant must point out the place [of the transaction] or cite another means of proof. (8.52)
He who gives false testimony, he who, having testified, retracts his statement, and he who does not understand the contradictory meanings of what precedes and follows; ||8.53||
Furthermore, he who, having stated what was to be stated, subsequently evades it;
and who, when questioned about a matter properly set forth, does not accept it. (8.54)
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer when questioned, or he who runs away; 8.55.

If, when told "Speak!", he does not speak, or if he speaks but fails to clarify what has been said, or if he cannot discern the consistency between what precedes and what follows, he is defeated on that point. (8.56)

Having said, "There are witnesses who know [the facts] concerning me," if one who is established in dharma does not point them out when told to do so, one should declare him to be defeated on these grounds. (8.57)
If the plaintiff does not speak, he shall be punished with death according to the law;
if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated.
Whatever amount of wealth one may conceal, or whatever amount one may falsely claim, both of those ignorant of dharma shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount. (8.59)

But one who, having been questioned, denies [the debt] while his status as a debtor has been established by a creditor seeking his wealth, must be judged by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas. (8.60)
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be appointed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them. (8.61)

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, are fit to give testimony when summoned for the sake of the matter; but no others whatsoever are so fit, except in times of emergency. (8.62)
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be made witnesses in legal matters;
those who know all the laws and are free from greed should be appointed, while the opposite should be avoided. (8.63)

One should not employ those who have a financial interest, nor those who are trustworthy, nor companions, nor enemies; nor those whose faults are known, nor those afflicted by disease, nor those who are corrupt. (8.64)
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments. (8.65)
Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts;
neither an old man, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties. (8.66)
Neither one who is afflicted, nor intoxicated, nor insane; neither one tormented by hunger and thirst, nor oppressed by fatigue, nor distressed by desire, nor angry, nor even a thief. ||8.67||
Women shall give evidence for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men; virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes. (8.68)
But whoever is an eyewitness may give testimony for litigants in the case of a matter within a house, in a forest, or in the event of injury to the body. (8.69)
In the absence of a woman, the task may be performed by a child, an elderly person, a pupil, a relative, a slave, or even a hired servant. (8.70)
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick who speak falsely in witness-depositions is unstable, as is the speech of those with overexcited minds. (8.71)
In all cases of violence, theft, and adultery, as well as in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely. (8.72)

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, the king should accept the majority; but if they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and if there is a conflict even among those distinguished by virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.
Testimony is established by seeing or hearing in person;
a witness who speaks the truth therein does not fall away from dharma or worldly prosperity. (8.74)
A witness who speaks falsely in an assembly of noble men about anything other than what was seen or heard goes headlong to hell after death and is excluded from heaven. (8.75)
Even where one has not been formally appointed, if one should see or hear anything at all, even when questioned there, one should speak it exactly as seen and exactly as heard. (8.76)

A single witness who is free from greed may be accepted, but not women, even if they are many and pure; for the intellect of women is unstable, and others as well who are tainted by defects [should not be witnesses]. (8.77)
Whatever they may say by their very nature should be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is meaningless. (8.78)
When the witnesses have arrived in the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, the judge shall interrogate them, consoling them with this following procedure: || 8.79 ||
"Whatever you two know to have been done between yourselves regarding this matter, tell me all of it truthfully; for you are the witnesses here. (8.80)
A witness who speaks the truth in testimony attains abundant worlds;
and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this word is honored by Brahmā.
Speaking falsehood in testimony, one is bound tightly by the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred lifetimes, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony. (8.82)
A witness is purified by truth; righteousness increases through truth.
Therefore, witnesses must indeed speak the truth among all social classes. (8.83)
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self.
Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men. (8.84)
Evil-doers think, "No one sees us"; yet the gods see them, as does the inner person within themselves. 8.85
Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, sun, fire, Yama, wind, night, the two twilights, and Dharma are the witnesses of the conduct of all embodied beings. (8.86)

In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either northward or eastward. (8.87)
One should ask a Brāhmaṇa, "Speak"; a king, "Speak the truth"; a Vaiśya, with [threats of] cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, with these [same] crimes. (8.88)

Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the killer of women and children, and for the betrayer of friends and the ungrateful—those shall be yours if you speak falsely. (8.89)
"Whatever merit you have accumulated since birth, O Bhadra, it would all go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise. (8.90)
O virtuous one, as for this notion of yours that "I am alone," this sage who observes merit and demerit is ever-present within your heart. (8.91)
The god Yama Vaivasvata who dwells here within your heart—if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the Kuru land. (8.92)
Shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty, and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar. (8.93)
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner fall into hell, who, when questioned regarding the determination of dharma, speaks falsely in reply. (8.94)
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man. (8.95)
For the gods know no other man in this world to be more excellent than that learned man whose inner self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), has no suspicion regarding his speech. 8.96
Listen, O gentle one, in due order, to the number of kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony in each case. (8.97)
One kills five by lying about cattle, one kills ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and one kills a thousand by lying about men. (8.98)
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those already born and those yet unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak a falsehood concerning land. (8.99)
Regarding women's enjoyment and sexual intercourse, as well as aquatic gems and all those made of stone, they say: "It is like [the nature of] water on earth. (8.100)
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth, speak the truth directly, exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen. (8.101)
One should treat Brahmins who are cattle-herders, merchants, artisans, actors, servants, or usurers as Śūdras. (8.102)
A man who speaks thus regarding matters of dharma, even if he knows otherwise, does not fall from heaven; they call that the speech of the gods. (8.103)

In cases where the death penalty would otherwise be prescribed for a Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Brāhmaṇa due to the telling of the truth, one must speak an untruth; for that is superior to the truth. (8.104)
And they should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial offerings of cooked rice (caru) dedicated to the goddess of speech, thereby effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood. 8.105.
Or he should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the rule with *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses;
or he should offer it with the verse beginning "ud" (*ud u tyam*), or with the three-verse hymn addressed to the Waters (*abdavatya*).

If a man who is not ill fails to give testimony regarding a debt or other such matters within three fortnights, he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth from all sources. ||8.107||
If, within seven days of the testimony being given, a witness suffers from disease, fire, or the death of a relative, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine. (8.108)

But in matters concerning which there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another, if he cannot discover the truth in its actual state, he should cause it to be established even by means of an oath. 8.109.
Great ṛṣis and gods have taken oaths for the sake of their purposes;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before King Paijavana.
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death. (8.111)
In matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cows, fuel, and assistance rendered to Brahmins, there is no sin in taking an oath. (8.112)
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by his cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all the heinous sins.
Or he may cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or he may have him touch the heads of his sons and wife individually. (8.114)
He whom kindled fire does not burn, whom water does not cause to float up, and who does not quickly meet with misfortune—he should be known as pure in his oath. 8.115
For in the past, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother, the fire—the spy of the world—did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness. (8.116)
In whatever legal dispute false testimony has been given, that very case shall be reversed; even if it has been decided, it shall be as if it were never decided. (8.117)
Testimony is declared to be false when given out of greed, delusion, fear, friendship, lust, anger, as well as from ignorance or childishness. (8.118)
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony in any of these cases. (8.119)

For taking [something] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first *sāhasa* fine; for out of fear, two middle *sāhasa* fines; and for out of friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*. (8.120)
Ten times more [severe] than desire is the former [retribution], but three times more than anger is the latter;
from ignorance there are two full hundreds, but from childishness there is only one hundred.
The wise have declared these penalties for false testimony, intended to ensure that justice does not fail and to restrain unrighteousness. (8.122)
A righteous king, having punished them with a fine, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu, the son of the Self-existent, has declared ten places for punishment; these may be applied to the three social orders, but a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt. (8.124)
The genitals, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body. (8.125)

Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature, and having considered both the capacity [of the offender] and the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. (8.126)
Unjust punishment in this world destroys one's reputation and ruins one's fame; it also prevents access to heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it. 8.127
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it, incurs great infamy and goes to hell. (8.128)
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of public reproach;
thirdly, the punishment of a fine, and after that, the punishment of corporal punishment. (8.129)
But when he is unable to restrain them even by execution, then he may employ all these four measures against them. (8.130)
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold that are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transactions. (8.131)
When the sun shines through a lattice, that subtle particle of dust which is seen is declared to be the first of all measurements, the *trasareṇu*. (8.132)
Eight *trasareṇus* should be known as one *likṣā* in measurement;
three of those [likṣās] are a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those are a *gaurasarṣapa*. (8.133)
Six mustard seeds make one middle-sized barleycorn; three barleycorns make one *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *suvarṇa*. (8.134)
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together should be known as one silver *māṣaka*. (8.135)
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* shall be one *purāṇa*; furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, or a *paṇa*. (8.136)
Ten *dharaṇas* should be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* should be understood by its measure as consisting of four *suvarṇas*.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement; five hundred should be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest. (8.138)
When a debt is admitted as due, one deserves a fine of five percent; if it is denied, that fine shall be doubled—such is the ordinance of Manu. (8.139)
A moneylender may stipulate an interest that increases his wealth as ordained by Vasiṣṭha;
he may take one-eightieth part of a hundred per month. (8.140)
Remembering the duty of the virtuous, he may take two percent;
for by taking two percent, he does not become a sinner regarding wealth. (8.141)
One may take interest at the rate of two, three, four, five, or ten percent per month, according to the order of the social classes. (8.142)
But one shall not receive interest on a secured loan if it is accompanied by a benefit;
nor, due to the lapse of time, may there be the alienation or sale of the pledge. (8.143)
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value, otherwise he becomes a thief of the pledge. (8.144)
Both an open pledge and a sealed deposit ought not to suffer the lapse of time;
if they remain for a long duration, both may be forfeited. (8.145)
Things enjoyed with mutual affection never perish:
a cow, a camel, a draft horse, and any animal employed as a beast of burden. (8.146)
Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while remaining silent in its presence, he does not deserve to recover it. (8.147)
If he is not an idiot and not a minor, and his property is enjoyed by another through legal transaction, that enjoyer deserves the wealth as it was consumed. (8.148)
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, the property of the king, and the property of a Vedic scholar do not perish through adverse possession. (8.149)
The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must relinquish half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment. ||8.150||
Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double the principal;
for grain, fodder, wool, and beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount. (8.151)
An interest exceeding the legal rate is not permitted;
they call that the path of usury, for it is held that five percent is the maximum one may claim. (8.152)

One should not take back interest exceeding that of a year, nor that which is not sanctioned; likewise, compound interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, and corporeal interest [are forbidden]. (8.153)
He who is unable to pay a debt and wishes to make a new agreement shall, after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the contract. (8.154)
Without showing the gold, he may exchange it right there; he ought to pay back as much interest as has accrued. (8.155)
One who has ascended to the increase of the wheel, established in the proper place and time, will not obtain that fruit if he transgresses the requirements of place and time. (8.156)
Those skilled in sea voyages, who perceive the proper place, time, and purpose, establish whatever profit there may be; that constitutes the attainment in that case. (8.157)
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance, he shall pay that person’s debt from his own property if he fails to produce him. (8.158)
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous debt, what is owed for gambling or liquor, or the remainder of a fine or a tax. (8.159)
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
however, if the surety for payment has died, the judge shall compel even the heirs to pay. (8.160)
Furthermore, when the debtor has not paid, the creditor may seek the debt from the surety once the nature of the obligation is known;
but if the surety dies afterwards, by what means could he seek it? (8.161)
But if the surety has been designated as having sufficient wealth, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one who has been designated. (8.162)

A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by disease, or dependent, or by a child, or by an elderly person, or one that is invalidly executed, is not valid. (8.163)
A speech does not become true even if it is well-established, if it speaks of things external to the fixed, conventional nature of phenomena. (8.164)
Whatever has been mortgaged, sold, given away, or received through fraud, or wherein one perceives deceit—that entire transaction he shall annul. (8.165)
If the borrower has perished and the expenditure was made for the sake of the family, that debt must be paid by the relatives from their own property, even if they are divided. 8.166.
Whatever legal transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family, whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not overturn it. (8.167)
"Whatever is given by force, whatever is enjoyed by force, and whatever is even recorded by force—Manu has declared all such matters effected by force to be as if they were not done. (8.168)
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a guarantor, and a family;
whereas four prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king. (8.169)
A king, even if he is impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor should he, even when prosperous, relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be. (8.170)
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the king's weakness is proclaimed; he perishes both in this world and after death. (8.171)
From the enjoyment [of his subjects], from the blending of castes, and from the protection of the weak, the power of the king is born; he prospers both in this world and after death. (8.172)

Therefore, like Yama himself, a master should personally abandon both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and conduct himself with the impartiality of Yama, having conquered anger and subdued the senses. (8.173)
But that evil-minded king who, out of delusion, should conduct affairs according to unrighteousness, his enemies will soon bring him under their control. (8.174)
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives his interests through righteousness, his subjects follow him just as rivers flow toward the ocean. (8.175)

If someone reports to the king that a creditor is recovering his debt by his own will, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of that amount to the king, and the debt itself shall be returned to the debtor. 8.176.
A debtor should repay the creditor with interest at the same rate as the principal;
one of equal or lower caste may pay it back directly, but one of superior caste should pay it gradually. (8.177)
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of equality the legal cases of men disputing with one another, as established by the testimony of witnesses. 8.178
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a great following, wealthy, and honorable. (8.179)
Whatever object a person deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the receipt. (8.180)
If one who is asked for a deposit does not return it to the depositor, he shall be summoned by the judge in the absence of that depositor. (8.181)
In the absence of witnesses, having truly deposited gold with trustworthy persons endowed with age and beauty under various pretexts, [he should cause it to be recovered]. (8.182)
If he should act according to what was entrusted and as it was done, there would be nothing therein for others to accuse him of. (8.183)
If he does not deliver that decision to them according to the rule, he shall be compelled to pay by being restrained by both parties; such is the settled law. (8.184)
A sealed deposit and an open deposit must never be given to a next-of-kin;
they are lost in the event of his death, but they are not lost if he does not die. (8.185)
But he who should himself give [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased must not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the relatives of the depositor. (8.186)
One should seek that object with sincerity and with affection;
having investigated his conduct, one should settle the matter through conciliation alone. (8.187)
This same rule shall apply to the recovery of all types of deposits;
however, one shall not recover anything from the ocean if it has not been brought back from there. (8.188)
If it has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire, he need not give it back, provided that he does not take anything from that [place] himself. (8.189)
One should seek out the thief of a deposit and likewise the person who did not entrust it, by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths. (8.190)

He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands it without having made a deposit—both of them should be punished like thieves, or compelled to pay a fine equal to the value of that [deposit]. (8.191)
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit (upanidhi), without distinction.
But whatever man should steal another's property by means of fraudulent tests, he, along with his accomplices, shall be put to death publicly by various modes of execution. (8.193)
Whatever deposit was made by someone, and in whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses—that same amount it must be recognized as; one who speaks falsely deserves punishment. (8.194)
If a gift was made by someone privately, or received privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking. (8.195)
In such cases, the king should reach a decision regarding deposited wealth as well as that which was entrusted out of friendship, without causing hardship to the holder of the deposit. (8.196)
One who sells another’s property as his own, being neither the owner nor authorized by the owner, one should not admit him as a witness—he is a thief who considers himself no thief. (8.197)
He shall be liable to forfeiture of his property along with his family, and a fine of six hundred panas;
if he has no family property and no means of escape, he shall incur the guilt of a thief. (8.198)
But whatever gift or sale is made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings. (8.199)
Where enjoyment is observed but no scriptural authority is seen anywhere, there the scriptural authority is the cause, not the enjoyment; such is the established rule. (8.200)
If one should receive any wealth from a sale in the presence of the family, he indeed acquires that wealth lawfully through purchase, for it is thus purified. (8.201)

Now, if the original owner cannot produce the root source [of his title], but the sale was public and he has cleared himself [of wrongdoing], he shall not be punished by the king; the claimant shall lose his suit and the purchaser shall recover his wealth. 8.202
One form mixed with another is not fit for sale;
nor is that which is defective, nor that which is deficient, nor that which is distant, nor that which is concealed. (8.203)
If, after showing one girl, another is given to the bridegroom, Manu has declared that he may marry both for the price of a single dowry. (8.204)

A giver does not deserve punishment if he has previously declared the defects [of the girl], provided she is not intoxicated, not afflicted with leprosy, and has not already had sexual intercourse. (8.205)
If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should fail to perform his own duty, a share corresponding to that work must be given to him by the co-performers. (8.206)
If, after the sacrificial fees have been distributed, he causes his own work to be neglected, he shall receive his entire share even if he has it performed by another. (8.207)
In whatever ritual those specific fees for individual components have been prescribed, he alone shall take them, or alternatively, all [the officiants] may share them together. (8.208)
The Adhvaryu priest shall take the chariot at the establishment of the sacred fires; the Brahman priest, the horse;
the Hotṛ priest may also take the horse; and the Udgātṛ priest, the cart at the time of the purchase [of the Soma]. (8.209)
Of all these, the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that [quarter];
those entitled to a third receive a third part, while those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part. (8.210)
When men here perform their respective duties in association with one another, the apportionment of their shares must be carried out according to this method. (8.211)
If wealth has been given by someone to another who asks for it for the sake of the Dharma, and if that wealth subsequently does not serve that purpose, it should not have been given to him. (8.212)
If, however, he should recover it out of pride or greed, he shall be made to pay one *suvarṇa* by the king; that is the atonement for his theft. (8.213)
Thus has been declared the lawful method for the non-repayment of what has been given;
hereafter, I shall explain the non-payment of wages.
If one who has been hired, being not ill, should out of pride fail to perform the work as prescribed, he shall be fined eight kṛṣṇalas, and his wages shall not be paid. 8.215
But one who was distressed should, once restored to health, perform the work exactly as stated from the beginning;
even after a very long period of time, he shall certainly receive that wage. (8.216)
As it has been said: "Whether he be afflicted or healthy, if one does not cause that work to be performed, his wages must not be paid, even for work that is only slightly incomplete. (8.217)
This law regarding the non-payment of wages has been declared in its entirety;
hereafter I shall proclaim the law concerning those who violate their agreements.
A man who, having made a formal agreement by oath with a village, a district, or an assembly, should break that agreement out of greed, the king shall banish him from the realm. (8.219)
Having restrained him, the king should compel that violator of the agreement to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one śatamāna of silver. (8.220)
In this manner, a righteous lord of the earth shall administer the rule of punishment for those who violate the agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies. (8.221)
If, after having purchased or sold anything here, one should have cause for regret, he may return that object or take it back within ten days. (8.222)
But after ten days have passed, one should neither give nor cause [the goods] to be given;
both he who takes them and he who gives them shall be fined six hundred by the king. (8.223)
But if a man gives away a girl who has defects without disclosing them, the king himself shall impose upon him a fine of ninety-six paṇas. (8.224)
If a man, out of malice, declares a maiden to be non-virgin when she is actually a virgin, he shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas], provided he does not demonstrate her fault. (8.225)
The mantras of marriage are established for maidens alone;
they are never for women who are not maidens, for such women have lost their eligibility for religious rites. (8.226)
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand are the definitive mark of wifehood;
their completion, however, should be understood by the learned to occur at the seventh step. (8.227)
In whatever matter one may have a subsequent regret after it has been performed, one should establish that person on the path of righteousness according to this procedure. 8.228
I shall now fully declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the legal dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock. 8.229

During the day, the responsibility for what happens lies with the keeper; at night, it lies with the owner, provided the animal remains in that house. Otherwise, if the security of the property is otherwise compromised, the keeper shall incur the responsibility. (8.230)
A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be the wages for a herdsman who receives no other pay. (8.231)
If an animal is lost, destroyed by worms, killed by a dog, or dies in a dangerous place, or if it is deficient in human effort, the keeper alone shall make restitution. (8.232)
If cattle have been stolen by thieves after being publicly proclaimed, the herdsman is not liable to pay, provided he informs his own master of it within the proper place and time. (8.233)
When animals have died, one should give their ears, hide, tail-hairs, bladder, sinews, and bile to the owners, and one should also show them the identifying marks. (8.234)
But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid, whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the fault of the herdsman. (8.235)
If, among those cows being grazed together in the forest, a wolf should spring upon and kill one while they are penned, the herdsman is not at fault in that matter. (8.236)
There shall be a buffer zone of one hundred bows all around a village, or else three throws of a yoke-pin; for a city, however, it shall be three times that amount.
If cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed there, the king shall not inflict punishment upon the guardians of the animals. (8.238)
One should construct a fence there such that even a camel cannot look over it, and one should block every opening through which the snout of a dog or a pig might pass. (8.239)

On a path, in a field that is enclosed, or at the edge of a village, one who has an owner is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; however, one should drive away animals that have no keeper. (8.240)
But in other fields, the animal deserves a fine of one paṇa and a quarter; however, in all cases, it is the settled rule that a portion of the crop must be given to the owner of the field. 8.241.

Manu has declared that one should not punish a cow that has recently calved and is within ten days of birth, nor bulls, nor animals dedicated to the gods—whether they are with their keepers or without them. (8.242)

In the event of a transgression by the landowner, the fine shall be ten times the share [of the crop]; for the servants, however, the fine shall be half of that if it occurred through the landowner's ignorance. (8.243)
A righteous lord of the earth should observe this rule regarding transgressions committed by owners of cattle, the cattle themselves, and their keepers. (8.244)
When a dispute has arisen concerning a boundary between two villages, he should determine the boundary in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the landmarks are clearly visible. (8.245)
He should establish boundary trees such as the *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *kiṃśuka*, *śālmali*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and other milky-sap trees. (8.246)
The boundary is not lost when there are various thickets, bamboos, *śamī* trees, creepers, and level ground, as well as reeds and *kubjaka* shrubs. (8.247)
Ponds, wells, tanks, and springs, as well as temples, should be constructed at the junctions of boundaries. (8.248)
And he should cause other boundary markers to be made concealed, having observed that in this world there is constant confusion among men regarding the knowledge of boundaries. (8.249)
Stones, bones, cow-hair, husks, ashes, potsherds, dried cow-dung, bricks, charcoal, gravel, and likewise sand— (8.250)
And whatever objects of this kind the earth would not consume due to their age, he should have them placed inconspicuously at junctions and on the boundaries. (8.251)
By these marks, as well as by long-standing possession and the constant flow of water, the king shall determine the boundary between two disputing parties. (8.252)
If there were doubt even when the marks are seen, the determination of the boundary dispute would depend solely upon the testimony of witnesses. (8.253)
In the presence of the village communities and of the two litigants themselves, witnesses shall be questioned regarding the boundary markers at the border. (8.254)
Once they have been questioned, he should establish the boundary exactly as they all unanimously declare it, and he should record them all by name. (8.255)
Bowing their heads to the earth, wearing garlands and red garments, and bound by oaths upon their own good deeds, let them lead you with justice. (8.256)
Those witnesses of truth who lead the case according to what has been stated are purified;
but those who lead it contrarily shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
But in the absence of witnesses, four neighboring villagers shall, being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king. (8.258)
But in the absence of neighboring villagers who are witnesses to the boundary, he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests: ||8.259||
He saw hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who dwell in the forest. (8.260)

Whatever those witnesses may say when questioned regarding the boundary markers at the junctions of the borders, the king shall establish that between the two villages in accordance with the law. (8.261)
The determination of boundaries and landmarks for fields, wells, tanks, groves, and houses is to be known as dependent upon the testimony of the neighbors. (8.262)
If the neighbors should speak falsely when men are disputing over a boundary, they shall all be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement. (8.263)
One who seizes a house, a pond, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if it was done through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred. (8.264)
When a boundary cannot be determined, the king himself, knowing the law, shall assign land to them for their benefit; such is the established rule. (8.265)
This entire law concerning the determination of boundaries has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the determination of verbal abuse. (8.266)
A Kṣatriya who reviles a Brāhmaṇa deserves a fine of one hundred;
a Vaiśya, one hundred and fifty or two hundred; but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment. (8.267)
A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for defaming a Kṣatriya;
for a Vaiśya, the fine shall be twenty-five; and for a Śūdra, the punishment is twelve. (8.268)
For offenses among the twice-born of equal caste, the fine shall be exactly twelve;
in cases where a debate is not to be spoken upon, that same fine shall be doubled.
But one of low birth who insults twice-born men with harsh speech shall suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is born from a base origin. (8.270)
But for one who utters their names or castes with malice, a ten-finger-long iron spike, glowing red-hot, shall be thrust into his mouth. (8.271)
If he should out of pride give instructions on the Dharma to Brahmins, the king shall cause hot oil to be poured into his mouth and his ears. (8.272)
One who, out of arrogance, speaks falsely regarding another's learning, country, caste, or even their physical body, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred panas. (8.273)
Whether one says of another that they are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly deformed—even if it be the truth—one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one kārṣāpaṇa. (8.274)
One who defames his mother, father, wife, brother, son, or teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to his teacher. (8.275)
A wise king should inflict punishment upon both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas:
for a Brāhmaṇa, the first amercement; but for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement. (8.276)

In the case of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is likewise determined that, with respect to their own respective castes, the administration of punishment shall be carried out exactly as prescribed, with the exception of corporal mutilation. 8.277.
This rule for punishment regarding verbal abuse has been declared according to the truth;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the determination of punishment for physical assault. 8.278
If a person of the lowest caste should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his must be cut off; such is the instruction of Manu. (8.279)
Raising his hand or a staff, he deserves the amputation of that hand;
striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the amputation of that foot. (8.280)
A person of low birth who seeks to sit upon the same seat as one of superior rank shall be branded on the hip and banished, or his buttock shall be gashed. (8.281)
If one spits out of pride, the king shall cause both lips to be cut off;
if one urinates [upon him], the penis; and if one passes wind [upon him], the anus. (8.282)
If someone seizes him by the hair, he should cut off both hands without hesitation; likewise if they seize him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles. (8.283)
One who breaks the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
but one who cuts the flesh shall be fined six niṣkas, while one who breaks a bone shall be banished. 8.284.
It is the established rule that for all forest trees, the punishment for injury should be inflicted in proportion to their utility. (8.285)
When one strikes humans or animals for the sake of causing them pain, the punishment should be made proportionate to the extent of that great suffering. (8.286)
In the case of crushing a limb, as well as in the case of [injuring] vital breath or blood, he shall be made to pay the expenses of recovery or even the full fine. (8.287)
If one should damage the property of another, whether intentionally or unintentionally, he must satisfy that person and pay the king a fine equal to the value of the object. (8.288)
For leather goods, articles made of leather, and those made of wood or clay, as well as for flowers, roots, and fruits, the fine shall be five times their value. (8.289)
They say there are ten cases where the vehicle, the driver, and the owner of the vehicle may escape punishment; in all other cases, a fine is prescribed. (8.290)
When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the vehicle turns sideways or faces backward, and likewise when there is a breakage of the axle or the wheel; ||8.291||
In the case of the breaking of a vehicle's harness, as well as its yoke-tie or reins, and when one cries out "Get away!", Manu has declared that there is no punishment. (8.292)
If a vehicle turns off course due to the driver's negligence, the owner shall be liable for the injury and shall be fined two hundred panas. (8.293)
If the driver is trustworthy, the driver alone deserves the fine;
if the driver is untrustworthy, all those seated in the vehicle shall each be fined one hundred [paṇas]. (8.294)
But if, being obstructed on the road by cattle or by a chariot, he should cause the death of a living being, the punishment in that case shall be without hesitation. (8.295)

In the case of killing a human being, one incurs guilt immediately, like that of a thief; for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and the like, the guilt is half [that of a human]. (8.296)
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
but for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
For donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five māṣas;
but for the killing of a dog or a pig, the fine shall be one māṣa.
A wife, a son, a slave, a pupil, and a uterine brother—when they have committed an offense, they may be beaten with a rope or a split bamboo cane. (8.299)
But one must strike on the back of the body and never on the head;
otherwise, striking in a different manner, one incurs the guilt of a thief. (8.300)
Thus has the determination of punishment for assault been declared in its entirety;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the determination of punishment for a thief.
A king should exert the utmost effort in the suppression of thieves;
through the suppression of thieves, his fame and kingdom increase. (8.302)
For that king who is a giver of fearlessness is always worthy of worship;
indeed, his sacrificial session (sattra) is ever-prosperous, having the gift of fearlessness as its fee.
A sixth part of all merit accrues to the king who protects;
likewise, a sixth part of the demerit accrues to him who fails to protect. (8.304)
Whatever one studies, whatever one sacrifices, whatever one gives, and whatever one worships—the king becomes a sharer of a sixth part of that through his proper protection. (8.305)
Protecting all beings according to dharma and executing those deserving of death, the king performs sacrifices every day with sacrificial fees of hundreds and thousands. (8.306)
That king who, failing to provide protection, takes tribute, taxes, tolls, fees for use, and fines, shall immediately go to hell. (8.307)
They say that a king who fails to protect his subjects, yet takes a sixth part of their produce as tax,
is the one who carries away the entire impurity of the whole world.
One should know that a king who disregards the bounds of propriety, who is an atheist, a plunderer, who fails to protect and instead devours his subjects, is destined for a downward path. (8.309)
One should diligently restrain the unrighteous by three means:
by confinement, by imprisonment, and by various forms of corporal punishment. (8.310)
By the suppression of the wicked and by the protection of the virtuous,
kings are constantly purified, just as the twice-born are by sacrificial rites.
A lord who seeks his own welfare should always forgive those people who bring lawsuits against him, as well as children, the elderly, and the sick. (8.312)
Because he endures insults when he is afflicted by suffering, he is glorified in heaven;
but because he does not endure them out of a sense of power, he goes to hell. (8.313)
The wise thief should go before the king with disheveled hair, confessing that theft: "I am a man of such deeds; punish me. (8.314)
Taking up a club, or a staff made of khadira wood, or a spear sharp at both ends, or even an iron mace; (8.315)
Whether by punishment or by release, the thief is freed from his theft;
but if the king does not punish him, he incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.316)
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief to the king. (8.317)
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds. (8.318)
But he who takes a rope or a water-pot from a well, or who breaks a water-trough, shall receive a fine of one māṣa and shall restore that [item] to its place. (8.319)
For one who steals more than ten jars of grain, the punishment is death;
for stealing less than that, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value as a fine, and that property shall be returned to its owner. (8.320)
Likewise, for goods measured by weight, such as gold, silver, and the like, and for the finest garments, there shall be execution if the amount exceeds one hundred. (8.321)
But for an amount exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for any remainder, one should determine a fine eleven times the value. (8.322)
One deserves the death penalty for stealing men of noble birth, women especially, and the most precious of gems. (8.323)
In the case of the theft of large cattle, weapons, or medicine, the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the circumstances of the act. (8.324)
For breaking the dam of a water-channel belonging to Brahmins' cattle,
and likewise for the theft of livestock, the punishment of cutting off half a foot shall be carried out immediately.
Of thread, cotton, and fermenting agents; of cow dung and molasses; of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass. || 8.326 ||
Likewise, for the theft of vessels made of bamboo or split cane, of salts, of earthenware, and of earth or ashes; (8.327)
Of fish, of birds, of oil, of clarified butter, of meat, of honey, and whatever else originates from animals. (8.328)
For other such items as these, for raw grain, for cooked rice, and for all kinds of cooked food, the fine shall be double their value. (8.329)
For flowers, green grain, shrubs, creepers, and trees, as well as for small quantities of unwinnowed [grain], the fine shall be five *kṛṣṇalas*. (8.330)
When grain, vegetables, roots, or fruits have been cleaned, the fine shall be one hundred paṇas if there is no prior connection, and fifty paṇas if there is a prior connection. (8.331)

An act committed by force, provided it is accompanied by a claim of ownership, would be *sāhasa* (violence); whereas taking what belongs to another without such a claim and then denying it constitutes *steya* (theft). (8.332)
But the king shall fine that man one hundred [paṇas] who steals these prepared materials, as well as he who would steal the fire from the house. (8.333)
With whichever limb a thief commits an offense against men, that very limb the king shall remove as a deterrent. (8.334)
Neither father, teacher, friend, mother, wife, son, nor domestic priest—there is no one who, failing to abide by his own duty, is exempt from punishment by the king. (8.335)
Where an ordinary person would be fined one kārṣāpaṇa, there the king should be fined one thousand; such is the established rule. (8.336)
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold. (8.337)
For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even a full hundred;
or twice sixty-four—know that he is one who understands both the faults and the virtues of those [qualities]. (8.338)
Manu has declared that taking roots and fruits from trees, wood for the purpose of fire, and grass for the fodder of cows, does not constitute theft. (8.339)
A Brahmin who seeks to obtain wealth from the hand of one who has not given it—even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching—is exactly like a thief. (8.340)
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to pay a fine. (8.341)
One who binds those who are unbound, or releases those who are bound, and one who seizes the slaves, horses, and chariots of others, shall incur the guilt of a thief. (8.342)
By carrying out the suppression of thieves according to this rule, a king shall obtain fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death. (8.343)
A king who desires to attain the station of Indra and imperishable, eternal fame should not overlook a man of violent deeds even for a moment. (8.344)
A man who commits violence through harsh speech, theft, or indeed by means of physical punishment, should be known as the worst among evildoers. (8.345)
But that king who tolerates one engaged in violence quickly goes to ruin and incurs hatred. (8.346)
A king should not, for the sake of a friend or from the acquisition of vast wealth, release those who act with violence and bring fear to all living beings. (8.347)
The twice-born may take up arms when their dharma is obstructed, or during a upheaval of the twice-born and the social orders caused by the exigencies of time. (8.348)
One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees, or in order to protect a woman or a Brahmin, does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma. (8.349)
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin, one should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation. (8.350)
No guilt whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an assassin, whether openly or in secret; it is fury that meets fury. (8.351)
The king, having branded those men who have set out to violate another's wife with punishments that cause terror, shall banish them. 8.332
For from that arises the confusion of castes among people, by which unrighteousness, which destroys the very root, leads to total ruin. (8.333)
A man who engages in private conversation with another's wife, having been previously accused of such offenses, shall incur the first amercement. (8.354)
But he who, having not been previously accused, speaks out for a valid reason, shall incur no fault whatsoever, for there is no transgression on his part. (8.355)
He who addresses another's wife at a sacred bathing place, in a river, in a forest, or even at the confluence of rivers, shall be guilty of adultery. ||8.356||
Performing services, playing together, touching ornaments and garments, and even sitting on the same bed—all this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (seduction). 8.357.
If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, consents to it, all such acts committed with mutual consent are recorded in the law as *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery). 8.358.
A non-Brahmin who commits adultery deserves a punishment ending in death;
for the wives of all four castes must always be protected most carefully. (8.359)
Beggars, bards, those initiated for sacrifice, and artisans may converse with women without being forbidden. (8.360)
One who has been forbidden shall not engage in conversation with women; but he who converses despite being forbidden deserves a fine of one suvarṇa. (8.361)
This rule does not apply to the wives of wandering performers, nor to those who live off their own labor;
for they entice women and keep them hidden away. (8.362)
But he who engages in conversation with such women, or with female slaves who eat only once a day, or with female ascetics in secret, shall be made to pay a small fine.
He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but a man who violates one who is willing, being equal to her in status, shall not suffer death. (8.364)
One should not cause a maiden who is associating with a superior man to pay anything at all;
however, one who is serving an inferior man should be kept confined in the house. (8.365)
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
one who has intercourse with a woman of equal caste should pay a fine, provided her father desires it. (8.366)
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force, shall have two fingers instantly cut off and deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas]. (8.367)
One who defiles a willing woman shall not suffer the same punishment as one who cuts off her finger;
rather, he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] in order to prevent the recurrence of such conduct. (8.368)
If a girl should defile another girl, her fine shall be two hundred;
she must also pay triple the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a rod. (8.369)
But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head, or else the cutting off of two fingers, and likewise being led away on a donkey. (8.370)

But that woman of the kinsfolk who, arrogant with the qualities of her caste and women, should transgress against her husband—the king shall have her devoured by dogs in a public place crowded with many people. (8.371)
They should cause the sinful man to be burned on a heated iron bed;
they should pile wood upon it, and there the evildoer shall be consumed by fire. (8.372)
For a wicked man who has been accused for a year, the fine shall be double;
likewise, it shall be the same for cohabiting with a Vratya woman or a Chandala woman.

A Śūdra who cohabits with a woman of the twice-born castes, whether she be protected or unprotected, shall have all his limbs cut off if she was unprotected; if she was protected, he is deprived of everything. (8.374)
A Vaiśya should be punished with the forfeiture of all his property after being imprisoned for one year;
a Kṣatriya should be fined one thousand [paṇas] and deserves to have his head shaved with urine.
If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman, the king should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand. (8.376)
But both of them, having violated that very Brahmin woman while she was protected, shall be punished like Shudras or burned in a fire of straw. (8.377)
A Brahmin who approaches a guarded Brahmin woman by force shall be fined one thousand;
he who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred. (8.378)
Shaving the head is prescribed as the punishment for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, for the other castes, the punishment shall be one that ends in death. (8.379)
One must never kill a Brahmin, even if he stands guilty of every possible crime; rather, one should banish him from the kingdom, leaving him with all his wealth and his body unhurt. (8.380)
No greater unrighteousness exists on earth than the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, a king should not even conceive the thought of his execution in his mind. (8.381)
If a Vaiśya should approach a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya a guarded Vaiśya woman, both of them deserve the same punishment as one who approaches an unguarded Brāhmaṇa woman. (8.382)
A Brāhmaṇa, however, committing adultery with guarded women of those two castes, shall be made to pay a fine of one thousand;
for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya committing it with a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand.
If a Kṣatriya has intercourse with an unprotected Vaiśya woman, the fine shall be five hundred;
however, the Kṣatriya shall undergo tonsure with urine, or else pay a fine. (8.384)

A Brāhmaṇa who approaches an unguarded Vaiśya woman, a Kṣatriya woman, or a Śūdra woman shall be fined five hundred; but if he approaches a woman of the lowest castes (antyaja), he shall be fined one thousand. 8.385.
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words,
and no perpetrator of violence or arson, shares the world of Śakra.
The suppression of these five within his own realm by a king brings him imperial power among his kinsmen and confers glory upon him in the world. (8.387)

If a sacrificer should abandon an officiating priest, or if an officiating priest should abandon a sacrificer—provided that the one is capable of the rite and free from fault—the punishment for both shall be one hundred [paṇas] each. (8.388)

Neither mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son deserves to be abandoned. One who abandons these, provided they have not fallen from their status, shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.389)

When twice-born men in their hermitages dispute with one another regarding their duties, a king who desires his own welfare and seeks to uphold righteousness should not issue a contrary judgment. (8.390)
Having honored these men as was fitting, together with the Brahmins, the king should first pacify them with gentle words and then establish them in their own duty.
If a Brahmin fails to feed his immediate neighbor and next-door neighbor when twenty worthy twice-born men are being fed at an auspicious occasion, he deserves a fine of one māṣaka.
If a learned man fails to feed another learned and virtuous man at auspicious rites, he shall be made to pay double the value of that food, as well as a silver *māṣaka*. (8.393)
One who is blind, mentally infirm, a cripple, or seventy years of age and infirm, as well as one who renders service to those learned in the Vedas, shall not be made to pay any tax by anyone. (8.394)
The king should always honor a learned Vedic scholar, those afflicted by illness or pain, children, the elderly, the destitute, those of noble lineage, and the virtuous. (8.395)
On a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood, the washerman should wash the garments slowly;
he should not rub one garment against another, nor should he let them dry together. (8.396)
A weaver shall give back ten palas of thread with an increase of one pala;
if he acts otherwise, he shall be made to pay a fine of twelve paṇas. (8.397)
At the toll-gates, those skilled in the valuation of all merchandise shall determine the price according to the goods; from that, the king shall take one-twentieth as tax. (8.398)
If one should, out of greed, carry away those articles belonging to the king which are well-known or prohibited, the king shall confiscate his entire property. (8.399)

One who evades a customs station, one who buys or sells at an improper time, or one who gives false accounts in the reckoning of goods, shall be made to pay a fine eight times the amount of the duty. (8.400)
Having investigated the import, export, and storage, as well as both the increase and decrease of all commodities, he should regulate their purchase and sale. (8.401)
Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed, the king should perform the formal offering of the guest-water (argha) in their presence. (8.402)
All weights, measures, and standards of measurement shall be well-marked;
they must be re-examined every six months. (8.403)
A vehicle shall be made to pay one paṇa at a ferry; a man, half a paṇa;
cattle and women, a quarter; and an empty-handed man, half a quarter. (8.404)
Vehicles filled with goods shall be made to pay a ferry-toll according to their value;
those with empty vessels, as well as men without belongings, shall pay whatever little they have. (8.405)
On a long journey, one should know that a crossing may be found according to the place and the time on the banks of rivers; however, there is no such sign at sea.
A pregnant woman in her second month or beyond, as well as a wandering mendicant, a sage, Brāhmaṇas, and those bearing religious marks, shall not be made to pay a ferry-toll at a crossing. (8.407)
Whatever on a boat may be damaged through the fault of the boatmen, that must be paid by the boatmen themselves, having assembled together from their own respective shares. (8.408)
This has been declared as the legal decision regarding those traveling by boat:
in the event of water damage caused by the fault of the boatmen, there is no punishment for what is due to fate. (8.409)
He should cause the Vaiśya to practice trade, money-lending, and agriculture, as well as the tending of cattle; and he should cause the Śūdra to perform service for the twice-born. (8.410)
A Brāhmaṇa should support with compassion a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for a livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties. (8.411)
If a Brahmin, out of greed, compels initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will by virtue of his superior power, he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (8.412)
But one may cause a Śūdra to perform service, whether he has been purchased or not;
for he was created by the Self-existent One solely for the service of the Brāhmaṇa. (8.413)
Even if released by his master, a Śūdra is not freed from servitude;
for that [status] is innate to him, so who can remove it from him? (8.414)

One captured under a banner, one who is a slave for food, one born in the house, one purchased, one given, one inherited from ancestors, and one enslaved as punishment—these seven are the origins of slavery. (8.415)
A wife, a son, and a slave—these three alone are declared to be without property.
Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they themselves belong. (8.416)
A Brahmin may confidently take property from a Śūdra, for he possesses nothing of his own; indeed, his wealth is to be taken by his master. (8.417)
One should cause the Vaiśyas and Śūdras to perform their own duties with diligence; for if these two fall away from their respective duties, they would throw this world into turmoil. (8.418)
Day after day, he should inspect his works and vehicles, as well as income and expenditure, the mines, and the treasury itself. (8.419)
Thus, by settling all these legal cases, the king, having cast off all sin, attains the supreme goal. ||8.420||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, in the *Saṃhitā* proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[The Ninth Chapter] For a man and a woman who abide in the path of dharma, I shall declare the eternal duties regarding their union and their separation. 9.1.
Women must be kept under control day and night by their own men; and when they are attached to sensual pleasures, they must be firmly established under one's own authority. 9.2.
The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth; in old age, the sons protect her. A woman does not deserve independence. 9.3
A father who does not give [his daughter] in marriage at the proper time is to be censured; a husband who does not approach his wife is to be censured;
and when the husband has died, a son who does not protect his mother is to be censured. (9.4)
Women must be guarded especially against even the slightest of attachments;
for if they are not protected, they will bring grief upon two families. (9.5)
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all social classes, husbands strive to protect their wives, even if they themselves are weak. (9.6)
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he indeed protects his own progeny, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma. (9.7)
The husband, having entered his wife, becomes an embryo and is born here; for that indeed is the "wifehood" (jāyātva) of the wife, because he is born again from her. 9.8.
For whatever kind of man a woman associates with, she gives birth to a son of that same kind;
therefore, for the sake of the purity of progeny, one should guard women with great effort. (9.9)
No one is able to guard women by force;
however, they can be guarded by the employment of these means. 9.10
He should employ her in the collection of wealth and in its expenditure, as well as in cleanliness, religious duty, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils. (9.11)
Those women who, though confined at home and guarded by trustworthy men, protect themselves by their own efforts, are truly well-guarded. (9.12)

Drinking, association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [at improper times], and dwelling in another’s house—these are the six things that corrupt women. 9.13.
They do not examine beauty, nor do they take account of age; whether he is handsome or ugly, they enjoy him simply as a man. (9.14)
Due to their profligacy, fickle-mindedness, and natural lack of affection, these women act perversely toward their husbands even when guarded with great effort in this world. (9.15)
Having thus understood their nature, which was produced by Prajāpati at creation, a man should exert the greatest effort toward their protection. 9.16
Manu assigned to women the bed, the seat, adornment, lust, anger, ignobility, a malicious disposition, and misconduct. (9.17)
"It is established as the law that women have no ritual action with mantras;
for it is settled that women are devoid of spiritual power, lack mantras, and are untruth. (9.18)
And likewise, many scriptural passages have been chanted even in the Vedas;
listen now to their form for the purpose of examining their specific characteristics. 9.19
"If my mother, wandering about unfaithful to her husband, lusted after another, may my father take that seed of mine"—this is the illustration for this [rule]. (9.20)
Whatever undesirable thing she contemplates in her mind for the sake of her husband, this is rightly called the concealment of such transgression. (9.21)
Whatever the qualities of the husband with whom a woman is united according to the prescribed rule, such qualities she comes to possess, just as a river does when it merges with the ocean. (9.22)
Akṣamālā, though born of a low womb, attained venerability through her union with Vasiṣṭha;
and Śārṅgī likewise attained honor through Mandapāla. (9.23)
These and other women in this world, though born of lowly descent, have attained eminence through their own respective auspicious qualities as wives. (9.24)
Thus has been declared the auspicious course of conduct for men and women at all times; now learn the duties regarding progeny, which yield happiness both in this world and after death. 9.25
For the sake of procreation, these highly fortunate women are worthy of honor and are the lights of the home;
between women and the goddesses of fortune (Śrī) in households, there is no distinction whatsoever. (9.26)
The procreation of offspring, the nurturing of those born, and the daily conduct of worldly life—women are the visible foundation for all this. (9.27)
Offspring, religious duties, service, and supreme delight depend upon the wife; likewise, heaven for both one's ancestors and oneself is dependent upon her. (9.28)
She who does not deceive her husband, being restrained in mind, speech, and body, attains the worlds of her husband and is called "virtuous" by the righteous. (9.29)
But through infidelity toward her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by sinful diseases. (9.30)
Listen to this meritorious discourse, beneficial to all people, which has been proclaimed by the virtuous and by the great sages of old concerning a son. (9.31)
They recognize the son as belonging to the husband; however, there is a conflict of scriptural authority regarding the progenitor.
Some say he belongs to the one who produces him, while others know him to belong to the owner of the field. (9.32)
The woman is considered to be the field, and the man is considered to be the seed;
from the union of the field and the seed arises the birth of all embodied beings. (9.33)
In some cases the seed is superior, while in others it is the female womb;
but where both are equal, that offspring is highly praised. (9.34)
Between the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior;
for the procreation of all beings is indeed characterized by the nature of the seed. (9.35)
Whatever kind of seed is sown in a field prepared at the proper time, that very kind of seed grows therein, manifested by its own inherent qualities. (9.36)
For this earth is called the eternal womb of all beings;
yet the seed does not nourish any of the qualities of the womb during its growth. (9.37)
Even in a single field on the earth, seeds sown at the proper time by farmers arise here in various forms according to their own nature. (9.38)
