Rice, śāli rice, mung beans, sesame, masha beans, as well as barley, garlic, and sugarcane—these all sprout according to their respective seeds. (9.39)
That one thing is sown and another is born—this is not possible;
for whatever seed is sown, that very same thing sprouts forth. (9.40)
Therefore, a wise and disciplined man, who understands both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom and desires long life, must never sow his seed in the wife of another. (9.41)
Regarding this, those who know the past recite verses sung by Vāyu:
"Just as a seed should not be sown by a man in what belongs to another... (9.42)
Just as an arrow shot into the sky vanishes when one shoots after it has already been pierced, so too does a seed sown in the possession of another truly perish. 9.43
Those who know the past recognize this earth as the wife even of Pṛthu; they call a field a "stump-cutter" and a deer one that "possesses an arrow. (9.44)
"The person is only this much: wife, self, and offspring—so the wise have said; likewise, he who is the husband is remembered as the woman. (9.45)
A wife is not released from her husband by means of a ransom or by abandonment;
thus we know the dharma established of old by Prajāpati. 9.46
A share of inheritance falls but once; a daughter is given away but once;
one says "I give" but once—these three things happen only once each. (9.47)
Just as one who fathers offspring from cows, mares, camels, slave-girls, buffaloes, goats, or sheep does not receive a share of their produce, so it is likewise with the wives of others. 9.48
Those who possess seed but have no field, and who sow it in another's field, never obtain the fruit of the crop that has grown. (9.49)
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain. (9.50)
In the same way, those who possess no field but sow their seed in another's field benefit the owner of the field; the owner of the seed does not obtain the fruit. (9.51)
But when no fruit is intended for either the owner of the field or the sower, the benefit belongs clearly to the owners of the field; for the womb is more powerful than the seed. (9.52)

But when this [fruit] is given for the sake of the seed because of an agreement on the action, then in this world both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen to be sharers in it. (9.53)
If a seed carried by the force of a flood sprouts in someone's field, it should be known as belonging to that owner of the field alone; the sower does not receive the fruit. (9.54)
This law regarding the offspring of cows, horses, female slaves, camels, goats, sheep, birds, and buffaloes should be understood. 9.55.
Thus has the essential and the worthless nature of seeds and wombs been described to you.
Hereafter, I shall declare the duty of women in times of distress. 9.56
The wife of an elder brother is the wife of a guru for the younger;
but the wife of a younger brother is considered the daughter-in-law of the elder. (9.57)

An elder brother who approaches the wife of his younger brother, or a younger brother who approaches the wife of his elder brother—even if they are authorized [to do so]—become outcasts, unless there is a time of distress (anāpadi). (9.58)
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring. (9.59)
But one appointed to a widow, being anointed with ghee and remaining silent, shall procreate a single son at night; by no means a second. (9.60)
Some who know the truth consider procreation with women to be the second [duty], seeing that the purpose of the appointment between those two has not yet been fulfilled according to dharma. (9.61)
But when the purpose of the appointment regarding the widow has been fulfilled according to the rule, the two should behave toward each other like a father-in-law and a daughter-in-law. (9.62)

If those two who have been appointed should act according to their own desire, disregarding the prescribed rule, they would both become outcasts, like one who violates his daughter-in-law or one who violates the bed of his teacher. 9.63.
A widow must not be appointed to another [man] by the twice-born;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma. (9.64)
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* mentioned;
nor, furthermore, is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies. (9.65)
For this practice of treating [beings] like cattle was rejected by learned brahmins;
yet it was declared even for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom. (9.66)
In former times, while ruling over the entire earth, that most excellent of royal sages,
his mind struck down by passion, brought about the intermixture of the social classes.
From that time forward, the virtuous censure any man who, out of delusion, employs a woman whose husband has died for the sake of obtaining offspring. (9.68)
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true, her own brother-in-law shall wed her according to this following rule. (9.69)

Having approached her according to the prescribed rule—she who is clad in white garments and pure in her vows—the two shall enjoy each other's company once in each fertile period until the birth of a child. (9.70)
A wise man, having given his daughter to one, should not give her again to another;
for by giving her away once more after she has been given, he incurs the sin of falsehood regarding a human being. (9.71)
Even after accepting her according to the prescribed rites, one may abandon a bride who is blameworthy, diseased, corrupted, or one who was presented through deception. (9.72)
But if one gives away a girl who has defects without having disclosed them, he should render void that gift of the evil-minded giver of the bride. (9.73)
A man who has business abroad should depart after providing for his wife's maintenance;
for a woman, even one of firm character, may fall into corruption when distressed by a lack of livelihood. 9.74.
If her husband has gone abroad after providing for her maintenance, she should live while remaining firm in her observances;
but if he has gone abroad without providing for it, she should live by means of blameless crafts. 9.75.
A man who has gone abroad for the sake of religious duties should be waited for eight years;
if for the sake of learning or fame, six years; but if for the sake of pleasure, three years. (9.76)
A husband should wait for one year for a wife who hates him;
but after a year has passed, he may take back her property and cease to live with her. (9.77)
She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings. (9.78)
There is no abandonment of a wife who is insane, fallen [from caste], impotent, sterile, or afflicted with a foul disease; nor is there any revocation of the gift [of her hand]. (9.79)

A wife who drinks liquor, is untruthful in conduct, or is hostile; one who is diseased, injurious, or constantly wasteful of wealth—such a woman may indeed be superseded by taking another wife. (9.80)

A barren wife may be superseded in the eighth year; one whose children have died, in the tenth; one who gives birth only to daughters, in the eleventh; but one who speaks unpleasantly, immediately. (9.81)
But a wife who is sickly, yet beneficial and endowed with good character, may be superseded by another only after she has been informed; she must never be treated with contempt. (9.82)
But a woman who, having been given in marriage, should depart from the house in anger, she must be restrained immediately or abandoned in the presence of the family. 9.83.
But she who, though forbidden, drinks liquor even on festive occasions, or goes to a theatrical performance or a social assembly, shall be fined six *kṛṣṇalas*. (9.84)
If twice-born men marry women both of their own caste and of other castes, seniority, honor, and the dwelling shall belong to them according to the order of their castes. (9.85)
The wife alone, and no one of a different caste under any circumstances, shall perform the service of her husband's body and his daily religious duties for all [the deceased]. (9.86)
But he who, out of delusion, causes it to be performed by another woman of his own caste, as is the case with a Brāhmaṇa-caṇḍāla, is exactly like that [previously mentioned] person. 9.87.
To one who is eminent, handsome, excellent, and worthy, one should give that maiden to him according to the prescribed rite, even if she has not yet reached marriageable age. (9.88)
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house at his pleasure until death;
yet he must never give her in marriage to one who lacks good qualities. (9.89)
A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
after this period, however, she may seek a husband of equal status. (9.90)
If she should approach a husband of her own accord when not being given away, she incurs no guilt whatsoever, nor does he whom she approaches. (9.91)
A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself any jewelry belonging to her father, her mother, or given by her brother; if she should take it, it would constitute theft. (9.92)
One who takes a girl who has reached puberty should not pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her menses, he would be overstepping his authority. (9.93)
A man of thirty years should marry a pleasing girl of twelve; or one of twenty-four years, a girl of eight, if he is in haste to fulfill his duty. (9.94)
A husband obtains his wife as a gift from the gods, not by his own will; he should always support her, if she be virtuous, acting thereby to please the gods. 9.95

Women were created for the purpose of procreation, and men for the purpose of continuing the lineage; therefore, in the Veda, religious duty is declared to be common to both, performed together with one's wife. 9.96.
If the giver of the nuptial fee dies after the fee has been paid for a maiden, she should be given to his brother, provided the maiden consents. (9.97)
Even a Śūdra should not take a bride-price when giving away his daughter;
for by accepting a bride-price, one commits a concealed sale of his daughter. (9.98)
But this is what neither others nor any other virtuous men have ever done:
that having given one's consent to one person, it is then bestowed upon another. (9.99)
Indeed, we have never heard of such a thing, even in previous births:
the sale of a daughter concealed under the name of a "bride-price. (9.100)
Let there be mutual fidelity until death;
this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief. (9.101)
Likewise, once they have performed their rites, the man and woman should always strive so that, even when separated from one another, they do not transgress against each other. 9.102.
This duty of women and men, connected with pleasure, has been declared to you, as well as [the rules for] obtaining offspring in times of distress; now learn the law concerning inheritance. 9.103.
After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive. (9.104)
The eldest alone, however, shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him just as they did upon their father. (9.105)
By the mere birth of the eldest son, a man becomes a father of sons and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, that son deserves everything. 9.106
He upon whom one pays off debts and through whom one attains infinity—he alone is known as the son born of dharma; others they know as born of desire. 9.107.

The eldest brother should protect his younger brothers like a father protects his sons; and they, in accordance with dharma, should behave toward their eldest brother as sons do toward their father. 9.108
The eldest son causes the family to prosper or, conversely, brings it to ruin;
the eldest is most worthy of honor in the world, and the eldest is not censured by the virtuous. (9.109)
He who is the eldest and behaves as an elder is like a mother and like a father;
but he who does not behave as an elder should be honored merely as a kinsman. (9.110)
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for dharma; dharma increases through separation, therefore separation is consistent with dharma. (9.111)
The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share, and whatever is the best among all the goods; half of that shall belong to the middle son, and a fourth to the youngest. (9.112)
The eldest and the youngest shall take their shares as prescribed;
those others who are between the eldest and the youngest shall receive the middle portion of the wealth. (9.113)
The eldest son shall take the best of all kinds of wealth; furthermore, he shall receive whatever is most excellent and a choice portion from ten [shares]. (9.114)
There is no share for those who have excelled in their own duties among ten [brothers];
however, something whatsoever should be given to the elder, which increases his honor. (9.115)
Thus, when the preferential shares have been set aside, one should allot equal portions;
but if no preferential shares are set aside, this shall be the allotment of shares for them. (9.116)
The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the next younger brother, one and a half shares; and the youngest brothers, one share each—thus the law is established. (9.117)
But the brothers shall each separately give to their sisters from their own shares an equal fourth part; those who are unwilling to give it shall become outcasts. (9.118)
One should never take unequal shares of goats, sheep, and one-hoofed animals;
however, it is ordained that the unequal share of the goats and sheep belongs to the eldest alone. (9.119)
If a younger brother should procreate a son upon the wife of the elder brother, the division of property in that case shall be equal; such is the established law. (9.120)
It is not consistent with dharma that the subordinate should take precedence over the principal;
since the father is the principal in procreation, one should therefore honor him according to dharma. ||9.121||
If a doubt should arise as to how the division [of the estate] should be made in a case where there is a younger son born of an elder wife and an elder son born of a younger wife: ||9.122||
The eldest son shall take one bull as his preferential share;
thereafter, the other bulls, inferior to that, belong to those who are junior according to their mothers. (9.123)
But the son born of the eldest wife shall take a bull as his sixteenth share;
thereafter, the remaining sons shall divide the property according to their mothers—this is the settled rule. (9.124)
Among sons born of wives of equal status, there is no seniority according to their mothers; rather, seniority is said to be determined by birth [from the father]. (9.125)
It is recorded in the Smṛti that even in the Subrahmaṇyā invocations, the summons is made according to birth-order;
and it is also recorded that between twins born from a single womb, seniority is determined by birth. (9.126)

A sonless man may, by this rite, make a daughter his appointed daughter (*putrikā*), with the agreement: "Whatever offspring may be born of her shall be the one who performs my ancestral rites. (9.127)
In accordance with this very procedure, the patriarch Dakṣa himself formerly created those daughters for the sake of the increase of his own lineage. (9.128)
With a joyful heart, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to King Soma, having honored them all.
Just as one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she remains as one's own self, how could another take away the wealth? (9.130)
Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that shall indeed be the portion of the unmarried daughter;
and the son of a daughter (dauhitra) alone shall take the entire estate of one who dies without a son. (9.131)
For the daughter’s son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather. (9.132)
In this world, according to the law of dharma, there is no distinction between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for both of them were produced from the bodies of their respective parents. (9.133)
But if, after a daughter has been appointed, a son is subsequently born, the division of the inheritance shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. (9.134)
But if an appointed daughter (putrikā) dies without leaving a son, her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation. (9.135)

Whether she was appointed or not, if a mother should obtain a son from a man of equal status, that grandson makes his maternal grandfather the recipient of the funeral cake; he shall inherit the wealth. (9.136)
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun. (9.137)
Because a son protects his father from the hell named Put, he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself. (9.138)
In this world, no distinction is found between a son’s son and a daughter’s son;
for even a daughter’s son saves him in the hereafter, just like a son’s son. (9.139)
The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother;
the second to her father, and the third to his own father. (9.140)
But he whose adopted son is endowed with all good qualities shall indeed inherit that estate, even though he has come from another lineage. (9.141)

An adopted son shall never take the family name or the inheritance of his biological father; for the funeral cake follows the family name and inheritance, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives it to the wrong lineage. 9.142

The son of an unauthorized woman, even if she has other sons, and the son obtained from a brother-in-law—both of these, being born of an adulterer and born of lust, do not deserve a share of the inheritance. (9.143)

Even if a man has procreated on an appointed woman, the son born contrary to the prescribed rule is not entitled to the paternal inheritance, for he was begotten by one who has fallen from his status. (9.144)

If a son is born from a woman appointed for that purpose, he is considered as one's own legitimate son; according to the law, that seed belongs to the owner of the field, and so does the offspring. (9.145)
He who takes charge of the wealth and the wife of his deceased brother shall procreate offspring for that brother and hand over that very wealth to him. (9.146)
If a woman, being authorized, obtains a son from a brother-in-law or another [relative], they declare that son to be born of lust, excluded from inheritance, and begotten in vain. (9.147)
This rule for the division [of inheritance] among sons born of a single wife should be understood; now learn that which applies to those born of many wives of various castes. 9.148.
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order [of castes], this is the rule recorded for the division [of the estate] among the sons born of them. (9.149)
A ploughman, a bull, a vehicle, an ornament, and a house—these should be given as the additional share (uddhārika) to the Brāhmaṇa, along with one principal portion. (9.150)
From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three shares; the son of a Kṣatriya, two shares;
the son born of a Vaiśya woman, one and a half shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (9.151)
Or he may divide the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts; one who knows the law should perform this righteous partition according to the following rule: 9.152.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (9.153)
Whether there be a virtuous son or even if there be no son at all, one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman. (9.154)
The son of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya does not inherit property;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth. (9.155)
Or, sons born of wives of equal caste for the twice-born shall all divide the inheritance equally after giving a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest. (9.156)
For a Śūdra, however, only a wife of his own caste is ordained, and no other;
those born of her shall share equal portions, even if there be a hundred sons. (9.157)
Of the twelve sons whom Svāyambhuva Manu has mentioned for men, six are kinsmen and heirs, and six are kinsmen but not heirs. (9.158)
The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son—these six are both heirs and kinsmen. (9.159)

The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the son of a Śūdra woman—these six are kinsmen who do not inherit. (9.160)
Whatever quality one acquires while crossing water with a leaky boat, such is the quality one acquires while crossing the darkness with bad sons. (9.161)

If there should be two sons, one legitimate (aurasa) and one born of the wife (kṣetraja), who are co-heirs, each shall take that paternal inheritance which belongs to his own father, and not the other. 9.162.
The son of the body alone is the master of the paternal wealth;
however, for the sake of kindness toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood. (9.163)
When dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) shall give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth share. (9.164)
The two sons, the body-born (aurasa) and the field-born (kṣetraja), are sharers of the father’s inheritance;
but ten others, in their respective order, are sharers of the lineage and a portion of the inheritance. (9.165)
But that son whom one should beget oneself upon one's own wedded wife, one should know as the legitimate (aurasa) son, the first in order. (9.166)
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or is diseased, to a woman appointed according to the sacred law, is known as the "son of the soil" (kṣetraja). (9.167)
If a mother or a father should give a son with water during a time of distress—one who is similar [in status] and given with affection—he is to be known as a "given" (dattima) son. (9.168)
But he whom one may make similar to oneself, who is discerning of virtues and faults, and who is endowed with the qualities of a son—he is to be known as the "adopted" (kṛtrima) son. (9.169)
He who is born in a house but is not known to belong to anyone is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him whose wife gave birth to him. (9.170)
A son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha* (abandoned son). 9.171
A son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father’s house, one should call him by the name *kānīna* (maiden-born); he is produced from the maiden, not from the husband. (9.172)
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition be known or unknown, the child belongs to the husband; such a child is called *sahoḍha* (one taken with the bride). // 9.173 //
If one should purchase a son from his mother and father for the sake of offspring, he is that man’s *krītaka* (bought) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [to him]. (9.174)
A woman who, having been abandoned by her husband or being a widow, bears a son after marrying again of her own will, is called *paunarbhava*. (9.175)
If she is still a virgin, or even if she has returned after having gone away, she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her husband from a second marriage. 9.176.
One who is bereft of parents, or has been abandoned by them without cause, and offers himself to another, is known as "self-given" (svayaṃdatta). ||9.177||
The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father on a Śūdra woman through lust is a corpse even while still alive;
therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava. (9.178)
If a son is born to a Śūdra by a female slave or the female slave of a slave, he may, with permission, take a share; such is the established law. (9.179)
The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja* as described above, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites. (9.180)
These sons who have been mentioned incidentally as born from the seeds of others belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else. (9.181)
If among brothers born of the same father, one should have a son, Manu has declared that they are all possessed of a son through that son. (9.182)
If among all women in a single row of seating one should have a son, Manu has declared them all to be possessed of sons by virtue of that son. (9.183)
In the absence of a superior [heir], one who is inferior is entitled to the inheritance;
however, if there are many of equal status, all are sharers of the estate. (9.184)
Neither brothers nor fathers, nor sons are heirs to the father's estate;
rather, the father shall take the inheritance of one who dies without a son, or else the brothers themselves. (9.185)
Water should be offered to three; the funeral cake proceeds to three; the fourth is the giver of these; a fifth does not exist. (9.186)
The wealth of each person shall belong to his nearest sapinda;
after him, it shall go to a sakulya, or else to the teacher or the pupil. (9.187)
But in the absence of all these, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled shall be the heirs of the estate; thus the Dharma is not violated. (9.188)
The property of a Brāhmaṇa is always inviolable by the king; such is the settled rule. But in the case of the other castes, the king may take their property when no heirs exist. (9.189)
For one who has died childless, one should obtain a son from a member of the same lineage;
whatever wealth there may be, that one should bestow upon him. (9.190)
But if two [sons] born of two [different men] should dispute over the wealth of their mother, each shall take that which belonged to his own father, and not the other. (9.191)
When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally. (9.192)
Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection. (9.193)

What is given before the nuptial fire, what is received from the father's house, and what is given as a token of affection; what is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman. (9.194)

What was given as a subsequent gift (anvādheya) and what was given by the husband out of affection—this shall be the property of the offspring of a woman who has passed away while her husband is still living. (9.195)
Whatever wealth exists in marriages of the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, or Prājāpatya types, that is held to belong to the husband alone when she dies without issue. (9.196)
Whatever wealth may have been given to her in marriages such as the Āsura and others, that is held to belong to the mother and father when she has passed away without offspring. (9.197)
Whatever wealth may belong to a woman, however given by her father, that a Brāhmaṇī wife shall take; or it shall belong to her unmarried daughter, or to the offspring of such a daughter. (9.198)
Women should not carry out any acquisition from the midst of the large family, nor even from their own wealth, without the permission of their own husband. (9.199)
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do so fall from their status. (9.200)

Those who have no share [in the inheritance] are the impotent, the outcaste, those blind from birth, the deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and whoever else is devoid of sense organs. (9.201)
However, it is right for a wise person to give to all of them according to his ability, at least food and clothing; for one who does not give becomes fallen. (9.202)
If, however, there should somehow be a desire for wives on the part of eunuchs and others, their offspring—provided they have produced progeny—are entitled to the inheritance. (9.203)
Whatever property the eldest son acquires after his father has died, the younger brothers have a share in it, provided they are devoted to learning. (9.204)
But if all those who were ignorant should acquire wealth through their own efforts, the established rule is that there should be an equal division of it, as it is not ancestral property. (9.205)
Whatever constitutes the wealth of knowledge belongs to that person alone;
the same applies to what is received from a friend, what is obtained at marriage, and what is offered as the honey-mixture (madhuparka). (9.206)
But he among brothers who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire wealth, shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence. (9.207)
That which has been acquired through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate, being obtained by one's own effort—that one is not obliged to give away against one's will. (9.208)
But whatever paternal property a father may acquire that was not previously obtained, he need not share that with his sons unless he so desires, as it is self-earned. (9.209)
If those who were divided while living together should divide their property again, the division in that case shall be equal; there is no right of primogeniture therein. (9.210)
If the eldest or the youngest [son] should be deprived of his share at the time of distribution, or if either of them should die, his portion is not lost. (9.211)
The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally; so too shall the brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters. (9.212)
If an eldest brother, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers, he shall lose his status as the eldest, receive no share of the inheritance, and be restrained by the kings. (9.213)

All brothers who are engaged in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the wealth; nor should the eldest brother make a separate provision for himself without having given anything to the younger brothers. (9.214)
If there should be a joint undertaking by brothers who have not divided their inheritance, the father must never, under any circumstances, allot unequal shares to their sons. (9.215)
But one who is born after the partition shall take only the paternal wealth; or, those who may have reunited with him, he shall divide that wealth together with them. 9.216.
The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring;
and upon the death of the mother as well, the father’s mother shall take the wealth. (9.217)
When all debts and assets have been divided according to rule, whatever may subsequently be discovered, all that should be brought into equality. (9.218)
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, and the management of property and security—they declare these to be indivisible. (9.219)

This division of property and the rule for the performance of rites for sons—beginning with the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the others—has been declared to you in due order; now learn the law concerning gambling. 9.220.
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
these two vices bring about the end of the kingdoms of rulers of the earth. (9.221)
Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress these two. (9.222)
That which is performed with inanimate objects is called "gambling" (dyūta) in the world; that which is performed with animate beings is to be known as "betting" (samāhvaya). 9.223.
The king shall cause to be executed all those who engage in gambling or betting, or cause others to do so, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born. (9.224)
He shall quickly banish from the city gamblers, actors, prostitutes, men belonging to heretical sects, those who follow forbidden occupations, and liquor-sellers. (9.225)
Existing in the kingdom as hidden thieves of the king, these men constantly afflict the virtuous subjects by their performance of forbidden acts. (9.226)
In ancient times, this gambling was seen to cause great enmity;
therefore, a wise man should not indulge in gambling, even for the sake of amusement. (9.227)
Whether it be done in secret or openly, whatever man should practice that [forbidden act], there shall be a variety of punishments for him according to the king's will. (9.228)
But a member of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra caste who is unable to pay a fine shall discharge the debt through labor; a Brāhmaṇa, however, shall pay it gradually, little by little. (9.229)
The king should inflict punishment upon women, children, the insane, the elderly, the poor, the helpless, and the sick by means of whips, split cane, ropes, and the like. (9.230)
But those who, having been appointed to official duties, ruin the affairs of the litigants while being consumed by the heat of wealth—the king shall deprive them of their property. (9.231)
He shall put to death those who forge royal edicts, those who corrupt the subjects, those who kill women, children, or Brahmins, and likewise those who serve his enemies. (9.232)
Whatever has been settled and adjudicated, wherever it may have occurred, one should know that to be established according to dharma; one must not reverse it again. 9.233
Whatever legal matter a minister or a judge might decide incorrectly, the king himself should settle that case and fine him one thousand [paṇas]. (9.234)
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—all these men are to be known individually as perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin). 9.235.
And for all four of these who do not perform expiation, the king shall prescribe a lawful punishment involving both body and property. (9.236)
For violating the teacher’s bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag;
for theft, the footprint of a dog; and for killing a Brāhmaṇa, the figure of a headless man. (9.237)
Indeed, being unfit to eat with, unfit to sacrifice for, unfit to study with, and unfit to marry, they shall wander the earth in misery, excluded from all righteous duties. (9.238)
But these, having been branded with the mark, must be abandoned by their kinsmen and relatives; they shall be without compassion and without the salutation—this is the instruction of Manu. (9.239)

But those of the higher castes who perform the prescribed penance as ordained shall not have a mark branded on their foreheads by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine. (9.240)
For these offenses against a Brāhmaṇa, the middle amercement shall be imposed; or he may be banished from the kingdom, along with his wealth and his belongings. (9.241)
But others who have committed these sins unintentionally deserve the forfeiture of all their property; however, if they did so intentionally, they deserve banishment. (9.242)
A righteous king must not take the wealth of one who has committed a mortal sin;
for by taking it out of greed, he becomes tainted by that very guilt. (9.243)
Having cast that staff into the waters, he should offer it to Varuṇa;
or he should present it to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and virtuous conduct. (9.244)
Varuṇa is the lord of punishment, for he is the wielder of the rod over kings;
the Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas is the lord of the entire world. (9.245)
Where a king avoids receiving wealth from evildoers, there men are born in due time with long lives. (9.246)
And the crops of the people ripen individually according to how they were sown;
children do not die prematurely, and nothing deformed is born. (9.247)
But if one born of a low caste should, out of desire, oppress Brahmins, the king shall slay him with various terrifying methods of execution. (9.248)
As much demerit is seen for a king in killing one who should not be killed, so much is seen in releasing one who deserves to be killed; but merit accrues to him who restrains [the wicked]. (9.249)
Thus has been set forth in detail the determination of legal procedure for two parties disputing with one another regarding the eighteen grounds of litigation. 9.250
Thus performing his duties in accordance with dharma, the lord of the earth should properly seek to acquire territories not yet obtained and protect those already acquired. (9.251)

But one who has settled in a well-chosen location and constructed a fortress according to the treatises should constantly exert the greatest effort in the removal of thorns (the suppression of enemies). 9.252.
By protecting those of noble conduct and by clearing away thorns,
kings who are devoted to the protection of their subjects go to the third heaven.
But that king who collects taxes while failing to punish thieves—his kingdom becomes agitated, and he is excluded from heaven. (9.254)
But that kingdom which is fearless and relies upon the strength of its arms increases constantly, like a tree being watered. (9.255)
The king, whose eyes are his spies, should recognize two kinds of thieves who steal the property of others: those who are open and those who are secret. (9.256)
Those who live by various wares are "open deceivers," while these people such as thieves and forest-dwellers are "concealed deceivers. (9.257)
Those who take bribes, those who practice fraud, deceivers, gamblers, and those who live by prescribing auspicious rites, together with those who subsist on the inspection of omens; 9.258.
And likewise, high officials who act improperly, physicians,
those skilled in the practice of arts and crafts, and clever courtesans— ||9.259||
One should recognize such people as manifest thorns in the world, as well as others who move in secret—ignoble men wearing the outward marks of the noble. (9.260)
Having identified them through secret agents who perform their duties with good conduct and by means of spies in various disguises, he should encourage them and bring them under his control. (9.261)

Having publicly proclaimed their faults according to the truth in relation to each of their respective duties, the king should duly administer punishment according to the gravity of the offense and the essential nature of the act. 9.262
For indeed, without punishment, it is not possible to restrain the wickedness of thieves who harbor evil intentions and move about secretly upon the earth. (9.263)
Assembly halls, water-stations, bakeries, brothels, taverns, and food-sellers; crossroads, sacred trees, public gatherings, and spectacles—(9.264)
Dilapidated gardens, forests, and the workshops of artisans, as well as empty houses, groves, and pleasure parks. (9.265)
The king should cause such regions to be patrolled by both stationary and mobile military outposts, as well as by spies, for the purpose of suppressing thieves. (9.266)
One should recognize and encourage him through his companions who follow him, who are skilled in various arts, and through clever former thieves. (9.267)
Under the pretext of providing food and drink, by means of visiting Brahmins, and under the pretext of discussing heroic deeds, they should bring about their meeting. 9.268.
Those who do not approach him there, and those who are rooted in enmity, the king should forcibly slay, along with their friends, kinsmen, and relatives. (9.269)
A righteous king shall not execute a thief without the stolen property; however, he may execute one caught with the booty along with the implements [of theft] without hesitation. (9.270)
Furthermore, whoever in the villages provide food to thieves, or give them space for their goods—all of those as well he should have executed. (9.271)
In the kingdoms, he should swiftly punish those appointed to guard them and the vassal lords who have been incited, if they remain neutral during attacks, just as one punishes thieves. (9.272)
And even one who lives by the Dharma, if he has fallen away from the commitment to the Dharma, he should indeed burn him with punishment, for he has strayed from his own duty. 9.273

In the event of a village raid, the breaking of a dam, or the sighting of a robbery on the road, those who do not rush to assist to the best of their ability shall be banished along with their belongings. (9.274)
He should cause those who steal the king's treasury, those who stand in opposition, and those who instigate enemies to be executed by various forms of punishment. (9.275)
But those thieves who commit robbery at night by breaking through a wall,
the king, having cut off their hands, shall impale them upon a sharp stake.
In the first instance of breaking a seal, one should have the fingers of the offender cut off;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves the death penalty. (9.277)

The Lord punished those who set fires, those who provided food [to thieves], as well as those who gave them weapons and shelter, and those who consigned stolen goods to storage, just as he would punish his own disciples if they were thieves. 9.278
One who destroys a tank should be killed by drowning in water or by some other pure form of execution; or he may repair it, and the king shall impose the highest fine.
One should indeed execute without hesitation those who break into storehouses, armories, or temples, as well as those who steal elephants, horses, or chariots. (9.280)
But he who diverts the water of a tank already established, or cuts off the inflow of waters, shall be made to pay the first amercement. (9.281)
He who, except in an emergency, should void excrement on the royal highway, shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away the excrement. (9.282)
One who has fallen into calamity, or one who is aged, or a pregnant woman, or even a child, deserve only a verbal reprimand; and that [offense] must be cleared away—this is the settled rule. (9.283)
For all physicians who practice deceitfully, there shall be punishment:
the first amercement for offenses against non-human beings, but the middle amercement for those against human beings. (9.284)
One who breaks the transition-arches, flagstaffs, or images shall repair all of that and pay five hundred [paṇas]. ||9.285||
For the spoiling of unadulterated goods, as well as for breaking them or boring gems in the wrong place, the punishment is the first amercement. (9.286)
For he who deals unequally with those who are equal, whether in respect to the goods or even the price, that man shall incur the first or indeed the middle amercement. (9.287)
And he should place all prisoners along the royal highway, so that those miserable, deformed evildoers may be seen there. (9.288)
One who breaks down a wall, fills up a moat, or destroys a gate should be banished immediately. (9.289)
In all cases of malevolent magic, a fine of two hundred [paṇas] shall be imposed, as well as for root-rites performed by those who are not authorized, and for various kinds of sorcery. 9.290.
One who sells seeds, one who steals seeds, and likewise one who breaks a boundary, shall suffer the punishment of mutilation or death. (9.291)
But a king should have a goldsmith who is the most wicked of all thorns, if he persists in unjust conduct, cut into pieces with razors. 9.292.
In cases of the theft of Sītā-grain, weapons, and medicine, the king shall determine the punishment after considering the time and the specific circumstances of the act. (9.293)
The sovereign, the minister, the capital, the realm, the treasury, the army, and likewise the ally—these seven constituent elements (prakṛtis) together are called the kingdom. 9.294.
Among these seven constituent elements of sovereignty, one should know that, in their respective order, each preceding one is more serious and its misfortune greater than the following. (9.295)
In this world, within the sevenfold kingdom supported like a triple-staff, nothing excels another because of the specific excellence of their mutual qualities. (9.296)
For in various specific tasks, this or that particular factor is distinguished;
whatever means accomplishes a given purpose is said to be the most excellent in that regard. (9.297)

Through one's conduct, through the application of enthusiasm, and indeed through the performance of actions, one should constantly know one's own power and the power of others, as well as that of oneself and the Supreme Self. 9.298
Having reflected upon the gravity and lightness of all oppressions as well as calamities, one should then undertake the task. (9.299)
One should indeed undertake actions again and again, even when exhausted; for prosperity attends the man who perseveres in his undertakings. 9.300
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages—all these are the conduct of the king; for the king is said to be the age itself.
When he is asleep, it is the Kali age; when awake, it is the Dvāpara age; when intent upon actions, it is the Tretā age; but when moving about, it is the Kṛta age. (9.302)
A king should conduct himself with the splendor of Indra, Arka, Vāta, Yama, Varuṇa, Candra, Agni, and Pṛthivī. (9.303)
Just as Indra pours down rain during the four months of the rainy season, so should one practicing the vow of Indra shower his own kingdom with the objects of desire. 9.304
Just as the sun draws up water with its rays for eight months, so should the king take tax from his realm; for that is the constant vow of the sun. (9.305)
Just as the wind enters all beings and moves through them, so too should one enter by means of spies; for this indeed is the "Wind-like" vow.
Just as Yama restrains both the beloved and the hated when their time has come, so too must subjects be restrained by the king; for that is the vow of Yama. 9.307
Just as one is seen bound by Varuṇa with his nooses, so should one restrain the wicked; for this is indeed the Vāruṇa vow. 9.308
Just as men rejoice upon seeing the full moon, so do the subjects rejoice in that king who observes the moon-vow (candravrata). //9.309//
One who is endowed with majesty, radiant, always intent upon evil deeds,
and a destroyer of wicked vassals— that is remembered as the Āgneya vow.
Just as the earth supports all beings equally, so too is the vow of a king who sustains all beings. (9.311)
Employing these and other means, always vigilant, the king should suppress thieves both within his own kingdom and in those of others. (9.312)
Even when fallen into the greatest calamity, one should not provoke the Brahmins;
for if they are angered, they could instantly destroy him along with his army and his mounts. (9.313)
By whom was the fire made all-consuming, the great ocean rendered undrinkable, and the moon made to wane and wax—who would not perish by provoking them? (9.314)
Who could prosper by harming those who, when provoked, might create other worlds and other world-protectors, and turn gods into non-gods? (9.315)
Upon whom the worlds and the gods always depend for their support, and for whom Brahman itself is wealth—who, desiring to live, would harm them? (9.316)
Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity;
whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is like fire, a great deity. (9.317)
Even in cremation grounds, the radiant fire is not defiled;
when offered oblations in sacrifices, it increases all the more. (9.318)
Thus, even if they engage in all kinds of undesirable actions, Brahmins are to be honored in every way, for they are the supreme deity. (9.319)
When the Kṣatriya power has increased excessively in every respect toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇical power alone shall be the restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa. (9.320)
Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone; the all-pervading energy of these subsides within their own sources. (9.321)
The Kṣatriya power does not prosper without the Brahmanical power; the Brahmanical power does not flourish without the Kṣatriya power.
But when the Brahmanical and Kṣatriya powers are joined together, they flourish both in this world and in the next. (9.322)
Having bestowed upon the Brahmins all the wealth arising from fines, and having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he should seek his end in battle. (9.323)
Acting thus, ever intent on the duties of a king and for the welfare of the world, the monarch should employ all his servants. 9.324
This eternal rule of action for the king has been declared in its entirety;
one should likewise know this rule of action for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra in due order. (9.325)
But a Vaiśya, having undergone the purificatory rites and taken a wife, should be constantly devoted to his livelihood through trade and to the protection of cattle. (9.326)
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya;
and he entrusted all subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and the King. ||9.327||
A Vaiśya should not have the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
if the Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else. (9.328)
One should know the relative value of gems, pearls, corals, metals, woven textiles, perfumes, and liquids. (9.329)
One should know the method of sowing seeds, as well as the defects and virtues of the field; one should understand the applications of measurement and all the applications of the balance. (9.330)
He [should know] the worth and worthlessness of goods, the merits and defects of regions, the profit and loss of merchandise, and the increase of livestock. (9.331)
He should know the wages of servants, the various languages of men, the methods of storing goods, and their purchase and sale. (9.332)
One should exert the highest effort to increase one's wealth through righteous means, and one should diligently give food to all living beings. (9.333)
For a Śūdra, service to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, householders, and illustrious, is indeed the supreme dharma leading to the highest good. 9.334.
Pure, devoted to excellent service, gentle in speech, and free from egoism, one who constantly takes refuge in Brahmins attains elevation according to their birth. (9.335)
This auspicious rule of action for the social classes in times of non-distress has been declared;
now learn, in due order, that which pertains to them in times of distress. (9.336)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

[The Tenth Chapter] The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study; however, it is the settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound [the Veda], and not the other two. 10.1.
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others and should himself likewise abide by them. (10.2)
Due to his distinctiveness, the excellence of his origin, his observance of the rules, and the particularity of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social orders. 10.3.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are twice-born;
the fourth is once-born, namely the Śūdra, but there is no fifth. (10.4)
Among wives of equal caste who have not lost their virginity, those born in the direct order of castes (ānulomya) should be known as belonging to that very same caste. (10.5)
Sons begotten by the twice-born on women born immediately after them in caste order are said to be their equals, being exempt from the defects of their mothers. (10.6)
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower. (10.7)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from a Śūdra daughter is born a Niṣāda, who is called a Pāraśava. (10.8)
From a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother is born a creature named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel. (10.9)
These six are recorded as base-born (apasada): those born from a Brahmin in the three [lower] castes, those from a Kshatriya in two castes, and those from a Vaishya in one caste. ||10.10||
From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden, a Sūta is born by caste;
from a Vaiśya father, the Māgadha and Vaideha are born as the sons of a royal and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.
From a Śūdra are born the Āyogava and the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men; these are the offspring of mixed castes born from Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa women. ||10.12||
Just as the Ambaṣṭha and Ugra are traditionally declared to be born from a one-interval union in the natural order,
so too are the Kṣattṛ and Vaidehaka born from a one-interval union in the inverse order.

Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [the wife of the same caste], as described in order, are designated by the name "anantara" (immediate) due to the defect of their mothers. ||10.14||
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra, but from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa. ||10.15||
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—these three base-born (apasada) sons are born from a Śūdra in the reverse order of castes. 10.16.
From a Vaiśya, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born; from a Kṣatriya, however, the Sūta alone is born.
These others are also three base-born (apasada) offspring, born in the inverse order. 10.17.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pulkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is traditionally known as a Kukkuṭaka. ||10.18||
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
one produced by a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhī mother is called a Veṇa.
Those sons whom twice-born men beget on wives of equal caste, but who are devoid of the sacred observances and excluded from the Sāvitrī, one should designate as Vrātyas. (10.20)
From a Vrātya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka, as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha. (10.21)
From the Vratya of the Rajanya caste are born the Jhalla, the Malla, the Licchivi, the Nata, the Karana, the Khasa, and the Dravida. (10.22)
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa, the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata. (10.23)
Through sexual misconduct, through the knowing of those who should not be known, and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises. (10.24)
I shall now describe in their entirety those of mixed origin who are born from inverse and natural unions, as well as those who are mutually intermingled. ||10.25||
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men;
the Māgadha, the Kṣattṛ caste, and likewise the Āyogava. || 10.26 ||
These six beget offspring of similar caste within their own wombs; they also procreate children of their mother’s caste when united with women of superior castes. (10.27)
Just as for the three castes, the offspring of two [of them] is born to this [man], so too is the sequence among the outsiders, due to the immediate proximity of their own species. (10.28)
And they also procreate many outsiders, even more corrupted than themselves, who take pleasure in one another's wives. (10.29)
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcast being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so too does an outcast beget one even more outcast upon a woman of the four castes. ||10.30||
Acting in opposition to their own nature, those of the outer castes further procreate even more outward and inferior offspring; thus, there arise exactly fifteen sub-castes.
A Dasyu begets upon an Ayogava woman a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply cosmetics and personal adornment, who is not a slave yet lives as one, and who subsists by the profession of a hunter.
But from a Vaideha is born a Maitreyaka, who subsists on madhūka fruit;
he constantly praises men at the rising of the dawn while ringing a bell. (10.33)
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a fisherman who lives by the work of boats; those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.
Among the Āyogavīs—who wear the clothes of the dead, are ignoble, and eat despised food—these three base-born castes arise separately. (10.35)
From a Niṣāda, however, a Kārāvara is born as a leather-worker;
from a Vaidehaka are born the Andhra and Meda, whose dwellings are outside the village.
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī woman is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. (10.37)
But from a Caṇḍāla, by a Pulkasī woman, is born the sinful Sopāka, whose livelihood consists of the root of ruin and who is always censured by the virtuous. (10.38)
But from a Caṇḍāla man and a Niṣāda woman is born a son called Antyāvasāyin, who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system. (10.39)
These castes resulting from intermixture, as shown by their fathers and mothers—whether they are concealed or manifest—are to be known by their respective actions. (10.40)
Six sons born of women of their own caste or of those immediately below it possess the status of the twice-born;
however, all others born of a violation of the order are recorded as having the same status as Śūdras.
And by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age. (10.42)
But through the gradual neglect of sacred rites and by the absence of Brāhmaṇas, these Kṣatriya lineages have become Śūdras in this world. (10.43)
The Puṇḍrakas, the Coḍas, the Draviḍas, the Kāmbojas, the Yavanas, the Śakas, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Cīnas, the Kirātas, and likewise the Daradas. (10.44)

Those castes in the world who are outside [the fold] of those born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—whether they speak the language of Mlecchas or the language of Aryas—are all remembered as Dasyus. 10.45.

Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions, should subsist by means of those very occupations of the twice-born that are held in contempt. (10.46)
The training of horses and charioteering for the Sūtas; medical practice for the Ambaṣṭhas; the work of women for the Vaidehakas; and trade for the Māgadhas. (10.47)
The killing of fish is the occupation of the Niṣādas, while that of the Āyogava is carpentry;
the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus subsist by the slaughter of wild animals. (10.48)
For the Kṣattrugras and Pulkasas, however, there shall be dwelling in holes, killing, and binding;
for the Dhigvaṇas, the work of tanners; and for the Veṇas, the playing of drums.
These learned ones, subsisting by their own prescribed duties, should dwell at shrines, near trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves. 10.50.
The dwellings of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, however, must be outside the village;
they are to be excluded from the use of vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.
Their garments shall be the clothes of the dead; their food shall be from broken vessels;
their ornament shall be black iron; and they shall always maintain the life of a wandering mendicant.
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them; their mutual dealings and marriages are only with those of their own kind. (10.53)
Their food should be given by others in a broken vessel;
they must not wander at night through villages or cities. 10.54

They should move about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out the disposal of corpses that have no kinsmen—such is the established rule. 10.55.
They shall constantly execute those condemned to death according to the scriptures and by the king's command;
they shall also take the clothes, beds, and ornaments of the executed. (10.56)
One should discern a man who is devoid of proper caste, unknown, and born of a defiled womb—an ignoble man with the appearance of a noble—by his own actions. (10.57)
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a disposition toward inaction reveal in this world a man born of a defiled womb. (10.58)
A son inherits the character of his father, or that of his mother, or indeed both;
however, one born of a low womb can never suppress his own innate nature. (10.59)
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth, that man will surely adopt the conduct of those [of low birth], whether to a small or a great degree. (10.60)
But where these corrupters of the social orders arise, causing total ruin, that kingdom, along with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly. (10.61)
The unconditioned sacrifice of one’s body for the sake of a Brahmin or a cow, or for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those of foreign lands. (10.62)
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, purity, and restraint of the senses—Manu has declared this to be the summary of the Dharma for the four castes. (10.63)
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with someone of a superior caste, he attains the caste of his superior parent up to the seventh generation. (10.64)
A Śūdra attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise falls to the state of a Śūdra;
one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya and likewise from a Vaiśya. (10.65)
If it should be asked: "Wherein lies the superiority between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father upon a non-noble woman, and one born from a non-noble father upon a Brāhmaṇī mother? (10.66)

One born of a noble father from a non-noble woman may become noble through his qualities; but one born of a non-noble father from a noble woman is certainly non-noble—this is the settled rule. (10.67)
The law is established that both of these are ineligible for sacramental rites:
the one prior to birth from a Vaishya woman, and the one subsequent [to such birth] through the inverse order. (10.68)
Just as good seed sown in a fertile field comes to fruition, so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement. (10.69)
Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established conclusion is as follows: ||10.70||
Seed sown in a field that is not fertile perishes right there within; and even a fertile field without seed becomes nothing more than a barren wasteland. (10.71)
Since sages born of animal species became honored and praised through the power of their seed, therefore the seed is praised. 10.72
Having carefully considered one who is ignoble yet performs noble deeds, and one who is noble yet performs ignoble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal. (10.73)
Those Brāhmaṇas who abide in the womb of Brahman and are established in their own duties should properly subsist by means of the six activities in their proper order. 10.74
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts—these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa). 10.75.
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts. (10.76)
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts. (10.77)
It is the established rule that these [duties] should likewise cease with respect to a Vaiśya;
for Manu Prajāpati did not prescribe those duties for them. (10.78)

The bearing of weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya; but the duty (dharma) consists of giving, study, and sacrifice. (10.79)

The study of the Vedas is the specific duty of the Brāhmaṇa, the protection [of subjects] that of the Kṣatriya, and the work of trade and agriculture that of the Vaiśya; these are their distinguished duties among their respective occupations. (10.80)
But if he cannot subsist by his own prescribed duty as a Brāhmaṇa, he may live by the dharma of a Kṣatriya, for that is the next best to him. (10.81)
But if he should find it impossible to live by either of these two, how should he act?
He should subsist by adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, namely, agriculture and cattle-rearing. (10.82)
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which is largely characterized by violence and dependent upon others.
People consider agriculture to be a good thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the iron-tipped wood destroys both the earth and those who dwell within it. (10.84)
But for one who, due to a deficiency in livelihood, abandons skill in the Dharma, this is the merchandise of a commoner—freed from its dross—to be sold for the increase of wealth. (10.85)
One should exclude all liquids, cooked food along with sesame seeds, stones, salt, animals, and human beings. (10.86)
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as garments made of hemp, linen, and wool—even if they are undyed—as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs. (10.87)
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes; milk, honey, curd, ghee, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass. (10.88)
All aquatic animals, fanged creatures, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals. (10.89)
Having personally undertaken agriculture with zeal,
a farmer may sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long.
Whatever else one does with sesame seeds other than giving them as food or as an ointment, one becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks there together with one's ancestors. (10.91)
One falls immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt;
a Brahmin becomes a Śūdra within three days by selling milk. (10.92)
But by selling other commodities here out of desire, a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights. (10.93)
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be bartered for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal.
A member of the royal caste, even when fallen into misfortune, may live by all these means;
yet he must never at any time take pride in a higher mode of livelihood.
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed, the king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately. ||10.96||
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the well-performed duty of another; for by living according to the duty of another, one falls immediately from one's caste. (10.97)
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may live even by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts, he should desist from it as soon as he is capable.
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having fallen into distress regarding his children and wife, may live by the work of artisans. (10.99)
Those crafts and various arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served—these are the works of artisans. (10.100)
A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the livelihood of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path and is distressed by a lack of means of subsistence, should practice this dharma when he is suffering. (10.101)
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that a means of purification should become defiled—this is not logically tenable according to dharma. (10.102)
No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, from officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts—even if they are censurable—for they are like fire and water. 10.103
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening crisis, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not tainted by that fault, just as the sky is not defiled by mud. (10.104)
Ajīgarta, being famished, approached to slay his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, for he was merely acting to counteract his hunger. (10.105)
Desiring to eat dog’s flesh in his distress, Vāmadeva—who was discerning of dharma and adharma—was not defiled, for he did so for the sake of preserving his life. (10.106)
But Bharadvāja, the great ascetic, being afflicted by hunger in the lonely forest along with his son,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛṣa.
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra, who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma, approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
Whether from receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or likewise from teaching, the acceptance of gifts is the lowest and is censured for a Brahmin after death. (10.109)
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those whose souls have been refined;
however, the acceptance of gifts is performed even by a Śūdra of low birth.
Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings;
however, that caused by accepting gifts is removed by renunciation and by austerity alone. (10.111)
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grain, even by the method of śiloñcha;
gathering grain (śila) is better than accepting gifts, and gleaning ears of corn (uñcha) is praised as even superior to that.
A lord of the earth should be entreated by *snātaka* Brahmins who are sinking into distress and desiring base metals or wealth; if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned. (10.113)

From a cultivated field, one may take unprepared grain; likewise, a cow, a goat, or a sheep; gold, grain, and food—among these, each preceding item is less blameworthy than the one following. (10.114)
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, professional labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. (10.115)
Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood. (10.116)
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may at will give a small amount to a more sinful person.
Even when taking a fourth part as his share in times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is liberated from sin. ||10.118||
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he should not turn his back in fear.
Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he may collect the lawful tribute.
For grain, the tax for commoners shall be one-eighth; for other goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
Śūdras who provide services, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [shall pay according to their work]. (10.120)
But if a Śūdra, seeking a livelihood, should wish to serve the Kṣatriya, or if he desires to live, he should do so by serving a wealthy Vaiśya. (10.121)
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both, he should propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his purpose.
Service to Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him. (10.123)
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family resources as is appropriate, having regard for their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they maintain. (10.124)
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, the dregs of grain, and old household utensils. (10.125)

There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve the purificatory rites (saṃskāra). He has no entitlement to religious duty (dharma), yet there is no prohibition against him from [performing] dharma. (10.126)
But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous, do not incur blame for [sexual union] except through mantras; rather, they receive praise. (10.127)
For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct, in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the next. (10.128)
For even a Śūdra who is capable should not amass wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas alone. (10.129)
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by properly performing them, they attain the supreme goal. (10.130)
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter I shall declare the auspicious rule for expiation. 10.131
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

[The Eleventh Chapter] One seeking to establish a lineage, one intending to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one seeking funds for the sake of a teacher, for the sake of parents, one desiring to study the Vedas, and one who is afflicted by illness. ||11.1||
One should indeed know those who beg for the sake of dharma as Brāhmaṇas who are *snātakas*; gifts should be given to these, who possess nothing, according to the excellence of their learning. (11.2)
For food, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, it is said that cooked food should be given outside the sacrificial altar (vedi).
The king, however, should bestow all kinds of jewels upon the Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, as well as sacrificial fees for the sake of the sacrifice, according to their merit.
He who, having already taken a wife, obtains another by begging her, gains only the fruit of pleasure; the lineage belongs, however, to the giver of the wealth.
He whose food for three years is sufficient for the maintenance of his dependents,
or even more than that, he is worthy to drink the Soma.
Therefore, the twice-born who drinks the Soma when his wealth is very small [commits a sin].
Even he who has not previously drunk soma does not obtain that fruit. ||11.8||
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own people live in misery—this is a mere semblance of dharma; it is like the taste of honey followed by the taste of poison. ||11.9||
He who performs funeral rites for the deceased by oppressing his dependents brings about an unhappy result both while he is living and after he has died. || 11.10 ||
If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be obstructed by a single limb,
especially that of a Brāhmaṇa, while a righteous king is in power— (11.11)
If there should be a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but performs no sacrifices and does not drink the Soma juice,
one may take that wealth from his household for the sake of accomplishing a sacrifice.
He may take three or two [grains] at will from the house of a Śūdra;
for a Śūdra has no proprietary right in sacrifices. (11.13)

If there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but has not performed sacrifices—one may take [wealth] from the households of even these two without hesitation. (11.14)
One may take from a non-giver who is constantly taking [from others];
in this way, his fame spreads and his merit increases.
In the same way, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one who follows the rule of not providing for the morrow may take food from a person of low conduct.
Whether from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever it may be found—if he asks, one must tell that to him who asks. (11.17)
A Kṣatriya must never seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa; however, he may take the property of a bandit or one who neglects his religious duties if he has no other means of livelihood. 11.18.
He who takes wealth from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous makes himself a raft and carries both of them across. 11.19
The wise know that the wealth of those who habitually perform sacrifices is the property of the gods;
however, the wealth of those who do not sacrifice is said to be the property of the asuras.
A righteous lord of the earth should not inflict punishment upon him;
for it is through the folly of the Kṣatriya that the Brāhmaṇa perishes from hunger. 11.21

Having ascertained his circle of servants and his own family members, and having understood their learning and character, the lord of the earth should provide them with a righteous means of livelihood.
Having provided for his livelihood, the king should protect him on all sides;
for from that protected person, the king obtains a sixth part of the merit.
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not beg for wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for a sacrificer who begs thus is born as a Caṇḍāla after death. ||11.24||
That Brahmin who, having begged for wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, does not bestow it all,
goes to the state of a crane or a crow for a hundred years.
He who, out of greed, misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of Brahmins—
that evil-souled man lives in the next world on the leavings of vultures.

At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice for the purpose of expiating any failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed. ||11.27||
The twice-born who performs a religious rite according to the rules for times of distress when he is not in distress does not obtain its fruit in the next world; this is certain.
By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great Ṛṣis, fearing death in times of calamity, a substitute for the sacred rule was established. (11.29)
The master of the primary rule who conducts himself according to a secondary rule—no fruit pertaining to the future life exists for that person of evil intellect. (11.30)
A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not report anything to the king regarding those human disciples who have done him harm; he should deal with them by his own power alone. 11.31
Between one's own effort and the effort of a king, one's own effort is more powerful;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies by his own effort alone. (11.32)
"One should employ the hymns of the Atharva-Angirases; this is settled.
For the word is indeed the weapon of the Brahmin; with that, the twice-born man shall slay his enemies. (11.33)
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through silent recitation and burnt offerings.
One who is a provider, a teacher, a speaker, and friendly is called a Brahmin;
one should not speak anything unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh speech. (11.35)

Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool; neither one who is afflicted by illness, nor likewise one who is uninitiated, should be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*. (11.36)
For these fall into hell, as does he for whom they offer;
