therefore, the *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas. ||11.37||

If a Brāhmaṇa, despite possessing the means, fails to give a horse as the sacrificial fee for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he remains one who has not established the fires. (11.38)
One who is faithful and has conquered the senses should perform other meritorious deeds;
however, one should never, under any circumstances, perform sacrifices here with meager sacrificial fees.

A sacrifice with meager sacrificial fees destroys one's senses, fame, heaven, longevity, renown, progeny, and cattle; therefore, one who possesses little wealth should not perform a sacrifice. (11.40)
If a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should abandon them out of desire, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that act is equal to the killing of a hero.
Those who, having obtained wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice—they are indeed the officiating priests of Śūdras and are censured among those who discourse on Brahman. (11.42)
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who are constantly ignorant and who serve the fire of the low-born (vṛṣala), the giver shall cross over all difficulties. 11.43.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured, and becomes attached to the objects of the senses, becomes liable to expiation. 11.44.
The wise know that expiation is prescribed for a sin committed unintentionally;
however, some say it is also required for a sin committed intentionally, based on the evidence of the Vedas.
A sin committed unintentionally is purified by the study of the Vedas;
but that which is committed intentionally through delusion is purified by various kinds of expiatory rites.

Having incurred the state of requiring expiation, whether by fate or by his own prior actions, a twice-born man shall not associate with the virtuous as long as that expiation has not been performed. (11.47)
In this world, some wicked-souled men undergo a transformation of their appearance due to their own misdeeds, while others do so because of what they have done in the past. (11.48)
A thief of gold suffers from deformed nails; a drinker of liquor, black teeth;
a killer of a Brahmin, consumption; and one who violates the Guru’s bed, a skin disease.
A slanderer becomes one with putrid nostrils; a backbiter, one with a foul-smelling mouth;
a stealer of grain, one with deficient limbs; and a mixer of goods, one with redundant limbs. (11.50)
The stealer of food suffers from disease; the stealer of speech suffers from dumbness;
the stealer of clothing suffers from leucoderma; and the stealer of a horse suffers from lameness. (11.51)
Thus, by the residue of their karma, they are born despised by the virtuous—
dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, and likewise deformed in appearance.
(11.53) Therefore, for the sake of purification, one must constantly perform penance.
For those whose sins have not been expiated are born endowed with censurable characteristics. ||11.54||
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife—these they call the great sins (mahāpātaka), as does association with those who commit them. 11.55
Falsehood regarding one's own excellence, backbiting directed toward the king, and the persistent speaking of falsehoods to a teacher are equal to the murder of a Brahmin. (11.56)
Abandoning one's Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten—these six are equal to the drinking of spirituous liquor. 11.57.
The misappropriation of a deposit, as well as the theft of men, horses, and silver, and of land, diamonds, and gems, is recorded in tradition as being equal to the theft of gold.

They consider the emission of semen within women of one's own lineage, among virgins, among those of the lowest castes, and among the wives of a friend or a son, to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed. (11.59)

Killing a cow, officiating at a sacrifice for those unworthy to sacrifice, adultery, selling oneself, abandoning one’s teacher, mother, father, or son, and neglecting one’s Vedic study or the sacred fires; 11.60.
The state of being superseded by a younger brother, as well as the act of superseding him;
the giving away of a daughter to those two, and officiating at a sacrifice for those very two. (11.61)
Violating a maiden, usury, falling away from one's vows, and the sale of a tank, a garden, a wife, or a child; 11.62.
The state of being a Vratya, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for a fee, receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that should not be sold. (11.63)
Authority over all forms [of crafts], the operation of great machines, the sale of harmful medicinal herbs, living off women, malevolent incantations, and root-rites. //11.64//
Felling trees that are not yet dry for the sake of firewood, undertaking activities for one's own sake, and likewise eating food that is censured; ||11.65||
Not maintaining the sacred fires, stinginess, non-discharge of debts, studying false scriptures, meanness, and engaging in vices. ||11.66||

The theft of grain, base metals, or livestock; the consumption of liquor and the consorting with women [of forbidden classes]; the killing of women, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, or Kṣatriyas; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka). 11.67.
Causing pain to a Brahmin, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants, dishonesty, and sexual intercourse with a male are recorded as acts that cause loss of caste. 11.68.

The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats and sheep, and likewise of fish, snakes, and buffaloes, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa). 11.69.
Accepting wealth from those who are censured, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras, and speaking untruths should be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa). ||11.70||
Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with intoxicants; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity. (11.71)
Learn now correctly those various vows by which all these aforementioned sins are individually expiated. (11.72)
A killer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years,
having built a hut and carrying a skull as his banner, subsisting on alms for the sake of self-purification.
Or he may become the target of weapon-wielders, according to his own wish;
or he may cast himself headlong three times into a blazing fire. (11.74)
Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Svarjit, or the Gosava;
or with the Abhijit and Viśvajit, or even with the Trivṛt-Agniṣṭut.
Or he may travel one hundred yojanas toward Japan or any other [sacred place], eating sparingly and with his senses restrained, in order to expiate the sin of killing a Brahmin. (11.76)
Or he should bestow his entire property upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas;
or wealth sufficient for a livelihood, or a house together with its furnishings. (11.77)
Or, subsisting on sacrificial food, he may follow the Sarasvatī upstream;
or, with his diet restricted, he may recite the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times.
Having shaved his head, he should dwell at the edge of a village, or in a cow-pen, or in a hermitage,
or at the foot of a tree, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one should properly sacrifice one's life;
the protector of a cow or a Brahmin is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Whether he attempts to prevent it for the third time, or wins back all his property, or recovers his life on account of that [property] belonging to a Brahmin, he is released from guilt. (11.81)
Thus, one who is firm in his vows, constantly practicing celibacy and remaining concentrated,
removes the sin of killing a Brahmin upon the completion of twelve years.
Or, having confessed his own sin before the gods of the earth at an assembly of kings, he is liberated from it upon bathing in the final purificatory bath of the horse sacrifice.
The Brāhmaṇa is said to be the root of Dharma, and the Rājanya its summit; therefore, by confessing one's sin in their assembly, one is purified. 11.84
By his very birth, the Brahmin is the deity even of the gods;
he is the authority for the world, for Brahmā himself is the cause in this matter.
Those three who know the Vedas shall declare the atonement for their sins;
that shall serve as their purification, for the word of the learned is indeed purifying. (11.86)
Therefore, by adhering to any one of these methods with a concentrated mind, a Brahmin,
through self-mastery, casts off the sin committed by killing a Brahmin.

Having destroyed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should observe this very same vow; as also in the case of killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who knows the Veda, or a woman who is the wife of an Ātreya. (11.88)
Having given false testimony, having reviled a teacher, having misappropriated a deposit, and having committed the murder of a woman or a friend; 11.89.
This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for the intentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa, no atonement is prescribed.
Having drunk liquor through delusion, a twice-born man shall drink liquor that is the color of fire;
when his body has been consumed by it, he is then released from that sin.
Or he should drink cow’s urine that is the color of fire, or water alone;
or milk, or ghee, or even the liquid from cow dung, until death. (11.92)
Or he should eat grains for a year, or consume oil-cake once at night;
wearing hair-cloth, with matted locks and carrying a skull-topped staff, for the purpose of expiating the drinking of liquor.
Liquor is indeed the impurity of foods, and evil is called impurity;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor. 11.94.
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī—liquor is to be known as threefold.
Just as one is, so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
The food of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas—namely liquor, meat, and fermented spirits—must not be consumed by a brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation of the gods. 11.96
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brāhmaṇa might fall into impurity, or he might recite the Veda, or he might perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication. (11.97)
He whose Brahman residing in the body is once drenched by liquor loses his status as a Brāhmaṇa and becomes a Śūdra. (11.98)
This manifold expiation for the drinking of spirituous liquor has been declared;
hereafter I shall proclaim the expiation for the theft of gold.
A Brahmin who has committed the theft of gold, having approached the king, should proclaim his own deed and say: "May Your Majesty punish me. (11.100)
Taking up a club, the king himself shall strike him once;
by this execution the thief is purified, or else a Brāhmaṇa is purified by austerity alone.
But a twice-born man who, desiring to remove by austerity the impurity born of stealing gold, should wear rags and perform the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brahmin. (11.102)
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he should expiate the sin of approaching the teacher's wife by means of these same vows.
Having spoken of the sin of violating the teacher’s bed, he should lie upon a heated iron bed, or he should embrace a blazing iron image; by death, he is purified. ||11.104||
Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his joined palms, he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until he collapses. (11.105)
Carrying a skull-topped staff or clad in rags, with a beard grown, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year with a concentrated mind in a solitary forest. (11.106)
Or, with his senses restrained, he should practice the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for three months,
subsisting on sacrificial food (havis) or barley-gruel (yavāgū), in order to expiate the sin of violating the Guru’s bed.
By these vows, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) may remove their impurity;
likewise, those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) [may do so] by means of these various kinds of vows. (11.108)
One who has killed a cow, being guilty of a minor offense (upapātaka), shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with the hide of that very cow.
For two months, with his senses restrained, he should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent seasonings and salt, at the fourth mealtime, and perform his ablutions using cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having served and paid homage to them, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
One should stand when they stand, follow when they walk, and likewise sit when they sit—self-restrained, free from envy. (11.112)
Whether she be afflicted by illness or beset by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or fallen or mired in the mud, he should rescue her with all his might. (11.113)
Whether it be hot, raining, or cold, or when the wind blows violently, one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability. (11.114)
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not report a cow eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor should one report a calf drinking. (11.115)
But he who, following this rule, attends upon cows, removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months. (11.116)
One who has successfully observed his vows should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

Twice-born men who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka) should perform this very same vow for the sake of purification, excluding the drinking of water from a leather bag, or else they may perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. 11.118.
But one who has broken his vow of chastity shall, at night, sacrifice to Nirṛti at a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure for the *pākayajña* offerings.
Having performed the oblations in the fire according to the rule, and finally with the verse beginning "sam",
he should offer oblations of clarified butter to Vāta, Indra, Guru, and Agni.
Those who know the Dharma and expound the Veda declare that for a twice-born man established in a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow. (11.121)
The four— the Maruts, Puruhūta, Guru, and Pāvaka— approach the ascetic who has extinguished his fires, for he possesses the splendor of Brahman.
When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three times of the day, he becomes purified in one year. (11.124)
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra; if done unintentionally, one should perform the Prājāpatya.
For acts causing mixture of castes or unworthiness to receive alms, the purification is the lunar penance (*aindava*) for one month;
for acts causing defilement, one should subsist on hot barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) for three days.
The fourth part of the penance for killing a Brahmin is prescribed for the murder of a Kṣatriya;
an eighth part for a Vaiśya who abides by his duty, and a sixteenth part should be known for a Śūdra. 11.127.
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born should give one thousand cows and one bull for the sake of his own purification.

Or, being self-controlled, wearing matted hair, and dwelling at a great distance from the village with his abode at the foot of a tree, he should perform the vow for the slayer of a Brahmin for three years. (11.129)
A twice-born man of the highest rank who has killed a Vaiśya established in his duty should perform this very same penance for one year, or he should give one hundred and one cows.
A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or else he should give ten white cows and a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog,
as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra.
Or he should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one yojana, or bathe in a flowing river, or mutter the hymn addressed to the waters (Ab-daivata-sūkta). || 11.133 ||
Having killed a snake, the best of the twice-born should give an iron spade;
for killing a eunuch, a load of straw and a māṣaka of lead.
For killing a boar, one should give a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a drona of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and for killing a curlew, a three-year-old calf.
Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, or even a peacock,
as well as a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should offer a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; for a bull, five dark-colored oxen; for an elephant, a goat and a sheep; and for a donkey, a one-year-old ox. (11.137)
Having killed carnivorous wild animals, one should give a milch cow;
for non-carnivorous animals, a heifer; but having killed a camel, one should give a *kṛṣṇala* of gold.

For the purification of those who have killed women of unstable character belonging to any of the four castes, one should administer separately the juices of the jīva, the bow (arjuna), and the bladder (bastā). 11.139.

If a twice-born man is unable to expiate the killing of snakes and other such creatures through charity, he shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each individual creature in order to remove the sin. (11.140)
But for the killing of a thousand boneless beings, or for filling a cart with boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra. (11.141)
But for killing a vertebrate creature, one should give something to a Brahmin;
for the injury of boneless creatures, one is purified by a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma). || 11.142 ||
For the cutting of fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses should be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food, born from moisture,
and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete purification.
For the destruction of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest, one should follow a cow for one day while observing a milk-vow. 11.145.

By these vows, indeed, the sin arising from violence—whether committed intentionally or unintentionally—shall be removed in its entirety; now hear [the rules] regarding the consumption of forbidden food. 11.146.
Having drunk liquor through ignorance, one is purified by the sacramental rite alone; however, for intentional drinking, the established rule is that it is inexpiable except by the end of life.
Having drunk water that has stood in a vessel for *surā* or likewise in a vessel for intoxicants,
one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights.
Having touched or given liquor, or having accepted it according to the rules,
or having drunk water left over by a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days.
But a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk Soma, having smelled the breath of one who has drunk liquor, becomes pure by suppressing his breath three times in water and consuming clarified butter. 11.150.
Having unintentionally swallowed feces, urine, or anything touched by liquor, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) once again. (11.151)
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
all these are discontinued for the twice-born during the rite of re-consecration.
But having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women or Śūdras,
or having consumed forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights.
Even after drinking fermented acids or astringent decoctions, though they are purifying, a twice-born man remains impure as long as that liquid has not passed downward. 11.154
Having consumed the urine or feces of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten dried meats, mushrooms from the ground, or anything found at a slaughterhouse that was unknown, one should observe this very same vow. (11.156)
For eating the flesh of carnivorous animals, pigs, camels, and cocks, as well as that of humans, crows, and donkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification. (11.157)
If a twice-born man who has not yet returned home from his teacher’s house should eat food given monthly (māsikānna), he shall fast for three days and remain in water for one day. 11.158
But he who, while observing a vow, should somehow eat honey or meat, having performed the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance, shall complete the remainder of his vow. ||11.159||
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, or a rat, or those of a dog or a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink the *brahmasuvarcalā* plant.
One who desires purity for oneself must not eat food that is unfit to be eaten;
if it has been eaten unknowingly, it should be vomited out or quickly purified by means of purificatory rites. (11.161)
This has been declared as the various rule for the vows regarding the eating of forbidden food;
now hear the rule for those vows which remove the fault of theft.

Having committed thefts of grain, cooked food, or wealth out of desire from the house of one belonging to his own caste, the best of the twice-born is purified by a year-long *kṛcchra* penance. (11.163)
But for the abduction of human beings, women, fields, and houses, as well as for [the theft of] water from wells and tanks, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed as the means of purification. (11.164)
Having stolen articles of small value from another's house, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance for the sake of self-purification after returning that property. (11.165)
In the case of stealing food that is chewed or eaten, as well as vehicles, beds, seats, and flowers,
roots, and fruits, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the means of purification.
For grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses,
clothing, leather, and meat, there shall be a fast of three nights.
For [the theft of] gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron,
bronze, and stones, one must subsist on grain-particles for twelve days.
For cotton, silk, wool, animals with cloven hooves, and those with solid hooves, as well as for birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, and rope, one must subsist on milk alone for three days.
By these vows, a twice-born man may remove the sin committed through theft;
however, he should expel the sin of approaching those who should not be approached by means of these same vows.

Having discharged semen into women of his own kin, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, he shall perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed. (11.171)

Having approached a daughter of his father’s sister, a daughter of his own sister, a daughter of his mother’s sister, or a daughter of his mother’s uterine brother, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (11.172)
A wise man, however, should not take these three as wives; they are not to be approached because of their kinship, for by taking them he falls low. (11.173)
Having discharged semen into non-human females, a woman in her courses, those who are not the natural womb, or into water, one shall perform the Sāṃtapanakṛcchra penance. (11.174)
But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman, a twice-born man shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a bullock cart, in water, or during the daytime. (11.175)

Having approached women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, or having eaten their food, or having accepted gifts from them, a Brahmin falls [from his caste] through ignorance; through knowledge, however, he becomes equal [to them]. (11.176)
A husband shall confine a corrupt wife in a single room;
he shall compel her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man who has committed adultery with another's wife. (11.177)
If, however, she should become defiled after being solicited by a man of equal status, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification. (11.178)
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a Vṛṣalī for a single night, he removes that by constantly subsisting on alms and reciting prayers for three years. (11.179)
This expiation has been declared for all four types of evildoers;
now hear these expiations for those who associate with outcasts. ||11.180||

By associating with an outcast for a year—through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or forming a matrimonial alliance—one becomes an outcast; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food. (11.181)
Whichever among these a man associates with through his own downfall, he must perform that very person's vow for the sake of purification from that association. (11.182)

The water libation for one who has fallen [from his caste] must be performed by his sapinda relatives together with other kinsmen on an inauspicious day in the evening, in the presence of agnates, officiating priests, and teachers. (11.183)
A female slave should overturn a jar full of water with her foot as if for a dead person;
the kinsmen, together with her, shall remain in a state of impurity for a day and a night.
But from that point on, there should be a cessation of conversation and shared seats, as well as the giving of inheritance and even ordinary social intercourse. (11.185)
Seniority shall cease, as shall the wealth acquired by virtue of seniority;
even the youngest son who excels in merit shall receive the portion due to the eldest. ||11.186||
But when the penance has been performed, they should bathe and together with him cast a new pitcher full of water into a sacred body of water.
Having thrown that jar into the water and entered his own home,
he should perform all the ancestral rites for his kinsmen as before.
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen from their status;
however, they should be given clothing, food, and drink, and they should live near the house. 11.189
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins until they have been purified; yet once they have undergone purification, one should never hold them in contempt. (11.190)

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman, even if they are pure according to the Dharma.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
This same penance should also be prescribed for those twice-born men who, having engaged in forbidden acts and being abandoned by the Veda, desire to perform expiation. (11.193)
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation, they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by silent recitation and austerity. (11.194)
Having recited the Sāvitrī three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.
But when he had returned again from the cow-pasture, emaciated by his fasts and bowing down before them, they would ask him: "O gentle one, do you desire equanimity? (11.196)
Having spoken the truth before the Brahmins, he should scatter fodder for the cows;
when the ford has been established by the cows, they should perform his formal reception.

Having performed sacrifices for Vrātyas, having performed funeral rites for others, and having performed malevolent magic (abhicāra) or the Ahīna sacrifice, one is purified by three Kṛcchra penances. ||11.198||
Having abandoned one who has sought refuge or having caused the Veda to be lost, a twice-born man removes that sin by subsisting on barley for one year.
One bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, or by domestic carnivorous animals, as well as by humans, horses, camels, or pigs, becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma). 11.200.

Eating only at the sixth mealtime for a month, the constant recitation of the *Saṃhitā*, and the daily performance of *Śākala* oblations are the means of purification for those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅktyas*). (11.201)
Having intentionally mounted a camel vehicle or a donkey vehicle,
a Brahmin who has bathed while naked becomes pure through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
If one who is afflicted has performed a bodily evacuation without water or even while in the water, he becomes pure by bathing outside with his clothes on and touching a cow. 11.203.
In the case of the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda, and upon the violation of the vows of a Snātaka, the penance is fasting. (11.204)
Having addressed a Brāhmaṇa with "huṃ" and an elder with "thou," one should bathe and, fasting for the remainder of the day, propitiate them by offering salutations. (11.205)
Having struck him even with a blade of grass, or having bound him by the neck with a garment,
or having defeated him in debate, one should appease him by prostrating.
But having merely threatened a Brahmin, one enters hell for a hundred years; having struck him, however, with the intent to kill, one enters hell for a thousand years. ||11.207||
For as many particles of dust as the blood of a twice-born man coagulates,
for that many thousands of years shall the one who caused it remain in hell.
Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra;
and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra.

But for the removal of sins for which no specific expiation has been stated, one should prescribe an atonement after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin. (11.210)
I shall describe to you those means by which a human being removes his sins—means practiced by gods, sages, and ancestors. (11.211)

For three days he should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, for three days he should eat food that has been unasked for, and for the final three days he should not eat at all; thus a twice-born man performs the Prājāpatya penance. (11.212)
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass, along with a fast for one night—this is known as the *sāṃtapana* penance. (11.213)
A twice-born man performing the Atikṛcchra penance should eat only a single mouthful for three periods of three days each as before, and should fast during the final three days. (11.214)
A Brahmin performing the *taptakṛcchra* penance should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days, bathing once daily and remaining composed in mind. (11.215)
For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is this penance called Parāka, which removes all sins.
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
touching water at the three sessions of the day, this is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (11.217)
One who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, being self-restrained from the beginning of the bright fortnight, should carry out this entire procedure in its entirety during the Yavamadhyama variety.
Restraining his self, one performing the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa penance should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food when the sun has reached the meridian. (11.219)
A composed Brahmin should eat four mouthfuls in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa.
By eating, with a concentrated mind, eighty-three morsels of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in any manner whatsoever for one month, one attains the same world as the Moon. ||11.221||
The Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Maruts, together with the great seers, observed this vow for the sake of liberation from all that is unwholesome.
One should personally perform the fire-oblation every day with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
one should practice non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and straightforwardness. (11.223)
Three times during the day and three times at night, he should enter the water with his clothes on;
and he should never speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts. (11.224)
He should pass his time standing or sitting; if unable, he may lie down on the ground.
He should be a celibate observer of vows, worshipping his guru, the gods, and the twice-born.
And he should daily recite the Sāvitrī and other purificatory texts according to his ability;
for in all vows, one who is intent on the purpose of expiation should act in this manner. (11.226)
The twice-born whose sins have been made public should be purified by these vows;
however, those whose sins have not been made public, one should purify with mantras and burnt offerings. 11.227.
By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by study, as well as by giving in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from that evil. (11.228)
To the extent that a man, having himself committed an unrighteous act, speaks of it, to that same extent he is freed from that unrighteousness, just as a snake is freed from its skin. || 11.229 ||
To the extent that his mind reproaches his evil deed, to that same extent his body is released from that unrighteousness. ||11.230||
For having committed a sin and felt remorse, one is liberated from that sin; by the resolve "I shall not do so again," a person is purified through abstention. (11.231)
Having thus reflected in his mind upon the arising of the fruits of action after death, he should constantly perform virtuous deeds through his thoughts, speech, and physical form. (11.232)
Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, having performed a reprehensible action, one who seeks liberation from it should not perform a second such act. (11.233)
In whatever action one has committed that causes a lack of lightness in the mind, one should perform penance for it until it becomes a source of satisfaction. (11.234)
"All this happiness, whether divine or human, has austerity as its root;
it has been declared by the wise who perceive the Vedas that austerity is its center and austerity its end. (11.235)
The austerity of a Brahmin is knowledge; the austerity of a Kṣatriya is protection;
the austerity of a Vaiśya is trade and agriculture; the austerity of a Śūdra is service. (11.236)
Sages of refined self-control, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air,
behold the three worlds with all their mobile and immobile beings through austerity alone.
Medicines, antidotes, sciences, and the various states of divine power—
all these are accomplished through austerity alone, for austerity is their means of attainment.

Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—all that can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed hard to surpass. (11.239)
Even those who have committed the great sins, as well as others who have performed improper acts,
are liberated from that defilement by means of well-performed austerity alone.
Insects, snakes, moths, beasts, birds, and even stationary beings go to heaven by the power of asceticism. 11.241
Whatever sin people commit through their mind, speech, or body, those whose wealth is austerity quickly consume it all by means of austerity alone. (11.242)
For a Brahmin purified by austerity alone, the denizens of heaven accept his offerings and fulfill his desires. (11.243)
The Lord Prajāpati created this scripture through austerity alone;
likewise, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity. 11.244.
Thus the gods proclaim this to be the great majesty of austerity, seeing that the arising of merit from all this comes from austerity. 11.245
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices, and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes. (11.246)
Just as fire, having reached its fuel, consumes it in an instant with its brilliance, so does the knower of the Veda burn away all evil by the fire of knowledge. 11.247
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava, performed day after day, purify even the killer of an embryo within a month. (11.249)
By reciting the Kautsa hymn beginning with "apaḥ," the Vasiṣṭha triplet, the Māhitra hymn, and the Śuddhavatī verses, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified. (11.250)
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once, one who has stolen gold becomes stainless in an instant. (11.251)
By practicing the *Haviṣpāntīya* hymn and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃ ha," and by reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the Guru's bed is liberated. (11.252)
Desiring to remove gross and subtle sins, one should recite for a year the verse beginning with "Having known" (avet) and the verse beginning with "Whatever this" (yat kiṃcedam). (11.253)
Having accepted what should not be accepted or having eaten forbidden food, a man is purified in three days by reciting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn. (11.254)
But by practicing the *Somāraudra* hymn many times for a month, one is purified;
likewise, by performing ablutions in a flowing river while reciting the three verses beginning with "aryamṇām. (11.255)
One who has committed an offense should mutter the seven verses beginning with "Indra" for half a year;
but having performed a blameworthy act, he should subsist on alms for a month while remaining in water.

Having offered clarified butter for a year with the *śākala* oblation mantras, a twice-born man destroys even the most grievous sin; or he does so by reciting the verse beginning with "namas. (11.257)
One who is joined with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) shall follow cows with a concentrated mind;
by practicing the Pāvamānī verses for a year while subsisting on alms, he is purified.
Or, having purified himself by reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā three times at the river's edge, he is released from all sins, having been cleansed by three *parāka* penances. (11.259)
If one, being self-controlled, fasts for three days while approaching water three times a day and recites the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, he is liberated from all sins. (11.260)
Just as the horse-sacrifice, the king of rituals, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
Even if he were to destroy these three worlds and eat food from anywhere at all, a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever. (11.262)
Having recited the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā three times, or the Yajus formulas with a concentrated mind, or the Sāmans together with their secret doctrines, one is liberated from all sins. (11.263)
Just as a clod of earth quickly perishes upon reaching a great lake, so does all misconduct sink away when immersed in the threefold Veda. 11.264
The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the various Sāman-chants—this is to be known as the threefold Veda; he who knows this is a knower of the Veda.
That which is the primordial Brahman of three syllables, in which the Triple Veda is established—that other secret one is the threefold Veda; he who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
[Chapter Twelve] O sinless one, you have declared this entire dharma of the four social orders.
Now, tell us truly and in its highest form about the production of the fruits of actions. 12.1
The righteous Bhṛgu, son of Manu, said to those great seers:
"Hear the definitive conclusion regarding this entire yoga of action. (12.2)
Action, arising from mind, speech, and body, yields auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
the destinies of men—superior, inferior, and middling—are born of action. (12.3)
One should know that for this embodied being—whether of these three types, or having three bases, or endowed with ten characteristics—it is the mind that is the instigator. 12.4
Coveting the property of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and adherence to falsehoods—this is the threefold mental action. (12.5)
Harshness, falsehood, slander in every form, and idle chatter—these constitute the fourfold nature of speech. (12.6)
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules, and adultery with another's wife—this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action]. (12.7)
One experiences the mental—whether auspicious or inauspicious—by means of the mind alone;
verbal action by means of speech, and bodily action by means of the body alone. (12.8)
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
through those of speech, to the state of birds or beasts; and through those of the mind, to the status of an outcaste.
The restraint of speech, the restraint of mind, and likewise the restraint of action—he whose intellect has these firmly established is called a "triple-staffed one" (tridaṇḍin). 12.10.
Having laid down this triple staff toward all beings,
and having restrained both desire and anger, a person then attains perfection.
That which is the instigator of this self is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field);
but that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) by the wise. ||12.12||
There is another internal self, distinct from the vital breath, innate to all embodied beings, by which one experiences all pleasure and pain throughout successive births. (12.13)
Both of these—the Great One (Mahat) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña)—are joined with the elements;
they abide pervading that which exists within high and low beings.
Innumerable forms issue forth from his body,
which constantly set various beings in motion.
After death, for those men who have committed evil deeds, another firm body arises from these very five elements for the purpose of undergoing torment. 12.16.
Having experienced those torments of Yama with this very body,
they dissolve part by part back into those same elemental constituents.
Having experienced those faults born of attachment to sense-objects,
which result in future suffering, he approaches those two of great splendor with his impurities removed.
Together with him, those two unweariedly perceive his merit and his evil,
by which, when joined with them, he attains happiness or misery both here and after death.
If one practices dharma for the most part and unrighteousness only to a small degree, then,
enveloped by those very elements, he enjoys happiness in heaven.
But if one mostly practices unrighteousness and righteousness only slightly,
abandoned by those beings, he undergoes the torments of Yama.
Having undergone those torments in the Yāmis, that living being, freed from defilement,
returns once more to those very five elements, each according to its own portion.

Having observed these destinies of the living being by means of his own mind— both those resulting from righteousness and those from unrighteousness— one should always fix the mind upon righteousness.
One should know that sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities of the self, by which the Great One (mahat) stands pervading all these states without exception. (12.24)
Whichever of these qualities is preponderant in the body in its entirety, it then makes that embodied being consist primarily of that quality. (12.25)
Sattva is knowledge, tamas is ignorance, and rajas is known as passion and hatred;
this is their pervasive nature, which rests within all beings. (12.26)
In that regard, whatever he perceives within himself as joined with joy, tranquil and appearing pure—that he should understand to be *sattva*. (12.27)
But that which is conjoined with suffering and is disagreeable to oneself, know that to be passion (rajas), ever carrying away embodied beings without obstruction. (12.28)
But that which is joined with delusion, whose nature consists of the unmanifest, which is beyond reasoning and unknowable—that one should understand as *tamas*. (12.29)
And I shall explain in its entirety the arising of the fruit for each of these three qualities—whether it be supreme, middling, or inferior. ||12.30||
Study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of dharma, and contemplation of the Self—these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva. 12.31.
Delight in undertaking enterprises, fortitude, adherence to improper actions, and constant indulgence in sense objects—these are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rājasa). 12.32.
Greed, sleepiness, lack of fortitude, cruelty, atheism, deviation from right conduct, a habit of begging, and negligence—these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas). 12.33.
And for these three qualities residing in the three [states], this should be known as the summary definition of their qualities in their respective order. ||12.34||

Whatever action one feels ashamed of after having done it, while doing it, or even when intending to do it—all that should be known by the wise as characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas). ||12.35||
That action by which one desires abundant fame in this world,
yet does not grieve when it fails to be achieved— that should be known as rajasic.

That which one desires to know in its entirety, that which one does not feel shame in practicing, and that by which one's own soul is satisfied—this is the characteristic mark of the quality of being (*sattva*). (12.37)

Desire is said to be the characteristic of *tamas*, while purpose is the characteristic of *rajas*; righteousness is the characteristic of *sattva*. Their preeminence follows this respective order. (12.38)
I shall now briefly describe, in their proper order, those qualities by which one enters into these various states of cyclic existence. 12.39

Those characterized by sattva attain the state of gods; those characterized by rajas, the state of humans; and those characterized by tamas, the state of animals eternally—such is this threefold destiny. (12.40)
This secondary course of rebirth should be understood as being threefold and of three kinds:
inferior, middling, and superior, according to the specific nature of one's actions and knowledge. (12.41)
Immovable beings, worms, insects, fish, snakes, reptiles, domestic animals, and jackals—this is the lowest state, characterized by darkness (tāmasī gati). ||12.42||
Elephants, horses, Śūdras, and despised Mlecchas, as well as lions, tigers, and boars, constitute the middling state of darkness (tāmasī gati). ||12.43||
Cāraṇas, Suparṇas, and deceitful men, as well as Rākṣasas and Piśācas—these are the highest destination among those in the quality of darkness (tamas). 12.44.
Jhallas, mallas, and actors, men of evil conduct, and those addicted to gambling and drinking—this is the first state, characterized by passion (rājasī). ||12.45||
Kings, Kṣatriyas, and the domestic priests of kings, as well as those whose primary concern is the science of war, constitute the intermediate Rājasī state. (12.46)
The Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and those who are followers of the gods,
as well as all the Apsarases— this is the highest destination among those belonging to the Rajas quality.
Ascetics, self-restrained yogis, Brahmins, and the hosts of celestial chariot-dwellers,
as well as the lunar mansions and the Daityas— this is the first, the Sāttvika, goal.
Sacrificers, seers, gods, the Vedas, the luminaries, the years, the ancestors, and the Sādhyas—this is the second, sāttvic goal. (12.49)
Brahmā, the creators of the universe, Dharma, and the Great Unmanifest—these the wise declare to be the highest state characterized by goodness (sāttvikī). ||12.50||
Thus has been fully described the entire transmigratory existence consisting of all living beings, which is threefold and of three kinds, corresponding to the threefold action of every sort.
Through attachment to the senses and by failing to practice the Dharma, the ignorant and lowest of men go to evil states of existence within saṃsāra. (12.52)
Learn now all that specific womb into which this living soul enters in this world, and by whatever particular karma, in due succession. (12.53)
Having experienced terrible hells for many series of years, those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakins) enter these transmigrations upon the exhaustion of that [karmic retribution].
The slayer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, or a camel; or that of a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, or a bird; or even that of a Caṇḍāla or a Pulkasa. (12.55)
A Brahmin who drinks liquor shall go among worms, insects, moths, birds that feed on excrement, and indeed among predatory creatures. (12.56)
A Brahmin who is a thief [becomes] thousands of times a spider, a snake, a lizard, aquatic animals, predatory beasts, and Piśācas. (12.57)
The violator of the Guru's bed becomes [the seed] of grasses, shrubs, and creepers, as well as of carnivorous beasts, fanged creatures,
and those who perform cruel deeds— by the hundreds.
Those who eat forbidden food become carnivorous beasts of prey or worms; thieves become creatures that devour one another; and those who consort with the wives of low-caste men become pretas. (12.59)
By entering into union with outcasts, by approaching the wife of another,
and by stealing the property of a Brahmin, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa.
Having stolen gems, pearls, and corals out of greed,
as well as various red objects, a human is born among goldsmiths.
By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; by stealing water, a water-fowl;
by stealing honey, a gadfly; by stealing milk, a crow; by stealing savory food, a dog; and by stealing ghee, a mongoose.
A vulture [eats] flesh; a madgu water-bird [eats] fat; a bird that feeds on oil [eats] oil;
a cricket [eats] salt; and a crane [eats] curd. (12.63)
Having stolen silk, one becomes a partridge; having stolen linen, a frog; having stolen cotton cloth, a curlew; for stealing a cow, an iguana; and for stealing molasses, a rat.
The chuchundarī [obtained] auspicious fragrances; the peacock, leafy vegetables;
the porcupine, various kinds of prepared food; and the hedgehog, unprepared food. (12.65)
By stealing fire, one becomes a cricket; by stealing household utensils, a house-builder wasp; and by stealing dyed garments, one is born as a pheasant. (12.66)
A wolf [dreams of] a deer; a tiger, a horse; a monkey, fruit and flowers; a bear, a woman; a *stokaka* bird, water; a camel, vehicles; and a goat, livestock. (12.67)
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property, or having consumed an oblation that was not consecrated by fire, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal. (12.68)
Women also, by taking [these things] according to this same rule, incur guilt;
they become wives to these very same creatures. (12.69)
Indeed, when the social classes fall away from their respective duties in times of no distress,
they pass through sinful transmigrations and enter into servitude among bandits.
A fallen Brahmin becomes a *preta* named Ulkāmukha who eats what has been vomited; a fallen Kṣatriya becomes a *kaṭapūtana* who eats impure matter and corpses. (12.71)
The Vaiśya Maitrākṣajyotika becomes a preta who feeds on pus;
but the Śūdra Cailāśaka, fallen from his own dharma, becomes a preta who feeds on rags.
To whatever extent those whose nature is directed toward sense objects indulge in them, to that same extent skillfulness in those very things arises within them. 12.73
Due to the repeated practice of those evil deeds, those of small intelligence encounter sufferings in various wombs here in this world. (12.74)
There is wandering through the fierce hells such as Tāmisra,
and [suffering] such as the Forest of Sword-leaves, along with being bound and having one's limbs severed.
And various torments indeed, such as being devoured by crows and owls,
the heat of sand mixed with grit, and the unbearable Kumbhīpāka hells.
And he experiences births in various wombs that are mostly full of suffering, as well as constant afflictions from cold and heat, and manifold fears. (12.77)
Repeatedly dwelling in the womb, experiencing dreadful birth, enduring painful bondages, and even being sent into the service of others. (12.78)
The separation from kinsmen and loved ones, as well as dwelling with wicked people; the acquisition of wealth and its loss, and the gaining of friends and enemies. (12.79)
And [he saw] old age, which is beyond remedy, and the torment of diseases, and those various manifold afflictions, and death itself, which is difficult to conquer. (12.80)
With whatever disposition one performs any particular action, with a body of that same nature one experiences its respective fruit. (12.81)
This entire arising of the fruits of your actions has been fully described;
now learn this rule of action for a Brahmin which leads to the highest good. 12.82
The study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, restraint of the senses, non-violence, and service to the guru are the supreme means for attaining the highest good. 12.83.
And among all these auspicious actions here, some particular action is said to be more conducive to welfare for a person. (12.84)
And for all of these, knowledge of the Self is remembered as supreme; for that is the foremost of all sciences, since immortality is attained through it. (12.85)
Of these six aforementioned types of action, it should be known that the Vedic rite is always more conducive to welfare, both after death and in this world. (12.86)
But in the Vedic path of action, all these [stages] without exception are included, respectively, within each specific injunction for ritual performance. 12.87.
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly prosperity and that which leads to the supreme good; it is also twofold, consisting of the active and the renunciatory.

Action performed with desire for results, whether in this world or the next, is called *pravṛtta* (active); but action free from desire and preceded by knowledge is taught as *nivṛtta* (withdrawn). 12.89.
By practicing active karma, one attains equality of power with the gods;
but by practicing renunciation, one indeed transcends the five elements.
Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, he who sacrifices to the Self attains self-sovereignty. 12.91
Even having abandoned the aforementioned ritual acts, the best of the twice-born should be diligent in self-knowledge, tranquility, and the study of the Vedas. 12.92.
For this indeed is the complete perfection of birth, especially for a Brahmin;
having attained this, a twice-born man has truly fulfilled his purpose, and not otherwise. (12.93)
The Veda is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings; it is inconceivable and immeasurable—such is the established nature of the Vedic scripture. (12.94)
Whatever scriptures are outside the Veda, and whatever false doctrines there may be—all these are fruitless after death, for they are said to result in darkness. (12.95)
Whatever other [teachings] there may be besides these, which arise and then fall away, they are fruitless and false because they belong only to the recent past. (12.96)
The four castes, the three worlds, and the four stages of life separately—the past, the present, and the future—all are established through the Veda. 12.97
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are established through the Veda alone; their origin arises from qualities and actions.
The eternal Vedic scripture sustains all beings;
therefore, I consider this to be the supreme means for the accomplishment of a living being. (12.99)
One who is learned in the Vedic scriptures is worthy of the command of an army, the sovereignty of a kingdom, the office of a magistrate, and even lordship over all the world. (12.100)
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees, so does one who knows the Vedas burn away the defects of his own karma. 12.101
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, dwelling in whatever stage of life he may be, becomes fit for union with Brahman even while remaining in this very world. 12.102
Those who merely memorize texts are superior to the ignorant; those who retain them in memory are better than those who merely memorize;
those who possess knowledge are superior to those who merely retain; and those who apply themselves with resolve are superior to those who merely possess knowledge. 12.103
Austerity and knowledge are the supreme means for a Brahmin to attain the highest good;
by austerity he destroys impurity, and by knowledge he attains immortality.
Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions—these three must be thoroughly understood by one who desires the purification of dharma. 12.105
He who investigates the instruction on dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures knows dharma, and no other. 12.106.
This action leading to supreme bliss has been explained in its entirety as prescribed; now the secret of this treatise of Manu is being taught. 12.107
If it should be asked how one should act regarding those dharmas not explicitly prescribed, that which learned Brahmins declare shall be the dharma, free from doubt. (12.108)

But those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been mastered in accordance with the Dharma, they are to be known as the cultured Brahmins, the authorities for the Vedas and direct perception. (12.109)
Whatever dharma a council of at least ten, or even three, who are established in virtuous conduct, may determine, one should not call that dharma into question. (12.110)

One who possesses the threefold knowledge, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma, and the first three orders of life—these constitute an assembly of at least ten members. 12.111

One who knows the Ṛgveda, one who knows the Yajurveda, and likewise one who knows the Sāmaveda—this assembly of at least three is to be known as the authority for resolving doubts concerning dharma. (12.112)

Even if he is alone, whatever dharma a supreme twice-born man who knows the Vedas determines should be known as the highest dharma; it is not [dharma] proclaimed by tens of thousands of those lacking knowledge.
For those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist on mere birth—even if they assemble by the thousands—no true assembly exists. (12.114)
Whatever those who are shrouded in darkness, the fools who do not know the Dharma, proclaim as such, that sin becomes tenfold and follows after those who spoke it. (12.115)
All this has been declared to you, which brings about the supreme good;
a Brahmin who does not fall away from this attains the highest goal.
Thus that Blessed One, the God, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, has told me all this, the supreme secret of the Dharma. ||12.117||
One who is composed should perceive everything—both the existent and the non-existent—within the self;
for by perceiving everything within the self, one does not direct the mind toward unrighteousness. 12.118
The self alone is all the deities; everything is established within the self.
For the self indeed produces the connection with action for these embodied beings. 12.119
One should place space within the cavities; the wind within movement and touch;
the supreme fire within digestion and sight; water within moisture; and earth within solid forms.
He placed the Moon in his mind, the Quarters in his ears, Viṣṇu in his stride, Hari in his strength, Agni in his speech, Mitra in his excretion, and Prajāpati in his procreation.
One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, radiant like gold, and attainable through the intellect in deep sleep. 12.122
Some call him Agni, others Manu, others Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, and still others the eternal Brahman. (12.123)
Pervading all beings with his five forms,
he perpetually causes them to revolve like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay.
Thus, he who perceives the Self within all beings by means of his own self, having attained equanimity toward all, reaches Brahman, the supreme state. 12.125
A twice-born man who recites this Mānava Śāstra proclaimed by Bhṛgu becomes eternally possessed of right conduct and shall attain his desired goal. (12.126)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.
